Anything else, the launch card, the status bar's label, Settings, the Review menu standing Setup in front of the dialog and a review that failed among them: the chapter, or whatever the page shows without Setup, with the focus back where it was when Setup opened when that is still on the page, as the status bar's label is (`focusReturnTarget`). The landing is cleared once the dialog or the guide has taken it (`setupLanding`).
   - **The privacy footer**: "<APP_NAME> never sees your Claude password or sign-in token. You sign in with Anthropic, in Claude Code and your browser.", with a link to Anthropic's setup guide, https://code.claude.com/docs/en/setup.
   - **The version**, last: "<APP_NAME> 1.0.0", the app's name and the version running (`setupFooterText`), from the updater's status (`update:get`'s `current`), which the page holds from its first moment (`release.9`).
6. **Checking again as the window comes back.** The author runs the command in a terminal and comes back. While the view has something to do and Claude is in use (the provider, or Setup open), the window coming back to the front checks again, at most every 3 s from the start of the last check, whatever started it, and never over a check that is running (`focusRecheckDue`, `recheckOnFocus` in `useAi`). A ready view, a usage limit, or ChatGPT as the provider with Claude's Setup closed (the OpenAI API key until `codex.6`), starts nothing.
7. **No sign-in of the app's own, for Claude.** The app never offers a sign-in form or a button that signs in to Claude, never starts a sign-in (`runClaudeCli` refuses anything but its two probes), never reads or writes Claude Code's credentials, and never runs a check with the vault as `cwd` (CLAUDE.md rules 2 and 6). `test/renderer/setupScreen.render.test.ts` renders every view and finds no button labelled like a sign-in. The Setup screen's ChatGPT view (5.7, `codex.2`) is the one place a button signs in: OpenAI documents that sign-in for open-source apps, where Anthropic's policy forbids one for Claude (Appendix A).
8. **Policy note for the README:** this app runs the unmodified Claude Code each user installs and signs in to themselves, with their own subscription or API key (C.42). Every user signs in with their own account through Anthropic's flow, in their own terminal; the app never intermediates credentials and never starts a sign-in (item 7, Appendix C "No in-app sign-in launcher"). The README's Connecting Claude and First run follow this section and section 7's welcome guide (written by `setup.13`, handed to `opensource.11`).

### 5.7 ChatGPT's sign-in: the ChatGPT view and the training warning (`codex.2`)

How the app signs in with ChatGPT, keeps the sign-in and warns about training (`codex.2`; what OpenAI's pages say is in Appendix A, read 2026-10-24, and what the build settled in Appendix C "What Sign in with ChatGPT settled where the plan left it open"). Reviews on the plan, its model list, its limits and its errors are 5.8's (`codex.3`). The words are `src/shared/ui/chatgpt.ts`; main's part is `src/main/chatgpt/` (`oauth.ts`, `idToken.ts`, `loopback.ts`, `store.ts`, and `index.ts`, which ties them together); the view is `src/renderer/components/ChatGptSetup.tsx` with `DataSettingsWarning.tsx`, and the page's state `src/renderer/state/chatgpt.ts`.

1. **The sign-in**, as OpenAI's sign-in page gives it. Sign in with ChatGPT refuses before anything opens when safeStorage cannot encrypt. Otherwise main makes the host id the first time (`ext_agent_host_id`: `urn:uuid:` and a version 4 UUID, kept in secrets.json through restarts, sign-outs and new sign-ins, since none of them is a new host), opens a listener on `http://127.0.0.1:<port>/auth/callback` on a port the system picks for each attempt, makes a fresh `state`, `nonce` and PKCE verifier (32 random bytes each; the challenge is S256), and opens `https://auth.openai.com/api/accounts/authorize` in the system browser (`systemShell().openExternal`, which the shell stub prints instead) with `client_id`, `ext_agent_host_id`, `response_type=code`, `redirect_uri`, `scope` (`openid profile email offline_access resource.invoke chatgpt.tokens.use.direct`), `resource=https://api.openai.com/v1`, `state`, `nonce`, `code_challenge_method=S256` and `code_challenge`. The first sign-in on a computer sends `client_id=dynamic_agent_client` and `agent_name_hint` set to `APP_NAME`, the app's own name; a later one sends the client id OpenAI issued and no name; `prompt=consent` goes only with the sign-in after one that did not grant the plan's use. No client secret, no partner key, and no header or parameter that names another client. The browser's answer is read in OpenAI's order: the state first (an answer with another state, two states or none is told "Not this sign-in" in its tab, and the wait goes on), then an `error` (`access_denied` reads "You did not allow <APP_NAME> on OpenAI's page, so you are not signed in."), then the code and, for a first sign-in, the issued client id, which must be there; a later sign-in's answer may leave the client id out and may not name another. The listener answers only a GET of its path whose Host is its own address. The code is exchanged at `https://auth.openai.com/api/accounts/oauth/token` (a form POST of `grant_type=authorization_code`, the client id, the code, the verifier and the same `redirect_uri` and `resource`); `invalid_grant` says the sign-in took too long. The ID token is checked against `https://auth.openai.com/.well-known/jwks.json` (RS256, the key named by `kid`): the issuer, the audience, which must be the client id the code was exchanged for, the expiry (with two minutes' grace for a clock that is off) and the attempt's nonce; its `sub` is the account. The scopes granted must include `chatgpt.tokens.use.direct`. Only then are the tokens kept, and the tab says "Signed in". The tab's pages are the app's own words and never anything the request carried, with no script. The wait ends after 10 minutes (`SIGN_IN_WAIT_MINUTES`), on Cancel, on a new sign-in, which replaces it, on Sign out, and on quitting (`registerController`).

2. **What is kept** (`secrets.json`, `store.ts`), beside the OpenAI key until `codex.6` took it out and alone since, a key from before then read past and dropped at the next write (`knownParts`): the host id; the registrations, each a client id OpenAI issued, with the account's `sub` once a sign-in with it has been checked, the account's data settings box and whether its next sign-in asks for consent again; the registration a plain Sign in with ChatGPT reuses (`lastClientId`); and the one sign-in kept, which names its registration and the plan and holds the access, refresh and ID tokens with the scopes granted and the access token's expiry as one safeStorage ciphertext. A first sign-in's client id is kept as soon as the answer brings it, so a code refused at the exchange does not register the app again. The email is not kept apart from the encrypted ID token. Every write of the file reads it and keeps the parts this version knows (`updateSecrets`, one write at a time per folder; the other credential until `codex.6`); off Windows the file is written 0600. A write never takes a read that failed for an empty file (codex.2 review): no file reads as empty; a file the system will not let be read, as while a sync, backup or antivirus tool holds it, refuses the write with `readFailure`'s words ("Windows would not let <APP_NAME> read secrets.json. ... <APP_NAME> has not changed anything.") and writes nothing; and a damaged file (not JSON, not an object, or another version) is first copied aside as `secrets.json.corrupt-<yyyymmddhhmmss>`, never over an earlier copy, or, when no copy can be made, nothing is written (settings.json's rule, `hardening.15`). The sign-in's decisions read it the same way (`readChatGptChecked`): which registration a sign-in uses, whose account a kept registration is, and whether there is a sign-in to end, so none is made on a read that failed. Only the status reads it leniently, and while it cannot be read it gives what was last read or written in the run, or nothing kept when nothing was. The privacy footer (item 6) says what is kept unencrypted.

3. **What the page sees** (`ChatGptStatus`): signed in or not; the plan, from `chatgpt_plan_type` in the ID token's `https://api.openai.com/auth` claim, as Codex reads it, named by `chatGptPlanLabel` ("Plus"), or none, since OpenAI's pages for this sign-in do not document it; the account's data settings box; whether a sign-in is waiting (`chatGptWaiting`: a page loaded while one it did not start waits, as after a reload, shows it too, and asks again every 2 s until it ends, `pollsForSignIn` and `SIGN_IN_POLL_MS`); whether a registration is kept, for Use another account; whether safeStorage can encrypt; and, in a development run, the sign-in server's address. Never a token, the client id, the account's id or its email (CLAUDE.md rule 2 b).

4. **Sign out** revokes the refresh token (since the `codex.3` review, that of a renewal held for its write when there is one, which is the one OpenAI takes, and the spent one on disk as well; 5.8 item 3) at `https://auth.openai.com/api/accounts/oauth/revoke` (a form POST of `token`, `token_type_hint=refresh_token` and the client id; a 200 means ended, an already ended token included; no answer or a 5xx is tried twice more, after 0.5 s and 1.5 s, and any other answer is not tried again), then removes the tokens whatever OpenAI answered, keeping the registrations and the host id. The view then says (`signOutOutcome`) "Signed out. The sign-in was removed from this computer, and OpenAI ended it." or, when OpenAI did not confirm it, in the warning colour, "Signed out on this computer, but OpenAI did not confirm that it ended the sign-in. To be sure, disconnect <APP_NAME> in your ChatGPT settings."

5. **A sign-in that is not kept.** Another account's `sub` on a kept registration ("You signed in as another ChatGPT account than the one <APP_NAME> was registered with on this computer, ... choose Use another account.") and a grant without the plan's scope ("OpenAI did not give <APP_NAME> permission to use your ChatGPT plan, ...", after which the next sign-in sends `prompt=consent`) are revoked at once; an ID token that fails a check is dropped without a request. Every reason has its sentence in `signInFailureMessage`, shown in red under the view's buttons and in the browser's tab; a cancelled sign-in says nothing (`signInFailureOutcome`). A request to OpenAI's token or key endpoint that fails says how (codex.2 review): no answer came (`no-answer`, the one sentence that says to check the connection), an error status (`server`, "OpenAI could not finish the sign-in: it answered with an error (status 503). Try again in a few minutes."), or an answer not in the form OpenAI documents, a token answer without its access or ID token or keys that are not JSON (`malformed`, "... Try again; if it happens again, <APP_NAME> may need an update."); `invalid_grant` keeps its own sentence.

6. **The ChatGPT view** (`ChatGptSetup`), the Setup screen's second view (`setupFor`, beside Claude's), in its layout (5.6 item 5), opened by Setup on Settings' ChatGPT account row; Done, Close and Escape go back to where it was opened from (5.6 item 5, `setup.19`; until then Close went back to the main view, wherever the view was opened from). "Set up ChatGPT" with Close; the status card, the live region: "Not signed in to ChatGPT" (`SIGNED_OUT_TEXT`) with Sign in with ChatGPT, blue, and Use another account beside it once a registration is kept; "Waiting for you to sign in" (`WAITING_TEXT`) with the sign-in button held (`heldButton`) and Cancel; "Signed in to ChatGPT" with "Your ChatGPT account is on the Plus plan." when the plan is known, `SIGNED_IN_TEXT`, then, once OpenAI's welcome has gone (5.8 item 9), OpenAI's label for the plan in use, "**Using ChatGPT plan.** Reviews count against your ChatGPT plan's usage limits, and nothing is billed per token." (`USING_CHATGPT_PLAN`, `CHATGPT_PLAN_NOTE`) with Manage usage as a link after it, and Sign out (the `codex.5` review: Review with AI had the label by the model choice, as OpenAI's guidelines put it, until `codex.5`, whose task said it stays on this view; until the review it stood here only as the welcome, until Got it, C.116); "<APP_NAME> cannot keep a sign-in here" (`NO_ENCRYPTION_TEXT`), in the warning colour, when Windows cannot encrypt, its button disabled. Sign in with ChatGPT and Sign out are one button, under one key, so the keyboard's focus stays on it as the sign-in comes and goes, and a focus left on nothing when the wait ends goes back to it. Cancel and Use another account are two buttons, each under its own key, so Cancel goes when the wait ends and takes the focus with it, which then goes back to the account button; until the codex.2 review they were one element, and with a registration kept a second Enter on Cancel pressed Use another account and registered the app again. The line under the buttons says how the last sign-in, sign-out, tick of the box or Open Data controls went, and each clears it as it starts. Under the card, the training warning (item 7), then Done, the blue button at the foot, which takes the focus once the sign-in has succeeded, wherever the focus was (`signInSucceeded`: main said there was no sign-in and now says there is one; a status read for the first time does not count; `setup.19`); the page keeps still while Done is wholly in view, so the card that says so stays where it was, and comes up just far enough to show Done when it is below the fold, as at 125% and 150% with OpenAI's welcome up, which a first sign-in always shows (`focusInView`, 5.6 item 5, the setup.19 review), then `CHATGPT_PRIVACY_FOOTER` ("... It keeps the sign-in's tokens in its data folder, encrypted with your Windows login, never shown and used only by its background process. Beside them, unencrypted, it keeps your plan, whether you ticked the data settings box, an id for your ChatGPT account, the id OpenAI issued <APP_NAME> for that account, and an id <APP_NAME> made for this computer.", exact since the codex.2 review, where it said the app kept only the tokens) and the app's name and version. Claude's ways to Setup (5.6 item 4) open Claude's view; since `codex.3` this one opens too from the Review menu's ChatGPT while no sign-in is kept, Review with AI's Open Setup on its account row (while there is no sign-in, since `codex.5`), the status bar's ChatGPT label, a review that found no sign-in or the box not ticked, and the welcome guide's Set up ChatGPT (5.8), and after the first sign-in it shows OpenAI's welcome under the status card until Got it (5.8 item 9).

7. **The training warning** (`DataSettingsWarning`; the author's requirement, Appendix D 23), on the view in every state and after the box is ticked, as a reminder: the dialogs' orange box (`role="note"`, named by its title), "ChatGPT may train on your chapters", `TRAINING_WARNING_TEXT` (on personal plans OpenAI may use what is sent to train its models unless Improve the model for everyone is turned off under Settings, Data controls; a review sends the chapter and the guidelines file; the app cannot see the setting), `TRAINING_CHOICE_TEXT` (it may be left on, but turning it off is recommended), then **Open Data controls**, which asks main to open ChatGPT's Data controls in the browser (`shell:open-external` with `chatgpt-data-controls`, `https://chatgpt.com/#settings/DataControls`), and the box **I have confirmed my data settings**, disabled while signed out and never while main writes it, kept for the signed-in account's registration (`chatgpt:confirm-data-settings`) through sign-outs and restarts; another registration has its own. Under the box: "Sign in first: the box is kept for the account you sign in with.", "Your first ChatGPT review needs this box ticked. It is kept for this account." or "Kept for this account.". Before the first review the same warning, with its box, stands in Review with AI, whose Start review waits for the box, and main refuses a review without it (`codex.3`, 5.8 item 5).

8. **Settings' ChatGPT account row**, under the Claude account (section 7; between it and the OpenAI key until `codex.6`): `chatGptAccountLine`, "signed in (Plus)", "signed in", "not signed in", "waiting for the browser" or "not read yet"; Setup; and its (?), `CHATGPT_ACCOUNT_TIP`.

9. **The log** (CLAUDE.md rule 9, 11.3 m): `chatgpt.sign-in.start` (`registration` new or saved, `consent`), `chatgpt.sign-in.done` (`registration`, `plan`, `durationMs`), `chatgpt.sign-in.failed` (`reason`, a fixed word, and the ID token's `problem`, or, for the token and key requests, `endpoint`, `token` or `keys`, and the `status` OpenAI answered with, `durationMs`), `chatgpt.sign-out` (`revoked`) and `chatgpt.data-settings` (`confirmed`); a failed sign-in is also `ipc.failed`, with its message. secrets.json adds `secrets.read-failed` (`code`), for a read refused before a write or a decision, and `secrets.unreadable` (`kept`, the copy's name, or `none` with the `code`), for a damaged file. Never a token, the code, the client id, the state, the nonce, the verifier, the host id, the account's id or its email; `scrub` takes out anything shaped like a signed token as well.

10. **Tested without an account.** `test/helpers/mockChatGptAuth.ts` stands in for OpenAI's sign-in server, and `MANUSCRIPT_REVIEW_CHATGPT_AUTH_URL` (11.3 b) points a development run at it. No agent has a ChatGPT account and none may sign in: the author's own first sign-in is the real check (`codex.2`).

### 5.8 ChatGPT's reviews on the plan (`codex.3`)

How a review runs on the author's ChatGPT plan once signed in (5.7): its request, its models, the renewal of its access token, the plan's limits and errors, and where the page shows them (`codex.3`; what OpenAI's pages say is in Appendix A, re-read 2026-10-24, and what the build settled in Appendix C "What ChatGPT's reviews settled where the plan left it open"). The provider is `src/main/providers/chatgpt.ts`; the renewal is `accessToken` in `src/main/chatgpt/index.ts`; the pure parts are `src/shared/ai/chatgpt.ts` (the model list, the limits) and `src/shared/ui/chatgpt.ts` (the words).

1. **The request**: the streamed `store: false` Responses request the API key's provider sent until `codex.6` (5.0; `reviewRequestBody`, `readReplyStream` and `checkedReply` in `providers/openai.ts`, which the ChatGPT provider alone uses since then): the system prompt as `instructions`, the strict schema as `text.format` (`json_schema`, `manuscript_review`, strict), the effort as `reasoning.effort`, `store: false` and `stream: true`, read to `response.completed`. `input` is the numbered chapter as the one user message of a list, as OpenAI's page on preview limitations asks; nothing that page lists as refused (`max_output_tokens`, `temperature`, `metadata` and the rest) is ever sent. The official `openai` package sends it to `https://api.openai.com/v1`, or to `MANUSCRIPT_REVIEW_OPENAI_BASE_URL` in a development run, with the sign-in's access token as the bearer, the package's own headers only, and no retries (`maxRetries: 0`, as OpenAI's example for this route). The reply is checked and parsed as an API key's was; a ChatGPT review has no cost, since the plan pays, and keeps its token counts. Whether the route takes `json_schema` structured output is the question 5.7 left open: the mock takes it, and the author's own review settles it; a refusal (`subscription_sharing_unsupported_capability` naming `text.format`) says so in its own words, and the fallback `codex.2` names, the user's Codex CLI, would be a task of its own.
2. **The models**: `GET /v1/models` with the bearer, read as OpenAI's page on models and inference gives it, a `models` array of `slug`, `display_name` and `visibility`, the `list` ones shown by their names in OpenAI's order (`readChatGptModels`; the `data` array the endpoint gives an API key is read too). The default, marked "(default)", is the first that `NOT_DEFAULT_MODEL` does not name, so no -pro, -codex, -deep-research or -chat model, else the first (`defaultChatGptModel`). The setting is `chatgptModel`, empty for the default (11.3 d); a review with none chosen lists the models first and sends the default, and when the list is empty fails, saying so. The list is fetched when Review with AI first shows ChatGPT, and forgotten when the sign-in changes, as it is the account's. A list that fails is said under the Model row with Try again, and asked for again as the dialog next opens; one that comes back empty is said there too (5.5, `codex.3` review).
3. **The access token**, asked for at call time (`accessToken`) and never kept by the provider. It is renewed with the refresh token when it ends within 60 s (`RENEW_BEFORE_MS`) or has ended, and when OpenAI refuses it with a 401, after which the request is sent once more: a form POST to the token endpoint of `grant_type=refresh_token`, the issued client id, the refresh token and the resource, with no scope, as OpenAI's page on sessions gives it. One renewal at a time, shared by every request waiting on it, since refresh tokens rotate; a review's Cancel stops waiting but not the renewal, which cut short after OpenAI had rotated the token would lose the sign-in, and quitting ends it. The answer's access token, rotated refresh token, scopes and, when it brings one, ID token replace the kept ones, encrypted, only while the kept sign-in is still the one renewed; a renewed ID token's account must be the kept one's, and the plan it names replaces the kept plan, read as it came from the token endpoint. A refresh error OpenAI's page lists as ending the sign-in (`invalid_grant`, `invalid_refresh_token`, `token_expired`, `refresh_token_expired`, `refresh_token_invalidated`, `refresh_token_reused`, and `invalid_client`, which also keeps a plain Sign in from reusing that registration; `ENDED_REFRESH_ERRORS`) removes the sign-in, keeping the registration and the host id, and the request fails as not signed in; so does a renewal for another account or without the plan's scope, which is ended at OpenAI, the latter marking the registration for consent (5.7 item 5), and a renewal made while the sign-in was ended or replaced, which is ended at OpenAI too. No answer, or an error status, keeps the sign-in and fails the request (`chatgpt-server`, or `chatgpt-failed` for a 4xx OpenAI's page does not list), as OpenAI's page says not to drop credentials for a failure of the network or its servers. A renewal that secrets.json will not take, as while a sync tool holds it, is held for the run and written with the next request, so the rotated refresh token is not lost. Once it is written, the sign-in kept is that renewal, and a renewal of it, when its token has ended by the next request or OpenAI refuses it, is compared with it (`codex.3` review: compared with the sign-in before, it read as replaced, its new refresh token was ended at OpenAI, and the next renewal, with the spent one, ended the sign-in); while the file still refuses it, the held tokens are renewed over the sign-in on disk, and the new renewal is held in their place. A renewal reads the kept sign-in again as it starts (`renewKept`), so a request whose read came before another request's renewal was written takes that renewal's token rather than renewing with a spent refresh token, which OpenAI would refuse as reused. Sign out ends a held renewal's refresh token (5.7 item 4), and a held renewal goes with the sign-in it renewed.
4. **Not signed in is never a failed review.** No sign-in, or one that has ended, fails a review with `chatgpt-not-signed-in` before the review's request is sent; the page reads the status again, opens the Setup screen's ChatGPT view and says why under its buttons in the warning colour (`notSignedInText`: not signed in, the sign-in has ended, the plan no longer allowed), with no card, and the status bar says "ChatGPT: not signed in" (`chatGptFailureRoute`). The Review menu's ChatGPT opens the view in place of the dialog while main says no sign-in is kept.
5. **The gate on the box** (5.7 item 7). Review with AI shows the training warning with its box while the account's box is not ticked, and keeps it shown for the rest of that opening once it is ticked there, so the box keeps its place and the keyboard's focus; Start review waits for a sign-in and the box, and the line beside it says which (`chatGptStartBlocker`). Main refuses a review without the box too (`chatgpt-data-settings`, which opens the view as not signed in does).
6. **The limits**, read from each answer's headers as Codex reads them (`readChatGptLimits`): `x-codex-primary-used-percent`, `x-codex-primary-window-minutes` and `x-codex-primary-reset-at`, or the older `x-codex-primary-reset-after-seconds`, and the same for `secondary`, which OpenAI's pages for this route do not document (Appendix A). The window names the limit (`windowKind`: 300 minutes the 5-hour limit and 10,080 the weekly one, as Claude's are named; 60 the hourly, 1,440 the daily, any other whole number of hours or days by its length). The notice is the limit reached, the one resetting last when both are, else the one most used, marked `provider: 'chatgpt'`, and the status bar words it with `describeRateLimit` as setup.9 words Claude's, from 80%: "5-hour limit 85% used, resets 15:45", "Weekly limit reached, resets Sat 09:00", with the tooltip "85% of your ChatGPT plan's 5-hour limit is used. It resets at 15:45, in 2 hours and 10 minutes." An answer with no limits sends a notice that says nothing (`CHATGPT_LIMITS_UNKNOWN`), so a limit reached does not outlive a review that went through. The page keeps the ChatGPT plan's notice apart from Claude's and shows it while ChatGPT is in use: the provider, unless Claude's Setup view is open, or ChatGPT's view.

With ChatGPT chosen the dialog shows Claude's rows and the account (`chatGptAccountLine`), with Open Setup while there is no sign-in, the warning before the first review, and the models; OpenAI's "Using ChatGPT plan" with Manage usage and the effort note stood there too until `codex.5` (5.5), and the first stands on the ChatGPT view's status card since its review (5.7 item 6). The status bar's label reads "ChatGPT ready (Plus)", "ChatGPT ready", "ChatGPT: not signed in", "ChatGPT: usage limit reached" or "ChatGPT: could not check" (`runtimeLabel`), and opens the view. With ChatGPT the provider, the welcome guide's first step says where the sign-in stands, in the view's words, with Set up ChatGPT and Use Claude instead. Copy diagnostics has a ChatGPT part: the last check's state, the plan and the last failure.

Manage usage in your ChatGPT settings.", OpenAI's words, with Manage usage and Got it, on the view under the status card while signed in until Got it, which is kept as the hint `chatgpt-plan-welcome` and hands the focus to the account button. Never a token, a refresh token, the client id, the account or its email.

The author's own review on his Plus plan is the real check, and settles the structured output question.

## 6. Files, watcher, review store (`src/main`)

### 6.1 Files

- List `*.md` and `*.txt` recursively under the manuscript folder (`listChapters`), sorted by their paths with numbers in order, skipping every file and folder whose name starts with a dot (`.obsidian`, `.trash`, `.git`, and Save's own temp files), folders named exactly `node_modules`, `out` or `dist` (`SKIP_DIRS`, there since before 1.0 and named nowhere in this plan until `files.12`; the welcome guide's folder line, `FOLDER_LISTS`, names of this list what an author meets, the guidelines file, Excalidraw drawings and names that start with a dot, and says a few are left out rather than that every file is listed (`files.23`), and the README's First run says the same and points to its full list), the reviews folder if nested, the guidelines file in use, drawings of Obsidian's Excalidraw plugin (`*.excalidraw.md`, in any case, `files.11`), which hold a drawing's data, not prose, and every symbolic link and junction, to a file or to a folder: the walk follows only entries that `readdir` reports as a plain file or folder (`entry.isFile()`, `entry.isDirectory()`), and on Windows Node reports both kinds of link as a symbolic link, neither file nor folder (Node 24.21.0, and the app's own walk), so a chapter folder or a chapter file linked into the manuscript folder is not listed (seen by the `files.12` review in a `dev:clean` window). Whether OneDrive's online-only files, which are reparse points too, are left out the same way is not known (`files.24`). Both extensions are read, saved and reviewed the same way; the empty state says "No .md or .txt files in that folder".
- **Sync hygiene (`files.11`, C.78).** The app points at what a sync tool or git leaves after a clash and changes nothing: nothing is hidden, moved or deleted. A conflict copy is listed and opens as any chapter does, and the list puts a "conflict copy" badge on a line under its name, so the name keeps the width any chapter's has, with a tooltip that names the tool and the chapter it copies (`conflictCopyLabel` in `src/shared/text/sync.ts`, section 7); only the names Obsidian Sync, Dropbox and Syncthing give their copies are known. A chapter holding merge markers, a line that starts `<<<<<<< ` or `>>>>>>> ` (`hasMergeMarkers`), opens as it is, markers and both versions on the page, with a warning card that says so (section 7, Notification cards); a reload from disk that brings markers shows it too, and one that takes them out closes it (6.2), as do a review opened from History and Save to chapter finding the file changed (6.3 step 2), which read the chapter again. When that change brought the markers, Save stops before anything is written, so the author sees them first (6.3 step 2, the `files.11` review).
- Read: bytes -> refuse anything over 4 MiB or not UTF-8 (`decodeText`, `files.3`, 11.3 l) -> detect BOM/EOL/trailing newline -> LF text -> sha256 of bytes. The refusal (`not-utf8`) says what the file most likely is (UTF-16, an older encoding, a few damaged characters, binary) and how to fix it, and ends "The app has not changed the file." Save re-reads through the same path, so a file swapped to another encoding after it was opened is refused rather than overwritten.
- Write, for Save to chapter only (`writeChapter`, 6.3, 11.3 h): the page composes the text (6.3 step 3) -> main reads the file and hashes it, and stops as `stale` with nothing written when it is not the file the review is based on -> restore EOL/BOM -> stop with nothing written when the bytes equal the file's -> copy the bytes being replaced into the backups, or stop with nothing written (6.5), then read once more and stop as `stale` if it changed -> write `.<file>.<12 random hex>.tmp` in the same folder, a dot-file the list skips, with the exclusive-create flag, and flush it to disk -> `rename` over the original (`atomicWriteFile` in `src/main/atomic.ts`). Remember the hash of what was written so the watcher can ignore the echo. A rename refused with EPERM, EACCES or EBUSY (a scanner, OneDrive or Obsidian holding the file for a moment) is retried after 50, 100, 200, 400 and 800 ms; before each retry the target is hashed again, and if someone else changed it the save stops as `stale` and their bytes stay (`files.4`). When the retries run out, `explainWriteError` says in plain words what Windows refused, including the Controlled folder access way out, and that nothing was written.
- **A read that fails is explained as a read (`apply.24`).** `toAppError` in `src/main/errors.ts` takes the operation, `read` or `write`, and these read paths in main throw `readFailure(err, name, options)`, whose words reach the page unchanged: opening or reloading a chapter (`readChapter`), the reads Save to chapter makes before it writes (steps 1 and 5 of 11.3 h, and the read after a `stale`), a review opened from History (`reviews:load`), the guidelines file (before a review, and its status), the drafts file (11.3 j) and Show backups (6.5). So does the review a chapter opens with (`reviews:load-latest`, `apply.25`): a review file in the chapter's folder that is there but cannot be read, or the folder itself, stops the open with a card that names the chapter before main's words ("Could not open Chapter 12.md: Windows would not let Lapidary read the review file ..."), and the page stays on what was open (6.4). `explainReadError` says what may be holding the file, what to try, and ends "Lapidary has not changed anything." On Windows EBUSY, EPERM and EACCES give "Windows would not let Lapidary read Chapter 12.md. Another program may have it open, such as a sync, backup or antivirus tool, or your Windows account may not be allowed to read it. Close it there, or wait a moment, and try again."; elsewhere "Lapidary is not allowed to read Chapter 12.md. Check that the file and its folder can be read, and that no other program is holding it, then try again." ENOENT and ENOTDIR give "Lapidary could not find Chapter 12.md. It may have been renamed, moved or deleted; if it was renamed or moved, open it again from where it is now." for a chapter (`readChapter` and Save's reads pass `reopen`), except that Save's reads keep `files.1`'s words for a chapter that is not there (`ENOENT`, `not-found`): "The chapter is no longer at <full path>. If you renamed or moved it in Obsidian, open it again from the list; its review comes with it." (`readForSave`); and they stop at "It may have been renamed, moved or deleted." for any other file, which cannot be opened again from somewhere else ("Lapidary could not find the review file 2026-10-17T12-00-00-000Z.review.json. It may have been renamed, moved or deleted. Lapidary has not changed anything."); EISDIR "... because it is a folder, not a file.", and any other code "Lapidary could not read Chapter 12.md (EIO). If it is on a network, USB or cloud drive, check that the drive is connected, then try again." Controlled folder access blocks only changes, so a read never mentions it. A file is named by its own name, a review file as "the review file <name>", the drafts file as "the file they are kept in" (its own name is a hash, and the card puts the words after "could not be read back:") and a chapter's backups as "the backup folder of <chapter>"; the name never starts a sentence, so a file name is shown exactly as it is. An error the IPC bridge receives unexplained is worded as a write that replaces a file, as before, and a refused rename keeps those words. The chapter list's read is explained too (`apply.25`): `listChapters` throws `readFailure` naming "the manuscript folder <name>" when the manuscript folder itself cannot be read or is not there, and the list shows those words where "No .md or .txt files in that folder." would be, with Try again (section 7); a subfolder it cannot read is still skipped. A list read that works, Try again's among them, also starts the watcher when the folder refused its start (6.2, `files.21`). Held by another program on Windows: "Windows would not let Lapidary read the manuscript folder Novel. Another program may have it open, such as a sync, backup or antivirus tool, or your Windows account may not be allowed to read it. Close it there, or wait a moment, and try again. Lapidary has not changed anything."
- **A write that makes something new says what it was making (`apply.25`).** Only a refused rename is retried (files.4), so only its words say "even after trying for a second and a half". `toAppError` takes the kind of write as well (`write`: `replace`, the default, `create`, `copy` or `folder`, the type `WriteKind` in `src/main/errors.ts`), and `writeFailure(err, kind, name)` turns a refusal into an `AppFailure` whose words reach the page unchanged, as `readFailure` does for a read; an error it has no words for (`EEXIST`, or `ENOENT` for a new file or a copy) is left as it is, so a caller can still test its code. `create` is a new chapter (`createChapter`'s `wx` write) and set-aside text (`setAsideDrafts`), `copy` the guidelines file made from its template (`ensureGuidelinesFile`), and `folder` the folder made before each of them, the drafts folder (`saveDrafts`), a chapter's review folder (`saveReview`, adoption) and the reviews folder itself (`makeReviewsFolder`, which every review operation runs first). Their words say what was being made, claim no retries, keep the Controlled folder access way out, since it blocks creating files too, and say "try again", never "save again", since none of them is Save to chapter: "Windows would not let Lapidary create Chapter 13.md. Another program may be holding its folder, or your Windows account may not be allowed to add files to it. Wait a moment and try again. If that keeps happening, Windows Security's Controlled folder access may be blocking Lapidary: allow it under Windows Security > Virus & threat protection > Ransomware protection > Allow an app through Controlled folder access. Nothing was written."; "... create GUIDELINES.md from the template. ..."; "... create the review folder of Chapter 12.md. Another program may be holding the folder it goes in, or your Windows account may not be allowed to add folders there. ..."; elsewhere "Lapidary is not allowed to create Chapter 13.md. Check that its folder is writable, then try again. Nothing was written."; a full disk "There is no space left on the disk for Chapter 13.md. Free some space and try again." (part of a new file may be left, so it does not say nothing was written) and a read-only drive "Lapidary cannot create Chapter 13.md, because the drive is read-only. Nothing was written.". A folder is named by what it is for: "the manuscript folder Novel", "the folder for GUIDELINES.md", "the folder they are kept in" (the drafts, after "could not be kept:"), "the folder for set-aside text", "the review folder of Chapter 12.md", "the reviews folder <path>". A folder is made with everything on its path, so `ENOENT` means its drive, or the share it is on, is not there, and `ENOTDIR` that a file is in its way, and a folder has words for both (`apply.25` review): the reviews folder can be on a USB, network or cloud drive, and while that drive is not connected no chapter opens (6.4), where Node 24 on Windows reports the missing drive as `ENOENT` with the path `\\?` and the card had shown only `ENOENT: no such file or directory, mkdir '\\?'`. Now "Lapidary could not create the reviews folder Q:\Reviews, because the drive or the folder it goes in is not there. If it is on a network, USB or cloud drive, check that the drive is connected, or choose another reviews folder in Settings, then try again. Nothing was written." and "... because a file has the name of one of the folders it goes in. Move or rename that file, or choose another reviews folder in Settings, then try again. Nothing was written."; only the reviews folder, which the author chooses in Settings, offers Settings (`makeReviewsFolder` passes `setting: 'reviews folder'`, `ErrorContext.setting`), and every other folder stops at "then try again". A new file and a copy keep `ENOENT` and `ENOTDIR` as they are. The temp file `atomicWriteFile` writes first is part of replacing a file, so it keeps `replace`, but a refusal to create it, which Controlled folder access gives in a protected folder before any rename, is never retried, and `explainWriteError` tells it from a refused rename by the error itself (a temp file's path and no `dest`): "Windows would not let Lapidary write the new version of Chapter 12.md into its folder. Another program may be holding the folder, or your Windows account may not be allowed to add files to it. Wait a moment and save again. If that keeps happening, ... Nothing was written; the file is as it was." Show in folder's own folders in the app's data folder keep the default words.
- **Main decides what Save may write (`files.2`).** `files:save` first runs `assertSavableChapter`: the file must be `.md` or `.txt`, must not be the guidelines file, and must lie inside the manuscript folder or have been read or created from inside it earlier in the run (`OpenedChapters`, so a chapter open while Settings changes folder still saves). Anything else is refused with `invalid-input` before a byte is read or written.
- **Create (`files:create`).** The New chapter dialog (7.5) creates a file in the manuscript folder through `createChapter`, which writes with the exclusive-create flag (`wx`): it can fail, but it can never overwrite. `checkChapterName` is the gate in front of it and refuses a path separator, a traversal, a reserved Windows device name, an illegal character and anything resolving outside the manuscript folder; `files:check-name` runs the same function plus an existence check, so the dialog can say "A file with this name already exists" while the author is still typing and keep Create disabled. A new file is written LF, no BOM, with a trailing newline; after that Save preserves whatever shape the file has.
- **The review folder name includes the extension** for anything but `.md` (`chapter-01` versus `chapter-01-txt`), so two files that differ only by extension cannot show each other's reviews. `.md` keeps the bare slug, which is what every review written before `.txt` support already uses.

### 6.2 Watcher

chokidar on the manuscript folder with `awaitWriteFinish: { stabilityThreshold: 300, pollInterval: 100 }`, 12 folder levels deep, ignoring every name that starts with a dot and `node_modules`. A chapter deleted, renamed or moved while open puts up a warning card, "The chapter was deleted, renamed or moved on disk. If you renamed or moved it in Obsidian, open it again from the list; its review comes with it.", and the page stays on the text it had; the list is read again, and the chapter opened again from it brings its reviews with it where they plainly are its own (6.4, "Reviews follow their chapter"; following a live rename was `files.18`, cut). On change to the open chapter: hash the file; if it equals the last written or last loaded hash, ignore; otherwise send `file:changed` to the renderer, which triggers rebase (4.5) and shows a card, one that each reload replaces (section 7, Notification cards): "Reloaded from disk. N suggestions re-anchored, M could not be found.", followed by "J suggestions kept out of the text, as they would now change Obsidian syntax." when the rebase kept some out (`files.20`) and "K decisions changed to match the file." when the rebase changed decisions to follow the file (C.5; `rebaseCardText` in `src/shared/ui/rebase.ts`, which words all four rebase cards: this one, a chapter opened on a review made before the file changed, an older review opened from History, and Save to chapter finding the file changed, `apply.23`). M counts only the suggestions this rebase took off the page (`newlyStale`), not those already under Unanchored, and this card and the one for a chapter opened on an older review warn only when M is above 0 (`rebaseCardTone`, `files.20`, C.74); until then M counted every suggestion under Unanchored, the kept-out ones included, and the card warned at every reload while there was one. Obsidian saves on a debounce while typing, so this can fire repeatedly; that is fine because rebase is idempotent. Since reloads come in runs, and each replaces the card, the card counts the run (`mergeReloadRun` in `src/shared/ui/rebase.ts`, the `files.20` review, C.74): while the reload card is still up, the next reload's card gives N as that reload left them, M as the suggestions any reload of the run took off the page that are still off it and not kept out, J as those any of them kept out, and K as the decisions any of them changed, each once, and warns while M is above 0. Counting only its own reload, a card that warned of a suggestion lost was replaced, at the next save two seconds later, by an information card saying "0 could not be found". A reload of another review, the card closed with its X, or a chapter or a review opened (App keeps the run with the card's id and drops it on an open) starts a new run. A reload also looks for merge markers (`files.11`, `mergeMarkersCard`): text that has them where the text before had none brings the warning card of 6.1, text without them closes it, and markers still there leave it as the author left it, so a card closed with its X does not come back at every save in Obsidian.

`createWatcher` (`src/main/watcher.ts`, `files.5`) takes chokidar, `broadcast`, the file reader and the log as dependencies, so it is tested with a stand-in and fake timers; `npm run test:slow` runs the real-chokidar timing tests in `test/slow/`, which `npm test` leaves out. Only .md and .txt files count: a change is reported unless its bytes are ones the app wrote or loaded (compared by `pathKey`), a chapter or folder appearing or disappearing refreshes the file list once per 300 ms burst, an added chapter is also hashed so an editor that saves by replacing the file still reloads the open chapter, and watcher errors are logged.

**Starting once the folder can be read (`files.21`, C.79).** Settings starts the watcher on the folder it holds (`start`, from `settings:get` and `settings:set`; from `settings:get` only once settings.json could be read, `hardening.15`, C.86), and starting the folder already in hand changes nothing. A manuscript folder another program holds at that moment makes chokidar report one error for the folder itself (`EBUSY` on `scandir`) and never get ready, and chokidar does not try again once the folder is free; so an error that names the folder itself before ready closes that watcher, is logged as `watcher.error` with `stopped=true`, and leaves the start failed, while an error for a subfolder, one that names no path, or one after ready is only logged, as before. Every event of a closed watcher is dropped. Every list read that works, `files:list` and `reviews:index` through `listAndWatch`, then calls `ensure`, which starts a new watcher when the folder read is the one Settings last gave `start` and that start failed, keeping the hashes of what was loaded and saved meanwhile: Try again, the folder chosen again and any later refresh start it once the folder can be read. A read of any other folder changes nothing, since a slow read of the old folder can end after Settings has changed folder or chosen none (the `files.21` review). Settings never tries a failed start again. chokidar says nothing of what happened before it was ready, so once it is ready every file whose hash is kept is read again (`catchUp`), and one whose bytes changed while nothing watched is reported as a change, and one that is gone as deleted, as chokidar would have: a chapter opened while the folder was held and edited in Obsidian meanwhile reloads, with the card above, once Try again works (the `files.21` review, C.79). Each start logs `watcher.start`, and chokidar being ready `watcher.ready` (debug). Main tells the page whether it watches, by `files:watching-changed` at each change and by `files:watching`, which the page asks once each list answer is in, so a page loaded again learns it too; until told otherwise the page takes it as watched. While it is not watched, the chapter list says "Lapidary is not watching the manuscript folder, so changes made outside Lapidary will not show until Try again succeeds." with Try again (`watchNotice`, section 7).

### 6.3 Save flow

`saveChapter` in `src/renderer/state/saveChapter.ts` (`apply.3`) is the one path from the page to the chapter file. The toolbar's Save to chapter, Ctrl+S, the review dialog's "Save N changes, then review" and Submit manual review's "Save N changes, then build" (`apply.20`, 5.5, 7.5), the leave prompt's Save first (`apply.7`, 7.7) and the close prompt's Save and close (`apply.9`, 7.7) all call it and can wait for how it ended: `saved` or `nothing-to-save` (the file now reads like the page), `cancelled` (Cancel to applying paragraph boxes), `blocked` (no chapter, a review of it running, or a box that cannot be applied) or `failed` (a card says why; a dialog that saved first, Review with AI or Submit manual review, also shows the card's words inside itself, 5.5 and 7.5). It reaches main through `SaveDeps` that App passes in (`files:save`, the review writer, a refresh of History and the list), so it is tested in node. Saves run one at a time, and `pendingSave()` hands a caller that must let one end first the save under way.

0. Nothing unsaved (`unsavedDecisionCount` is 0 and no paragraph box has changed text): a card says "The chapter already matches the page." and the file is not read or written. Paragraph boxes with changed text are applied first as accepted suggestions, after a question unless the caller already asked (`applyDrafts: 'apply'`, for a prompt whose Save reads "Apply and save first"); if one cannot be applied, nothing is written. A box still as it opened needs no question and is closed when something is written, since the save can renumber the paragraphs under it.
1. Re-read the file and hash it.
2. If the hash differs from the review's `base.hash`, rebase first and tell the user what changed, then try once more. A file that has changed again by then stops the save with nothing written: "The chapter keeps changing on disk. Close it in Obsidian and save again." under `SAVE_CARD`, and the save ends `failed`; so does a change found while another review has come on screen ("The chapter changed on disk before saving, and another review is open now, so nothing was saved."). Merge markers the change brought get their warning card here, as at a reload, since the rebase leaves the watcher's reload of the same bytes nothing to do (`files.11`, 6.1), and they stop the save there, before anything is written (the `files.11` review, C.78): the rebase card leaves out "Retrying." (`rebaseCardText('saving-stopped')`), a card under `SAVE_CARD` says "Nothing was saved: the change on disk brought merge markers. They are on the page now." (`STOPPED_FOR_MERGE_MARKERS`), and the save ends `failed`, so a dialog or prompt that saved first goes no further. The next Save goes ahead with them, as for a chapter that opened with markers, and markers the page already showed never stop a save.
3. Compose. When the bytes to write are the bytes already on disk, nothing is written (`SaveResponse.unchanged`, 11.3 h step 3), so the file keeps its modified time and Obsidian and sync tools see no change; the card then says the chapter already matches the page. Otherwise back up the bytes being replaced (6.5; no backup, no save), check once more that the file has not changed, and write atomically. Then update `base` to the written text (accepted hunks now have `baseSide: 'replacement'`, `savedReview`) and save the review. Comments and hunk paragraph labels follow their paragraphs into the new base (`remapAfterCommit`, C.44), so a save that splits, joins or deletes a paragraph does not shift them. A hunk the save leaves starting in the blank text before the first paragraph, as a paragraph added to a chapter of frontmatter alone does, moves to the paragraph's start, where the page draws it (`intoFirstParagraph`, the `files.22` review, C.76), so the review opens again with every decision on the page as it was. While the file is being written the store holds back decisions (`chapterSaving`): the new base folds in exactly the decisions that were written, so a click in that moment does nothing rather than being recorded as saved without being in the file. Opening a chapter or a History entry waits for a save under way to end (`pendingSave()`), and of several clicks made meanwhile only the last goes ahead. If the review on screen is replaced during the write all the same, by a load that began before the save: a copy of the same review on the same base whose decisions compose the same text is folded like the review itself (`isWrittenReview`); another chapter or review is left alone, the save is recorded off screen in the review it belongs to, and History is refreshed only for the chapter on screen; a copy of the same review that reads differently, such as one rebased onto other bytes, is left alone too, and the card says the review was reloaded while saving and to save again.
4. Obsidian notices external changes and reloads the file when it is not being edited there. Document that the same chapter should not be edited in Obsidian while accepting changes; the app cannot prevent it, only detect it.

**Ctrl+S**, or Cmd+S, runs the same save wherever the focus is (`saveShortcutAction` in `src/shared/ui/save.ts`, handled first in `state/keyboard.ts`, before the early return for modified keys). It does nothing behind a dialog, a question, Settings, the Setup screen or the welcome guide, on a held key's repeats, while a review of the chapter runs or a save is under way, or when there is nothing to save; from inside a paragraph box a card says to press Done first, and while the suggestion editor is open a card says to press that editor's Save first. Ctrl+Shift+S and Ctrl+Alt+S pass through.

### 6.4 Review store

`<reviewsFolder>/<chapter-slug>/<ISO-timestamp>.review.json`. The folder is named after the chapter's file name only, so same-named chapters in different folders share it; a review belongs to the chapter its `sourcePath` names, compared as the file system compares paths (`samePath`), never to whatever its folder suggests (files.1, C.45). The current review, the one the chapter opens with, is the one last on screen for it (`apply.26`, C.57), which is almost always the newest. Main records it in the chapter folder's `.last-open.json`, `{version: 1, chapters: [{sourcePath, file}]}`, one record per chapter path, since same-named chapters in different folders share the folder: when the page shows a review from History or the review selector (`reviews:shown`, sent once it is on screen, `recordShown`), and when `saveReview` starts a new entry, which is a new review arriving, whether the author is on its chapter or not, or the review on screen being written for the first time. A record is written only when it changes, never touches the review file or its times, and is honoured only for a `.review.json` directly in the chapter's folder that belongs to the chapter; a record that cannot be written is logged (`reviews.last-open-failed`) and the save it came with stands. While nothing is recorded for a chapter, or the file recorded is gone, it opens with the belonging review last decided in (`decidedAt ?? createdAt`): a decision is made only on screen, and that is the review every chapter opened with before `apply.26`, so upgrading switches no chapter to another review. When reviews follow a renamed or moved chapter, the record goes with them (`carryLastOpen`, run with the journal). `currentOf` in `src/main/reviews.ts` decides it for `reviews:load-latest` and for the chapter list's marks (`reviews:index`) alike. **A review file that cannot be read is not skipped like one that is not a review (`apply.25`).** `readEntry` tells a file that is there and that the system will not let the app read (another program holds it with no sharing, or the account may not read it) from a file that is gone, a folder, or json that is not a review, which are still skipped. Whose such a file is, and when it was decided in, cannot be told without reading it, so unless the record names a review that could be read, `reviews:load-latest` throws `readFailure` naming it ("Windows would not let Lapidary read the review file 2026-10-17T12-00-00-000Z.review.json. ..."), and it does the same for a chapter folder it cannot list ("the review folder of Chapter 12.md") and for the review chosen when that file was read before, its entry cached, and is held since; nothing is adopted in its place. `openChapter` shows any failure of `reviews:load-latest`, a reviews folder that cannot be made included (6.1), as a card and stays on what was open: no older review and no blank one comes on screen, so no decision can make a new review current over the one that could not be read. Main's words name only a review file or a folder, so the card names the chapter first (`chapterNotOpenedText` in `src/shared/ui/open.ts`, `apply.25` review): "Could not open Chapter 12.md: Windows would not let Lapidary read the review file 2026-10-17T12-00-00-000Z.review.json. ..."; a chapter file that cannot be read is shown in main's words alone, which name it. **A review behind the page does not open either (`apply.25` review).** A decision whose write failed is kept by the writer, not in the file ("Two save points" below), so a review read back from disk would come on screen without it, and the writer's next try would then put it back over what the page showed. Opening a chapter, or a review from History or the review selector, therefore first queues every failed review write again (`retryReviewWrites`) and then flushes, so a review whose file another program has let go gets its decisions before anything is read; if the review about to be shown still has a failed write (`reviewWriteFailureOf`, by the key of chapter path and review id), the open stops before anything on screen changes, with "Could not open Chapter 12.md, because your latest decisions in its review are not in the review file yet, and it would open without them. The review could not be saved: ..." or, from History or the selector, "Could not open the review from <date as History shows it>, because your latest decisions in it are not in its file yet, ..." (`unwrittenReviewText`). Another chapter, or another review of the chapter, still opens while one review cannot be written. A review file read before and unchanged since counts by its cached entry, held or not. History and the list's marks still leave such a file out. `saveReview` neither writes over such a file nor writes the review on screen into a new entry instead, which would become current: the write fails with the read words, and the writer tries again later ("Two save points" below). History lists every belonging review, the current one too, newest first by `createdAt`, and highlights the one on screen (`historyCounts`, `apply.5`); the review selector at the top of the side panel lists the same reviews (section 7). `raw` is never modified. A small `index.json` per chapter folder is not needed; list the directory, with summaries cached by modification time and size.

**Reviews follow their chapter.** When nothing belongs to a chapter that opens, the reviews of a chapter path that no longer exists are taken over if they plainly are this chapter's: the vault moved (the last two path segments match) or the chapter was renamed or moved in Obsidian (a review of exactly its current text, at least 500 characters). The whole history moves to the new folder with the new `sourcePath`, through a journal so a crash cannot split it, and a card names the old path (11.3 g). `saveReview` writes only a `.review.json` directly in the folder the review belongs in and holding no other chapter's review; any other path it is handed gets a new entry in the right folder instead.

**The reviews folder always resolves.** When Settings names no folder, reviews go to `<userData>/reviews`, created on demand (`resolveReviewsFolder` in `src/main/reviews.ts`). No review operation ever fails with "choose a reviews folder first": a generated review costs real money and minutes, and losing one because Settings was incomplete is the worst outcome the app can produce. Settings shows the folder actually in use, marks it as the default when it is, and offers Change and Show in folder.

**Two save points.** A review is written immediately after Claude answers, and again, debounced by 700 ms, after every decision. Both write through `reviews:save`; passing the known path overwrites that history entry rather than starting a new one. Each review has its own queue (`createKeyedWriter` in `src/renderer/state/persist.ts`, used by `reviewPersistence.ts`, `apply.1`): moving to another chapter or another History entry never cancels a write still waiting, one write per review is in flight at a time and the last one written is the newest, and opening a chapter, or a review from History or the selector, first queues failed writes again and then flushes what is waiting, so it never reads a review file that is behind the screen; a review whose write still fails does not open (above, `apply.25` review). The status bar shows "Decisions kept HH:MM" (local time, 24-hour clock) after each write of the review on screen, and only for that review: the time is stored with the file it was written to and shown while that file is the one open (`reviewKeptAt`), so a chapter whose review has not been written yet, or another review, shows no time. The tooltip is "Your decisions are kept automatically in the review. The chapter file changes only when you press Save to chapter." (`keptPhrase`, `KEPT_TOOLTIP`, `apply.4`; it said "Review saved", which read as the chapter). A failure raises a notification card once per distinct message rather than once per keystroke, and the review that failed is kept until a later write of it succeeds, so closing the window asks first and tries it again (`apply.9`, 7.7), as every open does (`apply.25` review). The card stays after a later write works, until its X is clicked.

**Writing the chapter is separate.** The toolbar button is called **Save to chapter** because it runs the only action in the app that changes the manuscript file, which Ctrl+S and the Save in the review dialogs and the leave and close prompts run too: it composes the page's decisions, copies the version it replaces into the backups (6.5) and writes atomically (6.3). Review json persistence needs no button, and nothing writes the chapter by itself. The button counts what the chapter file does not have yet (`unsavedDecisionCount`): "Save 3 changes to chapter", "Save 1 change to chapter", plain "Save to chapter" when the file already reads like the page; a dot in `--unsaved` before the chapter name and "3 not saved to chapter" in the status bar say the same (`saveButtonState`, `unsavedPhrase`, `apply.4`). So does the button's colour since `polish.9` (C.103): it is a primary button, in the turquoise, only while there are changes to write or a save of them is under way, and with nothing to save an ordinary one (`SaveButtonState.primary`, which goes with the dot outside a save; "Saving…" keeps it to the save's end, after the chapter file is written and the count is already 0). The chapter list puts the same dot, with the same tooltip, before every chapter whose current review holds decisions its file does not (`ReviewSummary.unsavedCount`), and before the open chapter while the review on screen does, so the dot outlasts leaving the chapter and a restart (`chapterListMarks` in `src/shared/ui/chapterList.ts`, `apply.5`). It goes by the review the chapter opens with, the one last on screen (`apply.26`), and so do Save, the status bar and the leave and close questions: changes left in another review of the chapter, which the author moved away from without a question, are not marked by the dot but counted on that review's entry in the review selector ("2 not saved to chapter", as last written; section 7). The list's marks are read (`reviews:index`) whenever the file list is (at start, after Save to chapter or a new review, when chapters appear or go) and also each time a chapter opens, after the reviews waiting to be written are on disk and before the new chapter shows, so the chapter just left is marked from its review as written; only the newest answer is kept. History counts the same way (`historyCounts` in `src/shared/ui/history.ts`, `apply.5`): the row of the review on screen, the one it highlights, takes its pending badge from the page, as the status bar does, and every other row its count as last written. History is read when a chapter opens, after Save to chapter and after a new review, and also when a History entry opens, after the reviews waiting to be written are on disk, so the row of the review just left keeps the count it showed on screen. There is no other unsaved flag: `store.dirty`, which also counted a decision made and turned back, is gone.

### 6.5 Backups

Before Save to chapter replaces a chapter file, the bytes it replaces are copied into the app's data folder (`apply.10`, 11.3 h, Appendix D question 10). The author may not use git, and the data folder is never synced or indexed. `writeChapter` in `src/main/files.ts` runs the copy as its `beforeReplace` hook, which main fills from `chapterBackupHooks` in `src/main/backups.ts`, after the file has been read and found to be the one the review is based on, and only when the save changes bytes: a save that would write what is already there writes and backs up nothing (6.3 step 3). **No backup, no save:** if the copy cannot be made, nothing is written and the card says "Could not back up the chapter before saving, so nothing was written:" and why, in plain words (no space left, a folder that cannot be written, and so on). After the copy the file is read once more, and if it changed meanwhile (Obsidian or a sync wrote it during the copy) the save stops as `stale` and rebases, as in 6.3, so bytes that are not in a backup are never replaced.

- **Where.** `<userData>/backups/<chapter slug>-<first 8 hex of sha256(pathKey)>/`, one folder per chapter file: the slug is the one the reviews folder uses (6.4), and the hash of the chapter's path key keeps two chapters with the same file name in different folders apart. A `chapter.json` holding `{sourcePath}` is written the first time and never replaced, so a person restoring by hand can tell which file a folder belongs to.
- **Never in the vault.** The backups root must lie outside the manuscript folder and outside the folder of the chapter being saved (`assertOutside`). That fails only when the manuscript folder contains the app's data folder, or a development userData override points into the vault, and the save is then refused with that reason, so no backup can be listed as a chapter, indexed by Obsidian or synced.
- **Names.** The local time of the save, then the chapter's file name: `2026-10-14 16.04.33 Chapter 12.md`, which opens in any editor as the chapter it copies and sorts by time. A second backup in the same second gets `-2` after the time, then `-3`. Each file is created exclusively, so no backup is ever overwritten, and holds the old bytes exactly: BOM, line endings and all. A copy that fails part way is removed. The names are made and read by `formatLocalStamp`, `backupFileName` and `parseBackupFileName` in `src/shared/backups.ts`.
- **Duplicates.** When the newest backup already holds exactly the bytes being replaced, as when the author put the old text back in Obsidian and saved again, no copy is added and that one stands for the save.
- **What is kept.** After every write, `afterWrite` prunes that chapter's folder: the newest 20 backups stay, and so does the oldest backup of each local calendar day from today back through the 29 days before; the rest are deleted (`backupsToPrune`). A name that is not a backup's, `chapter.json` and anything the author put there included, is never deleted. Pruning is best effort: the chapter is already written by then, so a failure is logged (`backups.prune-failed`) and the save stands.
- **The answer.** `SaveResponse.backup` gives the backup's `name` and whether this save made it (`created`), for the save card and Settings to point at (`apply.11`, which also records restoring a backup by hand). The log gets a line when a backup fails (`backups.failed`) or a prune does, and never a backup's contents (11.3 m).
- **Finding them** (`apply.11`). While a chapter is open, the toolbar's Actions menu holds **Show backups** as its last item (`polish.7`; from `apply.11` it was in a footer under the side panel's two regions), which opens that chapter's backup folder in File Explorer with its newest backup selected. The "Saved to the chapter file." card carries the same button whenever the answer names a backup, for the chapter it saved, whose newest backup is the one that save made or the one that stood for it (a later save of the same chapter replaces the card). Both send `shell:reveal` `backups` with the chapter's `sourcePath`, never a folder: main works the folder out itself (`chapterBackups` in `src/main/backups.ts`, through `backupFolderFor`), refuses a path that is not absolute and any folder that is not directly under the backups root (`assertChapterBackupFolder`), and answers `not-found` while there is no folder for the chapter's path. That is so until a Save to chapter first changes the file at that path, and also after the chapter was renamed or moved in Obsidian, or the whole vault was moved: the folder is named by the path, so the chapter gets a new one, and unlike its reviews (6.4, "Reviews follow their chapter") its backups do not follow it. Those made before stay in the old path's folder, whose `chapter.json` names the old path; after a vault move its name differs from the new one only in the hash. The page shows `not-found` as an information card, "No backups of Chapter 03 at this path yet. Save to chapter makes one each time it changes the file. If the chapter or its folder was renamed or moved, its earlier backups are in another folder, named after its old file name." (`noBackupsYet`), with **Show all backups** (`reveal-all-backups`), which selects the backups root as Settings does; it opens no other window. The card's key is `SHOW_BACKUPS_CARD`. A Show backups that works closes it, and so does a Save to chapter whose answer names a backup, made or standing for that save (the "reloaded while saving" card included, and whichever chapter the card named), so the card never stays above "Saved to the chapter file." saying there are none; a save that writes nothing or is refused leaves it. A folder whose backups were deleted by hand opens with nothing selected. Settings has a **Backups** row: the backups root (`EffectivePaths.backupsFolder`), Show in folder, which selects it in the app's data folder as the other rows do, and the note "Copies of your chapters as they were before each Save to chapter."; the note it had until `polish.4`, "Before every Save to chapter, the version it replaces is copied here. The last 20 saves and the first save of each day for 30 days are kept. Backups stay on this computer.", is now the tooltip of the row's (?), at the right end of the row (section 7). The words are in `src/shared/ui/backups.ts` and `src/shared/ui/settingsDialog.ts`.
- **Restoring by hand.** The app has no restore command. A backup is the chapter file as it was, byte for byte, so it opens in Notepad or any text editor; Obsidian opens only files inside a vault, so it cannot open a backup where it is. Do not drag a backup into Obsidian: that copies it into the vault, where a backup must never be (see "Never in the vault"), listed as a chapter, indexed and synced. Each chapter's backup folder holds a `chapter.json` naming the file its backups were made from, which tells apart two chapters of the same name, and a renamed or moved chapter's folder from its new one. To take back a passage, open the backup and copy the words into the chapter in Obsidian. To take back the whole chapter, first copy the chapter as it is now somewhere outside the vault, because the version on disk goes into a backup only when the next Save to chapter replaces it; then paste the backup's whole text over the chapter's in Obsidian, or replace the chapter file with a copy of the backup given the chapter's file name. A copy left in the manuscript folder under a backup's name is listed as a chapter and indexed by Obsidian. The app sees the changed file and moves the open review onto it (6.2), as for any change made in Obsidian, so suggestions the restored text no longer has go to Unanchored; the next Save to chapter backs up the restored text like any other.

### 6.6 Vault compatibility

What the app does to live inside an Obsidian vault, as M8 left it (`files.1` to `files.11`, `files.20` to `files.22`; written by `files.12`). It gathers 11.3 (g), (k) and (l) and the save guards in one place; the rules themselves stay where they are cited, and this section changes none of them. The README's "Working in an Obsidian vault" follows it, checked against the build by `opensource.11`, which also reworded the README's two sentences resting on what Obsidian does, marked unverified below, so that it claims only what the app does. Under Appendix D's friend defaults the app handles Obsidian syntax by leaving it alone: it shows it as typed and keeps the reviewer's suggestions off it, and Dataview and Templater get nothing of their own.

- **What is a chapter** (6.1). Every `.md` and `.txt` file under the manuscript folder, read, saved and reviewed alike. Left out of the list: every file and folder whose name starts with a dot (`.obsidian`, `.trash`, `.git`, Save's temp files), folders named exactly `node_modules`, `out` or `dist`, the reviews folder when it lies inside, the guidelines file in use, Excalidraw drawings (`*.excalidraw.md`), and symbolic links and junctions, whether to a file or a folder, which the walk does not follow (6.1): a chapter linked into the folder from elsewhere is not a chapter, so the chapters themselves must be in it. Attachments (images, PDFs, canvases and the like) are never listed, read or touched. A subfolder that cannot be read is skipped; the manuscript folder itself that cannot be read says so, with Try again (`apply.25`). One chapter per file: a file of several chapters is reviewed whole (`files.14` cut), with the long-chapter note from 12,000 words and the warning from 40,000 (`reviewSizeAdvice`, 5.5, `files.10`).
- **What the page shows** (section 7). The text exactly as typed, Markdown and Obsidian syntax as characters, nothing rendered or styled. The frontmatter is a grey block above the first paragraph: never numbered, sent, suggested on or edited in the app. The first body paragraph starts at `bodyStart`, past the line break that closes the frontmatter (4.1, `files.22`).
- **Reading a file (11.3 l, `files.3`).** UTF-8 only, a BOM allowed, at most 4 MiB (`decodeText`, `classifyBytes`, `encodingProblem`). UTF-16, an older single-byte encoding and UTF-8 with a few damaged characters are each refused in words that say what the file most likely is and how to fix it, which differs: re-save as UTF-8 in Notepad (VS Code elsewhere) for the first two, while for damaged characters the message gives the line of the first, says to retype them in Obsidian and save there, and warns against re-saving in Notepad, which would garble every accented letter. A file that looks binary is refused as not a text file, with no fix. Each message ends "The app has not changed the file."; a larger file is told to split. Line endings, the BOM and the final line break are recorded and the text kept LF (4.6). Save reads through the same path, so a file changed to another encoding while open is refused, not overwritten.
- **What the reviewer is sent** (5.2, 5.4, `files.8`). The body as numbered paragraphs, never the frontmatter, under the file name without folder or extension. A paragraph that holds nothing but `%%` or HTML comments, code or `$$` maths, white space aside, is sent as its number and "(author's note or code, hidden; skip it)", so its words never leave the computer; a comment beside prose is sent with the prose (C.75). The system prompt carries the Obsidian rule whatever the guidelines file says: leave links, embeds, tags, block IDs, footnote and callout markers, comments, code, maths, web addresses and HTML as written, correct the words a reader sees (an alias, a link's text, a footnote's words, a callout's title and body), and read angle-bracket dialogue as prose.
- **What a suggestion may change (11.3 k, `files.6`, `files.7`, `files.20`; C.72 to C.74).** `syntaxSpans` finds 17 kinds (`SYNTAX_KINDS`); some are protected whole (frontmatter, code, comments, maths, embeds, images, block IDs, tags, web addresses, HTML tags, horizontal rules, `[[target]]` without an alias), others by their markers only, so their words stay open (`[[target|` and `]]` around an alias, `[` and `](url)` around a link's text, footnote marks and the `^[` and `]` of an inline footnote, a callout's `[!type]`, the `>` of a quote and the `#` of a heading). A model's suggestion, from either provider, still pending and on the page, is kept out of the text when it lies before `bodyStart`, crosses or changes a paragraph break, overlaps a protected span, holds one of `[ ] % $ ^ # < > | ~`, a backtick or a line break (`MARKUP_CHARS`), changes the paragraph's syntax (`syntaxSignature`), or the whole chapter's where the paragraph reads differently inside it (a code block, comment or maths span crossing it, or an unclosed code fence or `<!--` before it), or starts exactly where the suggestion before it on the line ends (`combined`). It goes under Unanchored with the model's reason and "Kept out of the text: it would change Obsidian syntax (<label>). Make this change in Obsidian or with the paragraph pen if you want it." (`keptOutNote`). The screen runs when a review is made, when it is loaded, which screens reviews made before the guard, and at every rebase, which also places no hunk of any source before `bodyStart` (4.3 steps 7 to 9, 4.5). Not screened: the author's own edits (the paragraph pen, the suggestion editor), Submit manual review's suggestions, which are the corrected copy's own words, and a suggestion once accepted or dismissed, which is the author's (C.74). Not protected as spans: emphasis, bold, strikethrough and highlight markers, indented code, inline `$maths$`, tables and lists; `*`, `_`, `=` and `-` are not markup characters, so a suggestion may add or take away emphasis or a highlight, which the page shows before it is accepted, while one that adds `~`, `$` or `|` is still kept out. The guard's known cost is a few fair fixes kept out, such as a stray `#word` or "per cent" made `%` (11.5).
- **Writing a file: the save guards** (CLAUDE.md rule 1; 6.1, 6.3, 6.5, 11.3 h). Nothing autosaves: only `saveChapter`, reached from Save to chapter, Ctrl+S and the Save in the review dialogs and the leave and close prompts, writes a chapter. Main writes only a `.md` or `.txt` file that is not the guidelines file and lies in the manuscript folder or was opened from it in this run (`assertSavableChapter`, `files.2`). `writeChapter` reads the file and writes nothing when its hash is not the review's base: the page rebases onto the file as it is, says what moved and tries once more, and a second change stops the save ("The chapter keeps changing on disk. Close it in Obsidian and save again."), as merge markers that the change brought do (C.78). Bytes equal to the file's are not written, so the file keeps its modified time and a sync tool sees nothing. Otherwise the bytes being replaced are copied to `<userData>/backups`, never into the vault (`assertOutside`), and when the copy fails nothing is written; the file is read once more, then written to `.<name>.<12 hex>.tmp` beside it, flushed, and renamed over it, a rename refused by a scanner, OneDrive or Obsidian being tried again for about a second and a half with the file hashed before each try (`files.4`). What a save keeps: every character outside the decided suggestions, the frontmatter among them, the line endings, the BOM and the final line break (4.6; a file that mixes CRLF with LF is written all CRLF). What it does not keep: the file's creation time (File Explorer's "Date created").
