Checked from inside a Claude Code session: the launcher printed and removed the session's variables, the app reported `not-signed-in` with `--claude-config-empty`, and that folder's new `.claude.json` held no `oauthAccount`.

### C.44 Comments follow their paragraphs through a save (`files.21`, 2026-10-15)

A comment knows its paragraph only by number. `markSaved` folded the decisions into a new base and moved every hunk's offsets, but left comment numbers and hunk labels as they were. A save that split, joined or deleted a paragraph therefore shifted every later comment. The author split 42-43 with the pen, and his comments marked 63 and 77 ended up quoting text in 64 and 78.

`remapAfterCommit` in `src/shared/review.ts` maps each old paragraph's span through the committed hunks. A comment follows its paragraph; when the paragraph was split, it goes with the part that holds its quote; when the quote moved elsewhere, it goes to the nearest occurrence by position. Hunk labels are recomputed from their new offsets.

`repairCommentAnchors`, run by `upgradeLoadedReview` on every load, mends reviews saved before the fix: a comment whose quote is missing from its paragraph moves to the nearest paragraph that holds it. One whose quote is found nowhere stays put, and an untouched review keeps its identity.

Checked with unit tests (split, joins, deletes, a fast-check property over random splits and joins, the repair) and in a dev window: splitting paragraph 1 of samples Chapter 01 with the pen and saving moved its paragraph-10 comment to 11, where its quote now sits.

### C.45 Reviews are bound to their source path and follow moved or renamed chapters (`files.1`, 2026-10-15)

Reviews were filed by a slug of the chapter's file name and the newest file in the folder was taken as the chapter's review. Two chapters with the same name in different folders therefore shared one review, and a Save in one could write the other's accepted changes into it. A renamed chapter lost its review entirely.

A review now belongs to the file its `sourcePath` names, compared with `samePath`. `listReviews`, `loadLatestReview` and `reviewIndex` (now keyed by the chapter paths main lists, with summaries cached by modification time and size) only see belonging reviews. The current review is the one with the latest `decidedAt ?? createdAt`; `decidedAt` is set by the store on every decision, comment status change and save, and never by opening a review. (Since `apply.26`, C.57, a chapter opens with the review last on screen, recorded beside the reviews; this rule decides only while nothing is recorded.) `saveReview` writes an explicit path only when it is a `.review.json` directly in the right folder and holds no other chapter's review; anything else gets a new entry, `<stamp>-2.review.json` when the stamp is taken.

When nothing belongs to a chapter that opens, `findAdoptable` looks for a chapter path whose file is gone and whose reviews plainly are this chapter's: at least two matching trailing segments in the same folder (a moved vault), or a review of exactly the chapter's current text, 500 characters or more (a rename or move in Obsidian). A hash match outranks a path match, more segments outrank fewer, and two candidates equal on both adopt nothing; the plan's "then newest" was dropped, since newest cannot tell two different chapters apart. `adoptReviews` rewrites the whole history into the new folder with the new `sourcePath`, removing each old file after its copy is written, through a journal (`.adoption.json`) that the next store call completes after a crash. App.tsx re-homes every review it opens to the exact path it opened, shows "Reopened the review made when this chapter was at <old path>", and the unlink and missing-chapter messages say how to get the review back.

Checked by `test/main/reviews.test.ts` (33 cases, including a synthetic 0.1.0 review in `test/fixtures/review-0.1.0.json` that loads unchanged, saves back with only the decided fields changed and rebases keeping every field) and store tests for `decidedAt`. In a `dev:clean` window with A/ and B/ copies of samples Chapter 01: an accepted manual change in A left B opening clean; an accepted change saved in B changed only B's `Get-FileHash` (A stayed `950A07DB…`); renaming B in place while open showed the new unlink card, and reopening it from the list brought its review back, moved to `chapter-01-the-deluge`, with A's review left where it was.

### C.46 The launch check reads its answers properly (`setup.4`, 2026-10-15)

C.42 had already taken the model requests out of the launch check. What remained was how it read the answers: `looksLikeAuth` called any message that mentioned "auth" a sign-in problem ("the author" included), and the check said ready whenever `initialize` answered.

`src/main/providers/claudeRuntime.ts` now runs `--version`, `auth status --json` and the `initialize` handshake side by side and hands the answers to `classifyClaude` (`setup.2`). `auth status` is believed when it says signed out; the account decides what Claude Code signs in with; a handshake that failed for a sign-in reason wins; one that timed out falls back on `auth status`. The handshake (`claudeHandshake.ts`) gets 60 s on the first check and 20 s after, and its answer serves the model list for ten minutes. `looksLikeAuth` is gone: failures go through `classifyClaudeFailure`. `claudeDiagnostics` lists what was found and how it signs in, never the email or organisation. `test/shared/policy.test.ts` keeps `child_process` in `claudeBinary.ts` alone and Claude Code's credential file, `setup-token` and `logout` out of the source.

Checked in `dev:clean` windows against the author's Claude Code 2.1.266: plain, ready (subscription), a re-check answering in about 1 s; `--claude-config-empty`, not signed in; with `--api-key-dummy` added, ready (API key).

### C.47 Error results arrive as success with is_error (`setup.5`, 2026-10-15)

Claude Code reports some failures as a `result` whose subtype says `success` while `is_error` is true; signed out, it sends `{subtype: 'success', is_error: true, result: 'Not logged in · Please run /login'}`. The old mapping took the subtype at its word on one path, and `mapSubtype` and `mapAssistantError` each worded failures their own way.

`src/main/providers/claudeResult.ts` now decides: a refusal first, then both shapes through `classifyClaudeFailure` (`setup.2`), with Claude Code's own words kept in `detail`; a run with no result at all goes through the same classifier on its stderr. `mapSubtype` and `mapAssistantError` are gone, and `mapThrown` went with the SDK at `cli.1`. Start-up failure reasons (`cli_version_too_old` and the rest) are recognised anywhere in a result: Claude Code 2.1.266 does not send them, and the field a later version uses is not documented. In the renderer, `useAi` keeps the last failure through `nextLastFailure`, the status bar reads it, and a review that fails because Claude Code is missing, too old, signed out or its sign-in ended re-checks and opens Setup.

Checked by `test/main/claudeResult.test.ts`, and in a `dev:clean` window with `--claude-config-empty`: `ai:review` returned `claude-not-signed-in` with "Not logged in · Please run /login" as its detail.

### C.48 The scrollers have opaque backgrounds (LCD text while scrolling) (`theme.1`, 2026-10-16)

The author saw text turn heavier while scrolling, then sharpen (11.0, idea 18). Four of the elements that scroll had no background of their own: `.center` (the manuscript), `.body--single` (which holds the Setup screen), `.setup` and `.rows` (the suggestions list). At this machine's 96 DPI, Chromium gives a scroller a composited layer of its own, with LCD (ClearType) text on it, only when it can tell the scroller is opaque.

Measured on 2026-10-14 with the project's Electron 44.3.0 on a probe page (200 paragraphs of 17 px Georgia, 25 DevTools wheel steps of 400 px, a trace with `disabled-by-default-cc.debug`): a transparent scroller got no layer of its own and the window was re-rasterised as it moved, 153 RasterTask events; with `background: #f7f5f1` it got an `OverflowScrolling` layer whose contents layer had `contents_opaque=true` and `lcd_text_disallowed_reason: none`, and the same scroll took 41 RasterTask events.

Every scroller now has an opaque background in a colour token: `--bg` on `.center`, `.body--single` and `.setup`, and `--panel` on the side panel's scrollers after `panel.1` (C.49): `.rows`, `.side__lower` and `.side__body`, and since `ui.5` `.side__focus-body`, the focused suggestion's box. The colours equal what showed through before. `test/renderer/scrollers.test.ts` fails when a rule that scrolls has no `var(--…)` background (since `theme.4`, these checks are in `test/renderer/themeCss.test.ts`), and since the `theme.9` review also when that token is not a colour with alpha 1 in both themes, as the translucent `--hover-overlay` is not. `state/scroll.ts` does not round its scroll positions, because Chromium already snaps `scrollTop`.

Measured again in the app on 2026-10-16: a `dev:clean` window, viewport 1424x901 at 100%, a review with 115 suggestions and 15 comments, `LayerTree.compositingReasons`, then 25 wheel steps of 400 px over each scroller traced with `['cc', 'disabled-by-default-cc.debug']` after `Page.bringToFront`.

- **Before.** `.center` had no `OverflowScrolling` layer, only one promoted for `Overlap`, which was repainted as it scrolled: 192 RasterTask events, and its LCD reason switched between `none` (45 snapshots) and `background-color-not-opaque` (50). That switch between two kinds of antialiasing is a likely cause of what the author saw. The suggestions list sat on an `Overlap` layer with `background-color-not-opaque` throughout, so its text was always greyscale.
- **After.** `.center` has an `OverflowScrolling` layer and a contents layer with `contents_opaque=true` and `none` in all 29 snapshots; the same scroll took 31 RasterTask events. The list region and the details region each have their own `OverflowScrolling` layer, contents opaque, `none` throughout, and 0 to 2 RasterTask events. At 200%, where the short panel scrolls as one, `.side__body` has the same: an `OverflowScrolling` layer, contents opaque, `none` in all 32 snapshots. The list's text is now LCD at rest as well.

Floating cards over a scroller (the notification cards, the lock card, the tooltip and the edit popover) get layers of their own with `background-color-not-opaque`, so their text is greyscale-antialiased. That was seen on the probe page on 2026-10-14 and again for a notification card in the app on 2026-10-16 (the `.notes` layer), and is accepted.

Whether the effect the author saw is gone is for his eyes: in sitting C (`theme.10` b) he scrolls with `.center`'s background set to `transparent` in DevTools and back, and the result (gone, reduced or unchanged) is recorded here.

Measured again on 2026-10-22 with the app's own scrollbar (`polish.2`, C.106), which Chromium paints as a layer of its own beside the scroller's: a quiet `dev:clean --no-claude-code` window at the bottom of the stack, the page 1424x901, Chapter 01 with 37 suggestions and 12 comments and 30 filler chapters so the list scrolls, the same `LayerTree` read and 25 scrolls of 400 px over each scroller traced with `['cc', 'disabled-by-default-cc.debug']`, without `Page.bringToFront`. Before the change, with the browser's bar, in light at 100%: `.center`, `.rows` and `.side__lower` each had an `OverflowScrolling` layer whose contents layer was opaque with `lcd_text_disallowed_reason: none` in every snapshot. After it, the same in light and dark at 100% and in dark at 150% (`.center` 3 to 8 RasterTask events, the side panel's regions 2 to 6), and `.files`, the chapter list, the same once it scrolls; the layers are 1 px narrower at 100%, the bar's 16 px against 15. The new layers in the trace are the bars', all `no-text`.

### C.49 The side panel scrolls in two regions, or as one in a short window (`panel.1`, 2026-10-16)

The side panel scrolled as a whole and the suggestions list inside it scrolled too (`max-height: 42vh`), so two scrollbars sat side by side, and stepping through a long list moved the focused suggestion's details off screen.

`.side` no longer scrolls: it is `overflow: clip`, so script cannot scroll it either, and `min-height: 0`, which keeps its grid row to the window, as `clip` does not make it a scroll container. Inside it, `.side__body` is a flex column with two regions that each scroll. The list (`.side__list`) keeps its heading pinned and takes what it needs, up to 55% of the height; `.side__lower` below it holds the details, comments, resolved comments, Unanchored and History.

**Following the focus.** When the focus moves, by key or by click, `followFocus` in `state/scroll.ts` keeps the suggestion in view with the app's own timing, instead of `scrollIntoView`, which also scrolls ancestors that are not meant to scroll.

- **The row** is scrolled with `if-needed` (`shared/ui/scroll.ts`): a row already wholly in view stays where it is, and one partly or wholly out of view comes in with a 24 px margin, so j and k still show a row of context. As first landed it used `nearest`, which also moves a row that is in view but within 24 px of an edge: a click on the first or last visible row slid the list by about a row, and a click on that row's tick then accepted its neighbour.
- **The details.** With two regions, the Focused suggestion section is brought back into `.side__lower` the same way, so the details return when the author has scrolled that region down to read comments or History and then moves on; as first landed they stayed off screen. With one scroller only the row is followed: `.side__body` then holds both, and a second scroll would cancel the first. Since `ui.5` the details are a box of fixed height above the list, which no scroll of a region takes away, so only the row is followed and `followFocus` takes the row alone (section 7, The focused suggestion).
- **Tall details.** A section taller than its region keeps its top in view, so a long suggestion's reason and Edit button can sit below the fold until the region is scrolled (until `ui.5`, whose box scrolls a long reason inside itself, under the pencil). For a box that fits the view only without the 24 px margins, `nearest` and `if-needed` shrink them, so a section a few pixels shorter than its region shows whole.
- **Quick keys.** Whether a box needs a scroll is judged where a scroll in flight will land (`retarget`), not where it is mid-way, so a row in view now that the landing would carry away still gets its scroll.

**Short windows.** The panel scrolls as one when the window is less than 540 CSS pixels high inside: `@media (height < 540px)` makes `.side__body` the one scroller and lets the list run to its full length. Zoom changes that height; a chapter does not. The first version used a container query on the panel's own height, below 420 px (the plan said about 480), and that height changes from chapter to chapter: the filter chips take one row for 3 categories, two for 7 and three for 13 (36, 65 and 94 px in a 900x600 window at 100%), and the status bar takes two rows (51 px instead of 32) once it shows the save time, provider and model, effort, cost and a rate-limit notice. So the layout switched between chapters in the same window: panels of 451, 422 and 393 px in a 900x600 window at 100% (two regions, two, one), and 442, 413 and 384 px in a 1600x1000 window at 175% (two, one, one). The figures 420 was chosen from, 461 and 490 px at 900x600 and 312 to 342 px at 1440x940 and 200%, came from viewports of those sizes set with `Emulation.setDeviceMetricsOverride`, not from windows: the window frame takes 16 by 39 px here, so a 900x600 window, the smallest the app allows, is 884x561 inside. From the `polish.12` review to `polish.17` one container query read the panel's width, which the column or the drawer sets and no chapter changes, to leave the suggestion rows' status word out of a narrow panel (C.108), and the colour guard allowed it while failing a container on a height; it went with the word, and the guard fails any container again.

**The split** (`ui.6`, 2026-10-18). With two regions, a handle between them moves the line between them, and draws the line the region below's top border drew (section 7, The split; C.59). The one scroller hides it, draws the list at its full length whatever the setting, and gives the region below its border again. With two regions too short for it to move an arrow step, the handle is drawn as that line and is no control (C.59).

Measured on 2026-10-16 in `dev:clean` windows sized from outside with `SetWindowPos` (outer sizes; `GetClientRect` confirmed the inside), on Chapter 02 (3 categories), a long sample (7) and Chapter 01 with its suggestions spread over all 13, each with and without the status bar's extra items:

- **900x600** (561 px inside): two regions at 100%, panel 374 to 451 px; one scroller from 110% (510 px).
- **1440x940**, the default (901 px): two regions up to 150% (601 px; panel 445 to 493 px); one scroller at 175% (515 px; 330 to 407) and 200% (450 px; 224 to 322).
- **1280x800** (761 px): two regions at 125% (609 px), one scroller at 150% (507 px).
- **1600x1000 at 175%** (549 px): two regions, panel 364 to 442 px. 1600x985 (540 px) still has two, 1600x983 (539 px) one.

Every chapter got the same layout in each of these. 540 sits 21 px below the smallest window at 100% and 25 px above the default window at 175%. The smallest two-region panel measured was 356 px (13 categories and a two-row status bar, 540 px inside); in the smallest window at 100% it is 374 px, a list region of 206 px (about eight rows) and a details region of 168 px. The Focused suggestion section is 132 px with a one-line reason and 183 px with a three-line one, so in that window the latter needs a short scroll of its region to show the Edit button.

Checked first in a `dev:clean` window at 900x600 and 1440x940 viewports, at 100% and 200%, with 3 and 115 suggestions and 0 and 15 comments: 16 states, each stepped 45 rows down with j and 20 back with k where the list was long enough, with the panel measured every 5 steps and screenshots after opening, after j and after k, all looked at. No scroller was ever inside another or beside it, and the focused row was in view at every check. Those runs started with the details region at its top, so they did not catch the details staying off screen once it was scrolled.

Checked again after the review fixes, in a window sized as above, on the long sample (169 suggestions, 15 comments). At 1440x940 and 900x600 at 100%, 1600x985 at 175%, 1440x940 at 200% and 900x600 at 110%, the lower region was wheeled 1200 px down, then 45 j and 20 k were pressed 70 ms apart (25 ms apart as well at the first two sizes), with a second wheel before the k: at every fifth key the focused row was wholly in view and, with two regions, the details section was back in view, the region at 0 after the first j. Clicking the first and then the last wholly visible row, at 1440x940 and 900x600 at 100% (list at 88 px) and 1440x940 at 200% (panel at 300 px), left the scroll position unchanged with the clicked row still under the pointer, and at 1440x940 a click on the row's tick accepted that row; before the fix the first click moved the list from 88 to 64 px. A suggestion of 170 characters with a long reason gave a 376 px section in a 190 px region: heading and top in view, the rest below the fold. Screenshots of each chapter at 900x600 and 100% and at 1600x1000 and 175% were looked at.

### C.50 The theme rides on nativeTheme, not on a data attribute (`theme.5`, 2026-10-16)

A web page usually switches themes with a `data-theme` attribute on `<html>`, set by script, and the dark colours under `[data-theme='dark']`. The app does not. The main process sets Electron's `nativeTheme.themeSource` to the Appearance setting (`system`, `light` or `dark`; `src/main/theme.ts`), and `app.css` keeps its dark tokens inside `@media (prefers-color-scheme: dark)`. That one setting drives the three things that have to agree:

- **The page.** `themeSource` decides what `prefers-color-scheme` reports in the renderer, so the stylesheet picks its block with no script, before React has run. Each block's `color-scheme`, and `<meta name="color-scheme" content="light dark">` before the stylesheet loads, give select lists and form fields the same theme, and gave the scrollbars theirs until `polish.2` drew the app's own from the tokens (C.106).
- **The window.** `nativeTheme.shouldUseDarkColors` follows `themeSource`, and the computer's mode under `system`, so `currentWindowBackground()` hands `createWindow` the matching `--bg` (`WINDOW_BACKGROUND`, which a test pins to both blocks), and `installTheme` repaints every window when Windows switches mode.
- **The title bar.** On Windows, Electron sets the window's `DWMWA_USE_IMMERSIVE_DARK_MODE` attribute from the same source, so the frame matches with no code of the app's own.

Main sets `themeSource` from settings before the window exists, and the window stays hidden until its first paint (C.36), so no frame shows in the wrong theme. A data attribute could only be set once the page's script ran: until then the page would follow the computer, and the window background and title bar would each need handling of their own. A changed setting applies at once: `settings:set` calls `applyTheme`, which does nothing when that theme is already in effect.

Checked on 2026-10-16 in a `dev:clean` window on a scratch userData with `"theme": "dark"`: `prefers-color-scheme: dark` matched, the body was `rgb(28, 26, 23)`, and `DwmGetWindowAttribute(hwnd, 20)` on the app's window returned 1. After `settings:set {theme: 'light'}` the media query no longer matched, the body was `rgb(247, 245, 241)` and the attribute 0; `system` gave the same with Windows in light mode, and `dark` gave 1 again. The Windows setting was read, never changed.

### C.51 A rewritten saved suggestion is a change against the saved words (`apply.22`, 2026-10-16)

7.4 said only that rewriting a suggestion updates `replacement`. That is right until the suggestion has been saved into the chapter. After a save the base holds the replacement (`baseSide: 'replacement'`), and compose copies the base whenever the side a hunk wants is the side the base holds, so new replacement words reached the page, the side panel and the tooltip but never the file: `unsavedDecisionCount` stayed 0, and Save to chapter said "Saved to the chapter file." and left the old words in place. The other places that change words were already safe: a paragraph edit makes manual hunks over the base, and a rebase moves a hunk onto the side it finds.

A hunk has two texts, and the base must hold one of them, so a saved suggestion cannot keep the model's original, show the saved words and offer new ones all at once. `editSuggestion` now takes the base text and keeps what is in the file: the saved words become `original` and the base side, and the new words the replacement. The model's first words are given up. The file no longer holds them, the backup made before the save that replaced them does (6.5), and the alternative, a third text on every hunk that compose, rebase and commit would all have to carry, was more machinery than an undo to words already overwritten is worth. "Accept now" unticked used to send a saved suggestion back to pending with its model original, so Save would have put that original back; now the rewrite waits as a pending suggestion against the saved words, the page reads as the file, and Save writes nothing for it. A saved change the author had turned back (pending or dismissed, so that Save would restore the original) is treated the same way, so the page shows the saved words again: the one case where a rewrite unticked changes what the page reads.

Words that read exactly as the file does change nothing, so both sides become the file's words and `baseSide` follows the decision at that moment. That alone was not enough: the next ordinary decision moved `desiredSide` off `baseSide` again, and a hunk reading "begun → begun" counted as one unsaved change while compose still gave the base, so a click on the word or a dismiss brought "Save 1 change to chapter", a leave prompt and a History count, and Save answered "The chapter already matches the page." (the review of `apply.22`). So a hunk whose two sides are the same never counts as unsaved, whatever its decision (`changesBase`), and compose, commit and the page's live layout copy the base for it (`decidedText`), which keeps compose and the count in step even if such a hunk drifts after a fuzzy rebase: rewriting a saved suggestion and then back to the saved words leaves nothing to save, and so does whatever the author decides on it afterwards; a suggestion never saved but rewritten to the file's own words no longer counts as one unsaved change that would write nothing. Such a hunk reads "started → started" in the list, under a grey "was started" ghost on the page. Rewriting a saved change that was turned back to exactly its saved words keeps its `original`, which is still what turning it back restores. A stale hunk has no place in the base and only takes the new words.

### C.52 Deletions and insertions are placed by what surrounds them (`apply.23`, 2026-10-17)

A deletion has no text on one side, and neither has an insertion. `locate` searched only for text, so such a hunk was placed by its other side, and next to an identical word that went wrong both ways (the `apply.3` review). A saved deletion of one word of "the the frayed" (accepted, then Save to chapter, so `baseSide: 'replacement'` and zero width) came back after any change on disk as a suggestion to delete the "the" that remained, or another "the": the words it had deleted were the only text to search for, and C.5 let the disk win on any match. Accepting and saving would have deleted that word too. The other way round, an accepted deletion not saved yet but already made in the file was placed on the "the" that remained, and Save deleted it ("and frayed end"). Both were seen in a `dev:clean` window. Insertions had the same fault: a suggestion to insert "the " was taken as made, and accepted, on whichever "the" in the chapter had the best surroundings, and turning it back would have removed that word.

What `rebase.ts` does now:

- **An empty side is a place.** For a side that holds no text, `placeCandidates` looks for the text that surrounded the hunk in the old file: 48 characters either side together, then 24 and 12, then either side alone at those widths, so an edit right next to the place still leaves one side to find it by. A find inside a word is no find, since deletions and insertions are whole words. Each place is scored like a word, by how much of the 40 characters either side still reads as before, so the place a doubled word was taken out of, whose surroundings agree on both sides (80), outranks its twin, which agrees on one side at most (41 in the sample chapter).
- **The edges of the file count.** Where both texts begin, or end, within the 40 characters and agree all the way, that side agrees in full (`agreeBefore`, `agreeAfter`); where only one of them begins there, it agrees no further. Without this nothing within 40 characters of the start could agree in full, and an accepted insertion at the very start of a chapter went stale on any change.
- **Ties keep the decision.** Where the surroundings agree as well, the side the base holds now comes before distance (C.6 had distance first). Around a doubled word, the words and the place beside them often agree exactly as well, and distance, measured from the old offset, favoured whichever of them text removed above happened to shift towards.
- **The disk wins only plainly.** A candidate on the other side, which flips the decision (C.5), counts only where it plainly is the change made or undone there (`plainlyOnDisk`): a place whose surroundings read as before in full on one side, or for at least 12 characters of whole words on both, a side with less old text than 12 characters saying nothing (a place found only by "before", the last word of the file, recurring further up had 1 and 6 characters and outranked the deletion's own words by one, the `apply.23` review); words whose surroundings read as before on both sides; on one side, unless the words stood right beside a copy of themselves, since a doubled word's twin may then be all that is left of them; or, for a hunk whose own side has words, the only such words in the file, as before. A side counts only where the old file has text on it: the start of the file alone says nothing, so "Well, it rained." added at the top is not taken for a deleted "Well, " put back. When a candidate that is not plain ranks best, the hunk's own side is most likely gone from its place, so the hunk goes stale rather than fall back on a weaker match of its own side. This is the task's "never flip an accepted hunk with `baseSide: 'replacement'` to pending on an `ambiguous` match of `original` (leave it, or make it stale)", applied to every flip in both directions, with stale as the answer; a match its surroundings set apart is not taken as ambiguous, so a deleted word put back where it was still comes back as a suggestion.
- **A place is weighed against copies of the words near it** (`settleCopies`, the `apply.23` review). A place found by the text on one side can sit right beside the hunk's own words, or a word or two from them, and its score on the other side then runs into them or into whatever was typed beside them. The first version counted those letters wherever they happened to match the old text next to the hunk, so an edited neighbour let the place beat the words by a character or two: with "before the the storm" made "after the the storm", a suggested deletion of either "the" was taken as made ("1 decision changed to match the file."), and an accepted one too, so Save never deleted the word; a saved insertion became a suggestion to insert "had" beside the "had" in the file. In random edits of one or two words within eight words of a hunk whose words were left alone, that changed the side of about 1 in 15 deletions and saved insertions. Now every copy of the words within 40 characters of a place is weighed against it on the side the copy is on, counting whole words only (`wordsBefore`, `wordsAfter`: the "e" of "the" agreeing with the "e" of "before" is chance, and so is the space before a word). For a copy right beside the place: from the place, how far the new text reads as the old with the words taken out, against as the old with them in. For a copy further off: how far the text beyond the copy reads as the old text beyond the hunk, against the place's own score on that side. A copy that reads further takes the place away; a place that reads further against every copy stands, and a copy right beside it is the twin of a doubled word, which leaves the pool. A tie right beside the place counts for the place when the words stood twice in a row and stand once there now ("and the the frayed" made "but the frayed"), since the change is made whichever copy went; a tie further off counts for it when a copy right beside it lost; a copy whose own surroundings read further than the place's in all is no tie. Any other tie removes the place and keeps the words, but as no place for Save to write a decision: "river the before" made "night the to before" reads as well with "the" kept as with "the" taken out and "night the to" typed.
- **A place found on one side gives way to plain words.** An empty place the base holds, found by its surroundings on one side only, gives way to the other side's words found plainly: an insertion made by hand, with the word before it changed or another word typed after it, is taken as made rather than as one still to make, which Save would have written a second time.
- **Save writes only at a plain place.** A decision Save would write (an accepted change not saved yet, or a saved one turned back) stays on its own side only where that side is plainly in place (`placedPlainly`): words with one side of their surroundings as before, or the only such words when they did not stand beside a copy of themselves, and not tied with a place beside them; an empty place with one side as before in full and the other for at least 12 characters of whole words. Otherwise the hunk goes stale and nothing is written for it, as when a doubled word was deleted by hand together with the words either side of it and only its twin is left, or another word was typed right at the place of an accepted insertion ("Then later Mara", where the text before agrees for none). The first version asked an empty place for both sides in full, so an accepted insertion went to Unanchored after any edit within 40 characters on either side, "steps" made "stairs" 15 characters after it among them, and Save then wrote nothing for it (the `apply.23` review).
- **No place by a guess.** Only words are placed by the fuzzy search. A zero-width place found by surroundings that no longer read as before is a guess that can fall inside a word: a suggested insertion of "very " in "The ewes were always fine." went, after the file changed to "always good.", "quite good." and back, to "always| fine" with the "?" mark, and accepting it and saving wrote "alwaysvery  fine" (seen in a `dev:clean` window, the `apply.23` review; the old code did the same with both words changed at once, "quite gvery ood"). A deletion or an insertion with no place found exactly now goes to Unanchored, whatever its decision.
- **Stale stays stale.** A stale hunk's offsets are 0. A deletion or an insertion that went stale is not searched for again, since only its surroundings could place it: searched for around 0, it came back at the start of the chapter.

The cards that report a rebase (a chapter opened on a review made before the file changed, an older review from History, the reload after a change on disk, and Save to chapter finding the file changed) end with "K decisions changed to match the file." when `stats.adopted` is not 0 (`rebaseCardText` in `src/shared/ui/rebase.ts`); they read as before otherwise. What counts did not change: only a decision that changed, so an accepted deletion found already made is not counted, being accepted before and after.

What this gives up. A hunk the old code placed by its best guess now leaves the page, to Unanchored, when the file around it changed within 40 characters on both sides, as does a deletion or an insertion with no place found exactly; an accepted insertion, or a saved deletion turned back, also leaves it when the words right beside it on one side changed, so that less than 12 characters of whole words there read as before; and a saved change undone by hand becomes a suggestion again only where its words are plainly its own. Where a copy of a hunk's words stood right beside them and another editor took that copy out, the file reads exactly as with the hunk's own words taken out, so the change is taken as made: in the review's random edits, every side still changed was of this kind but 2 in about 28,000, where a word typed beside the hunk repeated the word on its other side. A dense run of decisions all applied in the file together can leave a deletion or an insertion among them without plain surroundings, so the round-trip properties with empty sides keep hunks 41 characters apart, and the properties over dense chapters check only that nothing is written or flipped by a guess. The anchor quality is unchanged: words that occur more than once are `ambiguous`, with the "?" after the ghost, even where their surroundings place them exactly.

Checked by unit and property tests, a mutation pass and `dev:clean` windows before and after the change; the figures are under `apply.23` in 11.2 (M6).

### C.53 Kept paragraph boxes belong to the chapter and go back by the page's text (`apply.16`, 2026-10-17)

11.3 (j) keeps a `reviewId` in each drafts file, and until `apply.7` the close prompt's line said boxes come back "with this review" (`apply.2`). The drafts file is named by the chapter's path alone, though, so it holds one review's boxes at a time, and tying them to that review would have meant either leaving them unseen while another review of the chapter is on screen, where the first box opened there would write over them, or setting them aside every time History or a new review replaced the one they were typed on. Going by the text loses less than either. Done applies a box against the page as it reads, whatever decisions produced it (`commitDraft` compares the block with `initial`), so a box that reads the same on another review applies there exactly as it would have on its own. So boxes go back on whichever review of the chapter comes on screen, by the page's text, and `reviewId` is written but never compared. Each time a review comes on screen, opened from the list, from History or adopted from a new review, the chapter's file is read back; meanwhile writes for that chapter wait, so a box opened in that moment cannot replace the file unread.

A file that cannot be read back at all, because another program holds it open or the app may not read it, is not written until it has been read (review fix, 2026-10-17). Before that fix, the next box typed in the chapter replaced it, and the boxes it held were gone. Now every write for such a chapter reads the file first; while it still cannot be read nothing is written, the write is held and counts as pending, and the next flush tries it again unless a newer write is waiting. A restore whose flush leaves a write held does not read the file back either: the held boxes are no longer on screen, and what the file holds would go back on the page without them. Once it can be read, what it held is carried after the boxes on screen, as a box that could not be set aside is, and goes back on the page the next time a review of the chapter comes on screen. It is not put back on the page at once: the file then also holds the boxes on screen, and placing it would set those aside as copies of themselves. Moving the file aside in main, as for a file that does not parse, was not enough: on Windows a file another program holds open without sharing cannot be renamed either, so the renderer has to hold its writes in any case. Main said why the read failed in words of its own, since the general error mapping explained a refused read as a refused write; since `apply.24` that mapping has words for reads (6.1), and `loadDrafts` uses them.

"Its paragraph" is read as its own index. A box whose paragraph moved, because one was added or removed above it, is set aside rather than placed on whichever paragraph now reads the same: short lines such as "Yes." or a scene break recur, and a box placed on the wrong one would rewrite that paragraph on Done. A set-aside .txt holds both what was typed and what the block read when the box opened, so the author can see what changed.

The card's button opens the .txt rather than showing its folder, since the author wants the words, not the file. `shell:reveal` still takes no path from the page: it takes the bare name the set-aside answered with, and main checks that it is a .txt in `drafts/set-aside` before it opens it, falling back to showing it in its folder when no app is set for .txt.

The prompts say so since `apply.7`. Their line about open boxes had said they come back "with this review", which held neither when the chapter opens with another review nor when the author leaves for a review from History. The leave and close prompts now say a box opens for editing again when the author comes back to the chapter, and leaving for a review from History says the boxes open there at once where their paragraph reads the same, and what was typed in the others is set aside in a text file. Since `apply.26` another review of the chapter, from History or the review selector, opens without a question, so only the first of these is said; the boxes go back on it by the same rule.

### C.54 Closing the window is a handshake with the page (`apply.8`, 2026-10-17)

A browser asks before a page closes through `beforeunload`, which puts the decision in the page. In Electron that handler shows no question of its own: it can only cancel the close silently, and a page that has stopped responding never runs it, so `win.close()` then waits on it. So the page holds no veto here. It pushes what a close would put at risk whenever that changes (`app:guard-state`), and main decides inside the window's `close` event, from the last push, whether to ask at all. With nothing at risk there is no IPC and no wait, so a clean close is as quick as before; a page that has pushed nothing since it loaded (every page before `apply.9`, or one still loading, after a reload too) has nothing at risk; and a page whose process has gone never holds the window.

When something is at risk, the page is asked once and given the two times of 11.3 (i): 3 s to say it has the request, which a page that is merely busy (a long compose or rebase) manages, and 10 s more to put its question up, which leaves room for its own 5 s race of the save and the writers (`prepareToLeaveApp`) and the "Still writing your decisions" question after it. Past either, a native box offers Wait and Close anyway, so a hung page cannot keep the window open. A second close before the page's question is up shows the box at once, since the author has asked twice. Wait sets no new timer, so a page that is slow but working shows one box and then its question (the check `apply.9` makes with a 15 s busy loop); another close brings the box back. Once the question is on screen there is no timer, because the author is reading it, and a further close only brings the window forward. A page that hangs after its question is up is therefore not offered Close anyway; the question's answers are quick (`apply.9`), and Task Manager remains for that case.

Every box carries an AbortSignal (`dialog.showMessageBox`'s `signal`). When the page answers after all, the box is taken away and whatever it was answered is ignored, even a Close anyway pressed in the same moment, since the page's own question is then on screen and one of its answers closes. Close anyway uses `destroy()`, because `close()` would wait on a page that may not answer. The page's true closes on the next tick, so the reply to its request reaches it before its window goes.

Electron cancels `app.quit()` when a window's close is held, so the guard keeps one quitting flag: `before-quit` sets it, and a close the author then agrees to, or Close anyway, calls `app.quit()` again. The page's false clears it, so a later plain close only closes the window, which on macOS does not quit the app. Restart now quits through the installer after its own question and must not be asked again, so `allowNextClose('update')` lets its close through (11.3 n).

A reload is a new page (a review fix the same day). It keeps the page's process, so no `render-process-gone` comes, and the guard used to keep the old page's last state and the stage of a close under way. In a `dev:clean` window, with a state at risk pushed through the bridge as `apply.9`'s page will push it: after Ctrl+R a WM_CLOSE was held and asked of the new document, which had no listener yet, and 3 s later "Lapidary is not responding" stood over a page that had only reloaded; with a close under way across the reload, the same box came 3 s after the first close, and after Wait the next close opened it again at once, while the new page had been sent nothing. So the guard now forgets the page when the main frame commits a new document (`did-navigate`), as it does for a new window, and a close under way ends without closing. It ends rather than closing as for a page that has gone, because the reload came after the close and the new page is alive: closing over it would undo the author's own Reload window, and a close they still want costs one more close, asked of the new page. `did-start-navigation`, kept to the main frame and to new documents, is the other way to hear a reload, but it also fires for a navigation that is then refused: in the same window a `blob:` address set as `location.href` fired it, then `will-navigate`, which refused it, and the page stayed where it was, so the guard would have forgotten a page that was still there. `did-navigate` fires only once the new document has replaced the old one. The page pushes its state as soon as it has loaded (`apply.9`), so a reloaded page that holds something at risk, such as boxes it opened again from the drafts file, is guarded from the start.

Checked by `test/main/closeGuard.test.ts`, with fake timers and a stand-in window that keeps Electron's rules, and for the reload in a `dev:clean` window as above; the page's half, and the window with real input throughout, are `apply.9`'s.

### C.55 Shutdown is never blocked (`apply.8`, 2026-10-17)

Windows ends a session (shutdown, restart or sign-out) by sending each window WM_QUERYENDSESSION, which Electron reports as the window's `query-session-end`, and then WM_ENDSESSION, reported as `session-end`, after which the process is ended. `preventDefault` on `query-session-end` would hold the shutdown up, and Windows would then show its "This app is preventing shutdown" screen, where the usual answer is Shut down anyway, which ends the app wherever it is, in the middle of a write too. So the guard never prevents either event. Both only send the page `app:flush`, so it writes the review and drafts writes it holds at once rather than at the end of their 700 ms wait; even without that, what the author does is on disk within those 700 ms (6.4, 11.3 j).

After `session-end` the session is ending, so every close then goes through at once and an open box is taken away: a close held then could only end by force. `query-session-end` alone changes nothing else, since another program may still refuse and the session go on.

Only Windows reports these two. On macOS a shutdown reaches the app as a quit, which the guard would hold and ask about like any other, holding the shutdown up; Linux is untried. Electron's `powerMonitor` reports a coming shutdown on both (`shutdown`), and is where a build for them should tell the guard the session is ending; `release.16` and `release.17` say so.

Checked by unit tests only; no shutdown was run.

### C.56 Claude Code ended with the app (`apply.18`, 2026-10-17)

The tracked spawner of the original design (`spawnClaudeCodeProcess`, a 4 KB stderr tail appended to the classifiers' text, `killClaudeChildren()` in `will-quit`) was to be built only if Claude Code outlived the app. It did not in the one run measured, so it was not built, and no code changed.

Measured once, on the unmodified build at 3df1552, in a `dev:clean` window with a scratch userData and a scratch copy of `samples/manuscript`. The app ran the author's installed Claude Code 2.1.302 (`%USERPROFILE%\.local\bin\claude.exe`) under his own sign-in, with model `haiku` (the dialog showed Haiku 5.5) and effort `low`, on a new chapter of three paragraphs:

- One typed edit came first, so the close had something to keep, then Review with AI and Review without it.
- 0.2 s later the review's `claude.exe` was a child of the app's main process, with the review's flags (`--model haiku`, `--effort low`, `--include-partial-messages`). In the one look, 0.9 s in, its tree was that `claude.exe` and the `conhost.exe` of its console.
- 0.9 s into the review, WM_CLOSE went to the window. "Close Lapidary?" came 13 ms later, saying the running review would stop, with Close, keep for later focused. The review was still running when it was answered.
- After Close, keep for later, the task's command, `Get-Process claude -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue | Where-Object { $_.Path -like '*claude-agent-sdk*' }`, found nothing at +0.07 s, +1.2 s, +4.5 s and +10 s.

That command can no longer find the app's Claude Code: its filter names the SDK's bundled binary, which went with C.42. So each check also looked for three more things: every process the run had started, by process id and start time (the review's `claude.exe` and `conhost.exe`, Electron's four processes, the `node.exe` of the launcher and of the dev server, and the dev server's two `esbuild.exe`); any process whose parent was one of them; and any `claude.exe` from `%USERPROFILE%\.local\bin` that had not been running before the launch. All three were empty at the first check, begun 7 ms after the click, and stayed empty. At +10 s no `claude` process on the machine was new since the launch. The review on disk kept the typed edit, as Close, keep for later says.

Which of three things ended it was not separated. Close, keep for later stops a running review (`apply.9`), and Cancel ends its process tree with `taskkill /T /F`. `will-quit` aborts whatever is still tracked (`abortAll`), which does the same. And Node starts a child without `detached` inside a job object that ends it when the app's process ends. That job lets a child's own children break away: a Node process that started `cmd /c ping` and exited took `cmd.exe` with it, while `ping` and the console's `conhost.exe` ran on. So a process Claude Code started would be ended only by `taskkill /T`, which a crash of the app would skip. None was seen in this run, and after the close no process whose parent was one of the run's was left. With `--tools ""`, `--strict-mcp-config` and `--setting-sources=` it has no tool, MCP server or hook to start one with, but no flag stops Claude Code itself from starting one.

### C.57 A chapter opens with the review last on screen, recorded beside the reviews (`apply.26`, 2026-10-17)

The author replaced the rule of `files.1` (the review last decided in, C.45) and the "Open the review from <date>?" question that `apply.7`'s review built on it: a chapter opens with whatever review was last on screen for it, and a select at the top of the side panel shows which, with a warning mark when it is not the newest. Changing reviews asks nothing.

**A record beside the reviews, not a time in them.** The task left the choice open between a per-chapter pointer and an `openedAt` on the entry. The pointer won: the page writes a review file again after every decision from its own copy, which has no such field, so a time main put in the file would be written over unless the page carried it too, and writing a review file because it was shown would change its modified time, which the store's cache goes by and a sync tool sees. So each chapter folder has a `.last-open.json`, `{version: 1, chapters: [{sourcePath, file}]}`, keyed by the chapter's path because same-named chapters in different folders share the folder (C.45). Its name starts with a dot, like `.adoption.json`, and the store lists only `*.review.json`, so it is never taken for a review. It is written atomically, only when it changes, and is honoured only for a review file in that folder that belongs to the chapter; a record that is unreadable, or names a file that is gone or another chapter's, counts as none.

**When it is written.** The page sends `reviews:shown` once a review it opened from History or the selector is on screen, not when it asks for the file (`reviews:load`), so a load that never reaches the screen (a chapter file that cannot be read, say) records nothing. `saveReview` records every new entry it starts: a review that arrives on screen, one that finished while the author was in another chapter (which is then what that chapter opens with, as 7.6 already said), and the review on screen written for the first time. Opening a chapter writes nothing: it already shows what is recorded or what the fallback picks, and a reviews folder may sit inside the vault, where a write on every open would touch synced files for nothing. A record that cannot be written is logged as `reviews.last-open-failed` and otherwise ignored; the review save it came with stands (a test puts a folder where the record goes: Windows refuses the rename, and the write gives up after `atomicWriteFile`'s retries).

**The fallback is the old rule.** While nothing is recorded for a chapter, it opens with the review last decided in (`decidedAt ?? createdAt`), not simply the newest. A decision is made only on screen, so that is the last review on screen as far as the files can tell, and it is what every chapter opened with before this change, so upgrading moves no chapter to another review. Once a record is written for a chapter, the fallback applies there only if the file it names goes.

**Reviews that follow a renamed or moved chapter** take the record with them: `carryLastOpen`, run inside `runJournal` after the moves, points the new path at the moved file the old path's record named and drops records whose file is gone, so a folder the move emptied holds no record and is removed as before. It reads the old records after the moves, so a journal finished after a crash carries the record too.

**What went.** `currentReviewId` and `ReviewTimes` in `src/shared/ui/save.ts`, `olderReviewFrom` and `openedBy` in `src/renderer/state/leave.ts`, `PromptContext`, the older-review line of the leave and close prompts ("Your decisions are kept in the review from <date>. The chapter opens with another review, so reopen this one from History."), the paragraph line for a review from History, and the "Open the review from <date>?" title. A `LeaveTarget` for a review no longer carries its date, and `LeaveDeps` and `CloseGuardDeps` no longer take History. `leavePrompt` answers null for any review target, and `beforeLeaving` still lets a save under way end first and lets only the last of several clicks go ahead.

**The selector.** `reviewPicker` in `src/shared/ui/history.ts` lists the chapter's History entries newest first, labels them as History shows them and, since the review fixes, with the changes not saved to the chapter (`reviewChoiceLabel`), counts the one on screen from the page, adds the review on screen when History does not have it yet, leaves out another chapter's entries still listed a moment after a chapter opens, and gives the mark's words (`notNewestText`) when the one on screen is not the newest by `createdAt`. A chapter with no review shows "No reviews yet", disabled.

**The selector and the review keys** (review fixes the same day). As first landed, the select kept the focus after a choice, as a select does whether the choice was made with the mouse or the keyboard, and nothing moved it. `isTypingTarget` in `src/renderer/state/keyboard.ts` counts a select as typing, so j, k, a, u, d, e and n did nothing until the author clicked elsewhere. And the arrows, Home, End and Page Up and Down change a closed select at once on Windows: ArrowUp and ArrowDown, review keys for moving between suggestions, opened another review at every press, with no question, and moved the record with it. In the window, with A chosen and the select still focused, j left the focus where it was, a accepted nothing, and ArrowUp opened B and moved `.last-open.json` to B, ArrowDown back to A. ArrowLeft, ArrowRight, Home, End, Page Up and Page Down and a typed digit each did the same. A History row is a button, which the review keys do not count as typing, so a History click never had this. Now a choice hands the focus back to the page (`event.currentTarget.blur()` in the select's onChange, before the review is opened), and the select holds back the eight stepping keys while no modifier is held (`pickerHoldsKey` in `src/shared/ui/history.ts`, `preventDefault` in its onKeyDown), so they do nothing while the closed select has the focus; Alt+Down, Alt+Up, F4 and Space are untouched and still open the list. Body rather than a row takes the focus because the review keys listen on the window and work from there, and because the new review is not on screen yet when the choice is made. Type-ahead is left as the select has it: a digit, the start of a date, picks the next review whose date begins with it, which opens it once and gives the focus back. That stays a deliberate act, not a review key.

**What the author may want to weigh.** Nothing now asks before the author moves from a review with changes not saved to the chapter to another review of the same chapter. Those changes stay in their review, but the chapter list's dot, the Save button and the leave question follow the review on screen; until `apply.26` the History question was the reminder. Since the review fixes, the selector's entry for that review says how many ("2 not saved to chapter", as last written), which History's rows do not, and README and 6.4 say the dot follows the review the chapter opens with. Only the selector shows them: once the author is on another chapter, nothing in the chapter list does. And the first-use Save hint (`apply.12`) hangs over the top of the side panel, so until Got it it covers the selector and its mark; in the window check it did whenever a change was unsaved.

Checked by `test/main/reviews.test.ts` (the rule, the record and its fallback, same-named chapters, a record that cannot be written, adoption into a new folder and within a shared one), `test/shared/history.test.ts` (the labels and their unsaved counts, the mark, the order, a review not in History yet, another chapter's History, no review, the keys the select holds back), `test/shared/save.test.ts`, `test/renderer/leave.test.ts` (with the select's onKeyDown and its blur before the choice) and `test/renderer/closeGuard.test.ts`. A scratch mutation pass broke twelve parts of the rule and the selector one at a time, and each failed at least one test; the fallback's first test passed by the order of the files in the folder, and now has a review first in the folder that is neither the newest nor the one decided in. The window check is in the task's done note.

### C.58 The side columns fold to strips and drawers, laid out in script (`ui.3`, 2026-10-18)

Round 5 gave the side columns `clamp()` widths, so that they narrowed "somewhat" as the window did. They could not narrow far: the chapter list kept at least 170 CSS px and the side panel 240, which in a 900 by 600 window at 150% left the centre column 179 px and the prose's text 25, and from 175% no text at all (`ui.2`, `ui.3`). The task asked for the columns to shrink or fold below a prose width of about 480 px and for section 7 to say how each gives way and how the author gets it back; that is section 7's Narrow windows. What the task left open, and why it went this way:

**480 px is the centre column, not the text.** The centre column holds the pane's padding, the paragraph rail and the position strip as well as the text, about 160 px between them with the scrollbar, but it is what the side columns take from directly and what the M5 review measured. Kept at 480, it leaves the text about 320 px at 100%, about 40 characters of Georgia at 17 px. When even both strips leave less than 480 (a 900 by 600 window from 175%, 1100 by 700 at 200%), the pane's own side padding narrows from 40 to 16 px, which gives the text 48 px more there.

**The chapter list folds first.** It is used to change chapters, which happens between reviews, not during one; the side panel holds the review selector, the focused suggestion, the comments and History, used all through a review. Both shrink a little before either folds (to 150 and 200 px), as a fold costs more than a few pixels of width. The default 1440 by 940 window never folds the side panel.

**Drawers, not columns that push the prose.** A folded column opened in place would take its width back from the prose: at 200% in a 900 by 600 window, the side panel at 240 px would leave the centre column 170 px and the text about 60. A drawer over the prose's edge leaves the prose as it was, and closes as soon as the author presses in the prose. It is under the first-use hint and the notification cards, so neither is ever hidden behind it; the hint keeps to the side panel's column wherever it is drawn, which with the panel folded is the drawer's place beside the strip, over the top right of the prose. A drawer has the page's background, which is what lies under the column in place, so the panel, faded while a review runs, does not let the prose show through it (`ui.3` review).

**The hint gives way to the prose with the side panel folded** (`ui.3` review). As first built, the hint lay over the prose until Got it: at 200% in a 900 by 600 window over the right 60% of it, its whole height, and over the paragraph editor's text, Cancel and Done wherever the paragraph sat, so Done could not be clicked, and over most of either drawer when one was open. That undid `apply.12`'s rule that the hint never meets the chapter's text, and the authors who zoom to 200% are the ones who most need the text clear. Two other ways were weighed. A full-width row under the toolbar, pushing the prose down, covers nothing, but the hint across the window's width is 91 to 111 CSS px tall, and with five chip categories the prose there has 287, 166, 112 and 68 px at 125%, 150%, 175% and 200%: from 175% the row would leave no prose. Showing it only in the Suggestions drawer would leave an author who never opens the drawer without it. So the hint still shows, once, where `ui.3` put it, and gives way as soon as the author goes on: it waits while a paragraph is open for editing, and the next press anywhere but on the hint, review key or drawer opened sets it aside while the panel stays folded, until the next start, writing nothing (section 7, First-use hint). The press or key that makes the first change comes before the hint shows, so the author always sees it once a session; with the panel in place it covers only the top of the panel, as before, and stays until Got it or a save.

**Escape never closes a drawer along with something else** (`ui.3` review). The find bar's box closes the bar on Escape in its own handler, which runs at React's root before keyboard.ts's window listener, and the Bulk menu and the legend close on it in window listeners added after keyboard.ts's. keyboard.ts found the bar already closed and closed the drawer as well, or closed the drawer under an open menu. An Escape something else has taken (`defaultPrevented`) now leaves the drawer alone, and so does one pressed while the menu or the legend is open (`popupTakesEscape`); the two also take the press they close on, so the order of the listeners does not matter. Left as it was before `ui.3`: with no drawer open, one Escape still closes the find bar and the Bulk menu or the legend together when both are open, since keyboard.ts closes the bar before their listeners run.

**Script, not media queries.** The widths depend on the window's width only, which CSS media queries could have read, but the strips are buttons with state (which drawer is open, the focus handed back on Escape), and the hint has to be placed again when the columns move. So the page measures `.body` with a ResizeObserver and computes the layout with the pure `columnLayout`, tested in node with fast-check properties (the widths add up, the centre keeps 480 px unless both columns are folded, a column folds only when nothing less would do and never as the window widens). It renders inside the observer's callback with `flushSync`, before the frame is painted, so a zoom step never shows the old layout. The widths reach app.css as custom properties on `.body`, whose defaults there are the `clamp()` widths of round 5 for the first moment.

**A verification note.** In a `dev:clean` window that Windows reports hidden (`document.visibilityState` is "hidden" while the window is covered, C.30), no frame is drawn and no ResizeObserver reports until something asks for a frame, so a zoom step's new layout appears only then; the drive scripts take a screenshot first. In such a window Chromium also does not open a select's list on a click, so the selector was checked by a real click, which takes the focus, and type-ahead.

### C.59 The split is a share of the height under the box, and the usual split is none (`ui.6`, 2026-10-18)

The task asked for the split "as a fraction of the panel height". It is the list's share of the height the list, the handle and the region below share: the panel less the review selector (44 CSS px), the focused suggestion's box (139) and the footer (40), all three of fixed height. A share of the whole panel would keep the line at the same share of a height that also holds those 223 px, so as the window, the zoom or the chips changed the panel's height, the two regions' own proportion would change; a share of their own height keeps it.

**The usual split is null, not 0.55.** The usual split is no fixed line: the list takes what it needs up to 55%, so a chapter with a few suggestions leaves the rest to the comments. A stored 0.55 would give such a list a region mostly empty. Double-click and Enter put the usual split back by writing null. A split the author sets is a fixed line, the list's region keeping its share however many rows it holds, so the handle stays where it was put when the chips or another review change the count.

**The limits are measured, and CSS draws the line.** Three rows each side depend on a row's height (22 CSS px here), the list's heading and padding (37), the region below's padding (20) and the handle's 7, which come from the fonts and the rules. The page measures them after every render and whenever the regions change size, and hands them to app.css as `--split-min` and `--split-gap` beside the share (`--split`); the list's height is `clamp(var(--split-min), calc(var(--split) * 100%), calc(100% - var(--split-gap)))`, which `splitHeight` in `src/shared/ui/split.ts` repeats for the keys and the drag. So a resize redraws the line with no script, even in a window Windows reports hidden, where no ResizeObserver reports until a frame is drawn (C.58's verification note); only the handle's value for a screen reader waits for one. app.css holds the measures at 100% as defaults until the page has its own.

**When the limits cross** (`ui.6` review, 2026-10-18). Three rows each side need the list's 103 CSS px, the handle's 7 and the region below's 86: 196 px under the box at 100%. The handle moves by the height under the box less 196 px, and not at all below that. As first landed, the least won wherever the limits crossed, so any split set drew the list at its three rows, and section 7 said each region kept three rows "whatever the split". The review found that a split set then left the comments less room than the usual split, which gives a full list 55%, in the windows where `ui.5` said the split was needed. Measured on the commit under review in a `dev:clean` window on Chapter 01 with 34 suggestions over 13 categories and 15 comments, the viewport set to the inside of each window: in the smallest window, 900 by 600, at 100% (884x561, the chips and the status bar on two rows each, 180 px under the box), a split set in the default window to favour the comments (Home, 0.18) drew the list at 103 and left the region below 50 px of what it scrolls, where the usual split drew 99 and left 54; End moved the list 4 px, and Home not at all. In the drawer of a 1000 by 900 window at 150% (656x574, the chips on three rows, 131 px), the same split left the region below 1 px, the usual split 32; at 884x545 (164 px), 34 against 47.

**The least is never more than 55%.** The clamp's least is `min(var(--split-min), 55%)`, and `splitMin` in split.ts is the same. Where the panel is too short for three rows each side, a split set draws the line where the usual split draws it under a full list, whatever the share, so it never leaves the region below less; between 187 and 196 px at 100%, where the list's three rows are under 55%, the list keeps them and the region below has a few pixels more than under the usual split. A list too short to fill its 55% still has more room under a split set than under the usual split, as in any window, since a split set holds its share however many rows the list has. The other choice was to ignore the split there, as the one scroller does; that needs the page to switch on a measure, which a window Windows reports hidden takes only at its next frame (C.58's verification note), where the cap in `clamp()` needs no script.

**A handle that cannot move an arrow step is no control.** Below 220 px at 100% (196 and one 24 px step) the handle has `aria-disabled`, leaves the Tab order and is drawn as the plain line, with no grip and the usual pointer, and a press, a drag, a double-click and its keys do nothing (`splitMovable`; section 7, The split), so a keyboard user does not reach a control that does nothing. It had been focusable with 4 px of travel. In the smallest window at 100% the handle moves only when the chips and the status bar take one row each (228 px, 32 px of travel); with the chips on one row and the status bar on two (209 px) it would move 13 px, with the chips on two rows and the status bar on one (199 px) 3, and below that not at all. In the default window at 150%, with this chapter's chips on two rows, the 243 px under the box let it move; Home took the list to its three rows, 100.67 px there.

Checked on the fix in the same `dev:clean` window. At 884x561, the split 0.18 and the usual split both drew the list at 99.05 px and left the region below 54; the handle had `aria-disabled`, tabindex -1, no grip and the default pointer, and 55% as its value and both limits; a real drag of 60 px on it and a double-click changed nothing, wrote nothing and left the focus on the page; with the focus on it, Home, End and Enter did nothing and ArrowDown moved the focus to the next suggestion. In real windows sized with `SetWindowPos`, 900 by 600 at 100% (884x561 inside) gave the same, and 1000 by 900 at 150% (984x861 inside, zoomed through `view:zoom`, the side panel in its drawer, 136 px) drew the list at 75 and left the region below 34 with the split set and without. At 884x611 (230 px) the handle moved: Home to 103, ArrowDown 24 px, End to 137.09 (230.11 less 93), a real drag of 60 px up stopped at 103 and one of 30 px down reached 133, and a double-click put back the usual split; shrunk to 884x561 with the split at End it was still and drew 99.05, and grown back it drew 137.09 again, and Tab from the last row reached it. The default window at 100% was as before: 103 to 475, and drags of 60 px up and 30 down moved the line by as much. Screenshots of the still handle in light and dark, looked at by eye, are in the session's scratch folder `u6f/out-after3`.

**540, not 420.** The task named the 420 px fallback of the first `panel.1`; since C.49 the one scroller is a window less than 540 CSS px high inside, and the handle follows that media query.

**Six places.** The share is written to six decimal places, within a hundredth of a pixel in any window; with four, a 24 px arrow step came out at 23.97 px in the default window.

### C.60 A comment that loses its paragraph keeps its number (`ui.7`, 2026-10-18)

`rebaseReview` gave a comment whose paragraph and quote had both left the file `paragraph: null`, the value a comment about the whole chapter has, so the side panel listed it among the open comments as "chapter" and nothing said where it had been. `ui.7` asks for "unanchored (was paragraph 12)" and a place in the list by that number, so the comment now keeps the index it had in `wasParagraph` (section 3). `paragraph` stays null, so the margin, the `n` key, Edit text, `remapAfterCommit` and `repairCommentAnchors` treat it as before, as having no paragraph; only the side panel reads the new field (`isUnanchored`, `commentPlace`, `sortComments`), and Edit text for its words (`commentEditBlocked`).

**The number is the one it had.** It counts in the text the comment lost its place in, as Unanchored's suggestions keep theirs ("Paragraph 4 in the original review"), and neither a later change on disk nor a save renumbers it. A deletion above the lost paragraph in the same change therefore leaves the number too high against the page's numbers: in the `ui.7` window, with "You knew." (5) and "Tomorrow we move the ewes" (8) deleted together, the second comment read "was paragraph 8" and sat where paragraph 7 now is, and so was listed after the resolved comment on the new paragraph 7. Working out where the lost paragraph would be in the new text, from the paragraphs either side that are still found, was left out: it would make "was" mean "would now be", the task's words are "the paragraph it last had", and the comment is still near the place it names.

**Nothing anchors it again.** As before, a comment without a paragraph is passed over by the next rebase, so it stays unanchored if the paragraph comes back.

**Older reviews.** A comment that lost its paragraph before this has no `wasParagraph` and still reads "chapter"; nothing in the review tells it from a comment about the whole chapter.

**Rendered in a test.** The side panel is checked by rendering `SidePanel` with `react-dom/server` in vitest's Node environment, with no DOM: the store's initial state is enough, and the effects, which measure and scroll, do not run on the server. The test file is named `*.render.test.ts`: tsconfig.web.json, which has JSX and the DOM library, type-checks such files, and tsconfig.node.json, which has neither, leaves them out.

### C.61 Quiet test windows (`dev.1`, 2026-10-18)

The verification runs kept opening the app in front of whatever the author was working in: the window took the foreground when it first showed, and a second launch or a held close brought it forward again. A development switch, `MANUSCRIPT_REVIEW_DEV_QUIET_WINDOW` (`npm run dev:clean -- --quiet`), read in `src/main/devSwitches.ts` and ignored by a packaged build like every other switch (C.39), keeps a test window out of the way. Everything it changes is in `src/main/foreground.ts`, which is also the only file in `src/main` that shows, restores or focuses the window, as a test checks. No CHANGELOG line: nothing changes for anyone who runs the app.

**Shown without the foreground.** `showInactive()` takes the place of `show()` at the first show (C.36), and nothing calls `focus()`, `moveTop()` or `restore()`; on Windows `showInactive()` is `SW_SHOWNOACTIVATE`. A window first shown this way keeps its place in the z-order, so a launcher that pushed it to the bottom while it was still hidden never sees it in front. The second launch (C.40) and the close guard's reveal (7.7) go through `bringForward`, which for a quiet window is `showInactive()` when it is not minimised and nothing when it is. The close guard does not flash a quiet window's taskbar button either: the flash asks for the attention the focus would have taken, so a check of the flash runs without the switch.

**Left minimised** (review fix, 2026-10-18). At first `bringForward` restored a minimised quiet window with `showInactive()`, since `SW_SHOWNOACTIVATE` also restores a window without activating it, and the one run of `dev.1`'s window check saw the foreground stay put and the window come back above the others. That was one run of an effect that comes and goes. The reviewer, with another program's window in front and second launches from a background process, saw the restored window take the foreground once in three tries and hold it, at z-order index 19 above the window that had had it, and come back at the bottom with the foreground untouched the other two times; a held close restored it at the bottom. In the fix's own check of the code before it, with a cover window of ours in front, six second launches, three from a background process and three from the cover's process, never moved the foreground, and the window came back above the cover twice and at the bottom four times. The likely cause is that Chromium's single-instance code, when a second copy hands over, gives the running copy the right to take the foreground (`AllowSetForegroundWindow`, which `electron.exe` imports), after which Windows may activate or raise a window it restores. So a minimised quiet window is now left minimised by both, and a test driver that needs it restores it itself, from a process that has no such right: the helper's `restore` (`ShowWindow(SW_SHOWNOACTIVATE)`, then `HWND_BOTTOM`). On the fix, in a `dev:clean --quiet` window with another program's window in front: three second launches left the minimised window minimised and two left the shown one where it was, at the same place in the z-order, with the foreground unmoved; a WM_CLOSE with typed text at risk left the minimised window minimised while the page put its question up, and no native box came; the helper's restore, five times, brought it back at the bottom without the foreground, and a CDP screenshot then showed the page. `apply.14`'s dev run (2026-10-21) saw the helper's restore fail that once: straight after a second launch had left the minimised window minimised, the restore gave it the foreground, though it stayed at the bottom of the z-order. Nothing in the drive checked for that then, and the window kept the foreground for about 10 s before the run handed it back. The drive gained the check for the packaged run: straight after a restore it reads the foreground and hands it back if the window has it (`backAfterRestore` in the run's scratch `drive.mjs`, in `phaseSecond` and `phaseMinClose`). In the packaged run the app's own `bringForward` did the restoring and took the foreground with it, and the drive handed the foreground back both times. In the reviewer's repeat the same day, the same sequence, a minimised window, a second launch and then the helper's restore, left the foreground alone, so this too comes and goes. The likely cause is the one above: the second launch had just handed the app's process the right to take the foreground, and the window used it as it was restored, whoever restored it. A driver that restores the window after a second launch checks the foreground straight after and hands it back.

**Outside the switch.** The switch covers what the app does to its own window, not the windows Windows draws for it. The native box of a held close (7.7, `dialog.showMessageBox` over the window) comes up in front. In the fix's check, on the code before it (the fix changes nothing here for a window that is not minimised), with the page paused in the debugger and WM_CLOSE posted to the quiet window at the bottom (index 266) under the cover, the box came 3 s later, took the foreground and pulled the window up to index 20, just under itself; when the page answered and the box was taken away, the window kept the foreground at index 19 until the cover took it back. It did so both times tried; the reviewer saw the window raised both times and the foreground taken once in two. The folder picker (`showOpenDialog`, Change folder) and Explorer (`shell.openPath`, Show backups) are separate windows that the switch cannot keep quiet either; they were not tried. A check that provokes any of them brings the window forward on purpose and sends it back after (`shots-app.cjs front`, then `back <hwnd>`). Skipping the box under the switch was considered and not done: the box is what a check of an unresponsive page looks at, and a quiet window without it would be checking something the author never sees.

**Rendering while covered.** Chromium works out from the desktop's windows whether its window is wholly covered (the `CalculateNativeWinOcclusion` feature) and then treats the page as hidden: `document.visibilityState` is `hidden`, no animation frames come and timers are throttled, the likely cause of C.30.
