Under the switch that feature is disabled on the command line at module scope, since Chromium reads its features when the app gets ready, and the window's `backgroundThrottling` is off. Without the switch, on this machine, a covered page was hidden and gave no animation frame within 2 s, but `Page.captureScreenshot` itself still returned in about 140 ms after 3 s and after 20 s covered, and showed a change made while covered, so the hanging screenshots the `ui.5` run saw did not happen again; a driver that waits for animation frames before a shot, as `shots.mjs` does, is what a hidden page holds up. With the switch the covered page stayed visible, its frames came, and a screenshot returned in 134 ms.

**The launchers.** The agents' scratch launchers (`shots-app.cjs`, `window-run.cjs`) pass `--quiet` and, through their user32 helper, push the window to the bottom of the z-order with `SetWindowPos(hwnd, HWND_BOTTOM, 0, 0, 0, 0, SWP_NOMOVE | SWP_NOSIZE | SWP_NOACTIVATE)` as soon as it exists, while it is still hidden, and again once it shows. An agent brings the window forward only for a step that needs real OS input and sends it back straight after; Windows refuses the foreground to a process in the background, so the helper joins the input queue of the window in front for that one call. A driver that takes the foreground, even for a stand-in window of its own, stops doing so once the author is at the machine (`GetLastInputInfo` says when the last input came): in the review fix's check the author came back mid-run, and the stand-in, taking the foreground back after each step, took it from them three times in 8 s before it was closed. A check that needs the page to believe it has the focus turns on CDP's `Emulation.setFocusEmulationEnabled`: without it, in a quiet window, `document.hasFocus()` is false and a focused button does not match `:focus`. A packaged build ignores `--quiet`, and in `apply.14` its window took the foreground at its first show at every launch, though the launcher ran in the background and pushed the window to the bottom (C.36's `show()`). Nothing watched for it at the first of the four launches, and that window held the foreground for about 10 s before the run handed it back. The three later launches ran beside a foreground watcher started before the launcher (the run's scratch `launch-pkg.sh` starts `fgguard.mjs` first, which polls the window and hands the foreground back as soon as the window has it), and the watcher handed it back within 30 ms each time. So a driver that launches a packaged build starts its foreground watcher before the launcher, from the first launch on: the build ignores `--quiet`, and the launcher's push to the bottom does not keep the window from taking the foreground. Its real click went only once the window was both the foreground window and the topmost one under the point, checked again just before the button went down; twice that check stopped the click, when the run's own foreground watcher, still running from the launch, sent the window back between `front` and the click.

### C.62 DevTools input gives a covered window's page the focus (verification note, `setup.7`, 2026-10-18)

A quiet test window (C.61) never has the foreground, so its page should believe it has no focus: `dev.1` found `document.hasFocus()` false there until focus emulation was turned on. That holds only until the first mouse event sent over DevTools. In `setup.7`'s window check, after trusted clicks through `Input.dispatchMouseEvent` (opening a chapter, then Setup), `document.hasFocus()` was true with the window at the bottom of the z-order and another program's window in front, and with no focus emulation in the session. Two things follow for a check.

- **A focus event needs the page to lose the focus first.** Bringing that window forward fired no `focus` event on the page, since it already had the focus; sending it back fired `blur`. Only the next time it came forward did `focus` fire, and with it the Setup screen's re-check. A check of what the window coming back does sends it forward and back once before it starts counting, or installs its probe before any DevTools input.
- **The clipboard is the system's.** With the page focused, a Copy clicked over DevTools in a window at the bottom may well write the system clipboard, the author's, without the window ever coming forward; it was not tried, for that reason. A check that clicks a Copy saves the clipboard's text first and puts it back after (only text: a picture or the HTML of a browser copy is not put back); a check of a Copy the clipboard refuses stubs `navigator.clipboard.writeText` in the page to reject, so the clipboard is never touched.

### C.63 Test the connection is a review's exchange with a one-line prompt, and answers rather than throws (`setup.8`, 2026-10-18)

- **One exchange for both.** `runCliReview` and the new `runCliTest` share `exchange` in `claudeCli.ts`: start Claude Code, send `initialize`, the one user message, read up to the `result`, always end the process. The test's `initialize` carries the system prompt "Reply with the single word OK." and no schema, its message is "This is a connection test.", and its command line is `claudeArgs({model: 'haiku', maxTurns: 1})`: the review's base flags, `--model haiku --max-turns 1`, no `--effort` (Claude Code's own for the model) and no partial messages. Its `result` is read by `resultToError`, as a review's is (C.47), so a test fails wherever a review would and in the same words. Any answer that is not a failure counts: the test is of the connection, not of the model's obedience, so the word is not checked. The model is the first key of `modelUsage`, else the one the `system` init message named.
- **The time limit is the caller's.** `testConnection` (`providers/connectionTest.ts`, no electron import) runs either provider's `test`, aborts it at 60 s and answers the timeout at once rather than once the process has gone; the abort ends Claude Code's process tree, or OpenAI's request, as Cancel does for a review. Its controller is registered, so quitting ends a test too. Whatever happens comes back as `{ok: false, error}`, never as a thrown error; an error that is not the provider's own is "The test failed: …" with the provider's failure code, never `toAppError`'s file wording.
- **The duration is the app's clock**, from the request to the answer with Claude Code's start-up included, not the result's `duration_ms`, which counts only the request: it is what the author waits for.
- **`test-ok` is `success`.** The task's word predates `setup.6`, whose `nextLastFailure` takes one `success` event for a review and a connection test alike; a test that went through sends that (`testSetupEvent`), one that failed sends `failure` with its code, and a cancelled one nothing.
- **The real test** (2026-10-18, the one request the task allowed, from a `dev:clean --quiet` window on a scratch copy of the samples): this machine's Claude Code 2.1.302 on a Max plan answered in 1.7 s by the app's clock, 1758 ms from the trusted click to the line on screen, as `claude-haiku-5-5`, and sent a `rate_limit_event` with status `allowed_warning` and type `seven_day`, which the status bar then showed as "allowed_warning (seven_day)" in its warning colour, as it does after a review; the words for it are `setup.9`'s.
- **"Connect" in the render test's sign-in check.** `setupScreen.render.test.ts` treats a button labelled like "Connect Claude" as a sign-in; its pattern now leaves out the noun, so "Test the connection", which signs no one in, passes, and the test pins it as the only button that names a connection.
- **The note follows the credential** (`setup.8` review). The task's note, "which counts against your plan like any other", stood in every view the test is offered in, so with an API key the card said reviews are billed to the key "not to a Claude plan" and, a few lines under it, that the test counts against your plan (seen in a `dev:clean --claude-config-empty --api-key-dummy` window). `connectionTestNote` picks the note from the check's `credential`: the task's words on a Claude plan, "is billed to your API key" with an API key, "is billed through your cloud provider" for Bedrock, Vertex and the like, and "counts against your plan or API key" where the check failed, which leaves the credential unknown (5.6 item 5). Each ends "like any other", as the task's does.
- **Held, not disabled** (`setup.8` review). A focused button that becomes `disabled` loses the focus in Chromium, which leaves it on the page. Seen in the window: Test the connection focused and pressed with Space, the focus was on the page while the test ran and after; Check again the same once its check ended. `heldButton` (`src/renderer/state/heldButton.ts`) gives both `aria-disabled` and no click handler while their work runs, and `app.css` draws `button[aria-disabled='true']` as `button:disabled` and leaves it out of the hover and press colours. The handler matters for Check again: unlike the test, `useAi.check` does not refuse a second check while one runs. The tests run without a DOM, so the render test pins the markup (no `disabled`, `aria-disabled="true"`), a unit test the props and `setupEntry.test.ts` that both buttons take them; the focus itself was checked in the window.
- **Quitting, pinned for either provider** (`setup.8` review). The test that quitting ends a test passed without `testConnection` registering its controller, since the Claude exchange registers one of its own through `deps.track`. OpenAI's test only listens to the signal it is given, so quitting during it rests on that registration alone. `connectionTest.test.ts` now also runs a stub that only listens, and OpenAI's test against the mock's `slow` key, each with `track: registerController`: one controller while the test runs, `abortAll()` aborts it, and the answer is `cancelled` (at once for OpenAI, whose reply the mock holds for 7.2 s).

### C.64 Usage notices are Claude Code's own figures, worded from 80% (`setup.9`, 2026-10-18)

- **What Claude Code sends.** The `rate_limit_info` of a `rate_limit_event`, as the zod schema inside this machine's Claude Code 2.1.302 defines it and the Agent SDK 0.3.283's `SDKRateLimitInfo` documents it: `status` (`allowed`, `allowed_warning` or `rejected`), `resetsAt` (Unix seconds), `rateLimitType` (`five_hour`, `seven_day`, `seven_day_opus`, `seven_day_sonnet`, `seven_day_overage_included` or `overage`), `utilization`, `isUsingOverage`, and fields the app does not read (`overageStatus`, `overageResetsAt`, `overageDisabledReason`, `surpassedThreshold`, `unifiedWindows` and more). The schema's own description gives `utilization` as the fraction of the window used, "usually 0-1", and above 1 when usage runs past a limit. In 2.1.302 it comes only with `allowed_warning`, Claude Code's own warning (`setup.9` review, read from the program): the notice built from the response's headers (`Jl`) has no share, a `rejected` one is passed on as it is (`DS`), and the share is added only where Claude Code warns (`nh`), when Anthropic's servers say a threshold was passed, or, by its own table, from 90% of the 5-hour limit in the first 72% of the window and from 75%, 50% or 25% of the weekly limit in the first 60%, 35% or 15% of the week. `isUsingOverage` is set on a `rejected` notice only, when the plan's limit is refused and extra usage still allows the request. A share for every window on every notice exists only in `unifiedWindows`, which the schema marks `@internal`, so the app does not read it. `readRateLimit` keeps the status, the reset, `kind`, `utilization` and `usingOverage`, and leaves out a field of the wrong type rather than guessing; `test/helpers/fakeClaude.ts` sends that shape, with no share on its `allowed` and `rejected` notices (it sent 0.42 and 1 at first, which Claude Code never does). Nothing here was sent to Claude to learn it: the schema was read from the installed program, and no review or test ran.
- **`message` is gone.** It was `${status} (${rateLimitType})`, which the status bar showed as "allowed_warning (seven_day)" after `setup.8`'s real test (C.63). Nothing reads it now.
- **Why 80%.** Claude Code raises `allowed_warning` from thresholds that depend on how far into a window it is, so early in a week it warns well below 80%, and a status bar that warned on the status alone would warn for most of a week. `describeRateLimit` follows the share instead, taken to a tenth of a percent and then rounded down, as Claude Code words its own warning ("You've used 85% of your session limit"), so the two never differ, 79.6% says nothing and 99.5% reads 99%, never 100% of a limit not reached (`setup.9` review: rounded to the nearest, 0.796 read 80% and 0.995 read 100%); capped at 100%; and it says nothing without one, unless a limit is reached (`rejected`) or extra usage is paying, which it always says, since that may be billed. As the share comes only with Claude Code's warning (above), the notice from 80% shows only while Claude Code is warning: late in a window, even at 85 to 99% used, an `allowed` notice has no share and the bar says nothing until the limit is reached.
- **Names.** "5-hour limit", as the task gives it, where Claude Code says "session limit"; "weekly limit", "weekly Opus limit", "weekly Sonnet limit"; "weekly model limit" for `seven_day_overage_included`, a weekly limit for one model that Claude Code names after the model (2.1.302: "Fable limit") and counts, with the Opus and Sonnet limits, as a model's limit; "extra usage limit" for `overage`; "usage limit" for anything else. The weekly Sonnet limit's name depends on the plan, as in Claude Code (`setup.9` review): 2.1.302 names `seven_day_sonnet` "weekly limit" on a Pro or Enterprise plan (its `JZt`), where it is the account's weekly limit and its message is "You've hit your weekly limit", and "Sonnet limit" on any other or none known. The app does the same from the check's `subscriptionType` (Pro as `isProPlan` reads it, Enterprise likewise), in the status bar, its tooltip and both cards' advice, which on those plans is to wait: told "Haiku and Opus do not count against the weekly Sonnet limit" there, a Pro user, whom the app sets up with Sonnet (`setup.1`), would have been sent to models the same limit holds.
- **Time.** The computer's own clock, 24-hour, as "Decisions kept 14:02". A reset that is not today gives its day, since a weekly limit's "resets 09:00" would read as today: "tomorrow 09:00", the weekday within the week ("Sat 09:00"), else the date ("29 Oct 09:00"). Days are counted by calendar date, so a change of the clocks in between does not shift them. The tooltip says it in full with the time left, from now to the minute its clock time names, counted up to the whole minute, so it is always the difference between that clock time and the computer's (`untilPhrase`, `rateLimitTitle`); from a day on it gives days and whole hours, the minutes left to the clock time before it. It was counted down from the reset at first, which the docstring claimed never promised a reset sooner than it is, but did the opposite: the status bar reads the clock with its seconds, so for all but the first second of each minute the time left was a minute short of the clock time it followed ("It resets at 22:29, in 2 hours and 9 minutes" at 20:19:27), and past a day a whole hour short ("in 1 day and 1 hour" for 26 hours; `setup.9` review).
- **Expiry.** The notice is about one window; once its reset has passed it is out of date, so `describeRateLimit` gives null. The status bar's `UsageNotice` words it again every 30 s while it shows, which keeps the tooltip's time left current and takes the notice away within 30 s of the reset. It shows only while Claude is in use (the provider, or Setup open): beside "OpenAI ready" a "5-hour limit 85% used" would read as OpenAI's.
- **The usage-limit card is both cards.** The task did not say which card. A review that stops at a usage limit puts up a card with Claude Code's own words (which name the limit and its reset) and the advice (`usageLimitCard`), and Setup's status card in the usage-limit view, which a connection test that stops at a limit also leads to, gives the same advice under its text. The advice depends on which limit was reached, from the last notice: Sonnet and Haiku can go on past a weekly Opus limit, Haiku and Opus past a weekly Sonnet limit (but not on Pro or Enterprise, where it is the weekly limit: Names), and any other model past the weekly model limit, which the model list's Fable makes real (`setup.9` review: it was told to wait); but a 5-hour or weekly limit holds every model, so there the advice is to wait, with Sonnet and Haiku to make the limits last, in the words of the Pro plan note (`proPlanNote`). A reached one-model limit's tooltip says which reviews stop, "so reviews with Opus stop until it resets" (Sonnet, "that model"), not "reviews with Claude", which contradicted the card. Only one of the plan's limits gets advice (`isPlanLimit`). Claude Code's words alone do not tell the plan's limits from the rest: "You've hit your" starts its plan-limit messages and also "You've hit your team's shared budget. Switch to another model … to continue.", "You've hit your monthly spend limit." and the channel's, and "You've reached your" only its message for usage credits on Fable, "You've reached your Fable limit." (2.1.302's `AS` and `VWo`). So words that already say to switch model, or a notice that says extra usage was paying or was itself the limit reached, rule the advice out; a notice that says a plan limit was reached rules it in; and otherwise only Claude Code's own names for the plan's limits do, "You've hit your" and "limit", "session limit", "weekly limit", "Opus limit", "Sonnet limit" or "Fable limit" (its `hie`; `setup.9` review: any message that started "You've hit your" or "You've reached your" counted, so a team's shared budget after an extra-usage notice got "Wait until the limit resets", against Claude Code's "Switch to another model"). The rest, a team's shared budget, a spend limit, usage credits with no plan limit reached, or a seat without usage, keep Claude Code's words alone, which say which limit it is and mostly what to do. Running out of credits is not the line: when a plan limit and the extra usage behind it run out together, 2.1.302 says "You're out of usage credits · resets 3pm" with the plan's reset after a notice that names the plan's limit, and waiting for that reset lifts it, so the advice is given (`setup.9` said such messages were ones "waiting does not mend"). Setup says what the card said: its view cannot read Claude Code's message later, so `useAi` records the card's decision with the failure, from the same message and notice read at once (`failureSetupEvent`, `LastFailure.planLimit`; a failed connection test, from its own message and notice), and the view gives the advice only for a plan limit, and for any other a text that does not say the plan's limit was reached, as does the review dialog's warning (`setup.9` review: Setup gave the wait advice for every usage limit, credits and extra usage included).
- **The card reads the notice from a ref.** Main broadcasts the notice before it answers the review with the failure, but the page's state may not be drawn by the time the failure is handled, so `useAi` keeps each notice in a ref as it arrives as well as in its state, and the card reads `latestRateLimit()`.
- **The window check** handed the notices to the page's own state over DevTools, as main's broadcast would, in a `dev:clean --quiet --no-claude-code` window, so no request was made: the words, the tooltips, both themes, the expiry, OpenAI hiding it, and the card. The review fix's check did the same with a ready runtime on a Pro plan and the last failure handed to the page's state too, which reaches Setup's usage-limit view that `--no-claude-code` otherwise hides, before the fix and after it (`setup.9` task note). A notice from a real Claude Code was last seen in `setup.8`'s test.

### C.65 Open in Obsidian names no vault (`setup.10b`, 2026-10-18; taken out by `polish.3`, 2026-10-22)

`polish.3` took Open in Obsidian out (C.101): at sitting C the author found it opened the file in Obsidian, but would rather have Open and Open folder (`theme.10`, 2026-10-22). It handed the system `obsidian://open?path=<full path>`, a link that names no vault, since Obsidian looks for the most specific vault it knows that holds the path. The link's builder, `src/shared/obsidian.ts`, its tests, main's check of the link and the button's refusal of a `.txt` file went with it, and so did this entry's notes on the link, its percent-encoding and that check; the history of `PLAN.md` keeps them. Nothing in the app hands the system an Obsidian link now. Open, the system's app for the file's type, is Obsidian when the author has made it the app for `.md` files.

- **Blank.** The task says the note shows when `styleSheet` is `blank`. `guidelines:status` reports a file that does not exist yet as `missing`, but the review creates it from the template, whose style sheet is blank, and that first review is when the note matters most, so `styleSheetNote` shows it then too. A file of the author's own with no "## Style sheet" heading (`missing`, existing) gets none.

### C.66 A shell that opens nothing (`setup.10b`, 2026-10-18)

The window check of `setup.10b` had to press Open in Obsidian and Open without starting Obsidian or an editor on a machine the author was using. The page cannot stand in for main: `window.api` is exposed by `contextBridge`, non-writable, non-configurable and frozen, so a drive cannot wrap `guidelines:open` in the page (tried first, and stopped before any button was pressed). Main can. A development switch, `MANUSCRIPT_REVIEW_DEV_SHELL_STUB` (`npm run dev:clean -- --shell-stub`), read in `src/main/devSwitches.ts` and ignored by a packaged build like every other switch (C.39), makes `systemShell()` in `src/main/ipc.ts` return `recordingShell` (`src/main/shellApi.ts`) in place of Electron's `shell`: `openExternal`, `openPath` and `showItemInFolder` open nothing and print `[shell stub] openExternal <link>` and so on to the terminal, and `openPath` answers as if it had worked. Every place main hands something to the system goes through `systemShell()`: `guidelines:open`, `shell:reveal` (Show in folder, Show backups, a set-aside text) and the window's web links in `index.ts`; `test/main/shellApi.test.ts` checks that neither file calls Electron's `shell` directly. Main prints "[shell stub] on: nothing is opened outside the app" as it starts, so a drive reads that line from the terminal log before it presses anything, rather than trusting the flag it passed. The folder picker is a dialog, not the shell, and is not covered.

### C.67 The Pro preselection belongs to the first welcome guide (`setup.11` review, 2026-10-19)

`proPreselection` (`setup.1`) took `onboardingDone: false` to mean a new user. Until `setup.11` nothing wrote that flag, so on a fresh install it stayed false for good, and Sonnet was preselected at the first check that found Claude ready on a Pro plan, whenever that came. `setup.11` writes the flag both ways, which changed this in two places.

- **Show the welcome guide again.** It wrote `onboardingDone: false` alone, so an install on Pro whose model was still Default, from before 1.0 or a fresh one that had skipped the guide, looked new, and the next check moved it to Sonnet (seen in a `dev:clean` window with a Pro plan's check put into the page: `default` became `sonnet` on disk). Section 1 says a settings file that names a model keeps it and that only a new user gets Sonnet. Show again now adds `pro-model-preselected` to `dismissedHints` in the same write (`welcomeAgainPatch`), so the guide comes back with the preselection settled. It is one write, so no settings reply holds `false` without the id.
- **Start or Skip before Claude is ready.** The guide invites starting with Connect Claude still to do. Two ways were open: keep the preselection pending until the first check that finds Claude ready, or let it belong to the first guide. Pending needs a mark that survives a restart and tells a fresh install that skipped from settings from before 1.0, which normalisation makes alike (`onboardingDone` true, no hints): a new settings key, or a "pending" id in a list of dismissed hints, which reads backwards. Chosen: the preselection happens only while the first guide is open (`proPreselection`'s `guideOpen`, App's `welcomeOpen`, which also counts a Start or Skip whose write failed as closed). After the guide has gone, a model setting never changes behind the author's back, and a Pro user left on Default still has the review dialog's note, beside the model list, that Opus models, Default included, use the limits fastest.

### C.68 Small changes are drawn bigger, never stored bigger (`small`, 2026-10-19)

The author's round 6 screenshot showed two changes trimmed to one character (4.3, step 5): an accepted hyphen-to-space in "double standard", a 4 px grey line under a space with a faint "WAS -" whose strike-through merged into the hyphen, and a pending comma after "Mira", a 2 px purple caret with a 3 px comma above it. On the line each was about 5 by 22 CSS px to hit, against 68 by 21 for the word "standard". Widening the stored hunk would have moved offsets, demoted neighbours in `resolveOverlaps`, let `touches()` supersede it more often and made the ghost repeat the whole word, so every change in 11.7 is drawn and nothing is stored: Save to chapter, Copy result, find and a copied paragraph read exactly as before, which `test/renderer/hunkDom.render.test.ts` guards for every shape and status.

Measured in quiet `dev:clean` windows on a fixture chapter with every shape of 11.7's table in each status, a word change with a comma touching it, two small changes two words apart and a dialogue line with six:

- **Caret.** Across 651 window widths from 900 to 1550 CSS px at 100%, the inline-block caret left the line of the character before it at 4 widths (after "it" in the dialogue line); the inline one at 0.8em at none, 2 by 15 px, and none at 80% or 200% either.
- **Targets.** A hit test at every CSS pixel of the line around each change: 34 small changes, 16 to 17 by 23 to 25 CSS px at 100%, 16 to 17 by 22 to 23 at 80% and 15 to 16 by 21 to 24 at 200%; case 2, a 4 px caret, is now 16 by 23. Word changes, 45 to 65 px wide, are as they were.
- **Capsule.** 12.75 CSS px wide at 100%. With every paragraph isolated, `.center` keeps its `OverflowScrolling` layer and LCD text (`none`, contents opaque) through 25 wheel steps.
- **Tints.** `--tint-small` 16% and `--tint-small-hover` 26% in both themes, by `theme.8`'s measure (11.3 e).
- **Keys.** With a box on every key, an accepted comma's "ADDED [,]" ran 11.6 px over the next "-> [I]" in the dialogue line at 100% and 200%; with the box kept only for named whitespace the two end 0.2 px apart.
- **Margin marks.** CSS anchor positioning works in Electron 44.3.0 with the isolation in place: each mark is 11 by 39.1 CSS px, flush against the text, its middle within 2 px of its line's at 80%, 100% and 200%. A paragraph join's live text is the break, whose box Chromium puts on the blank line between the paragraphs, so its bar sits there.
- **List rows.** In the default window a decided row has about 150 CSS px for its text beside its status, so a small change's row shows two words a side, at most 14 characters, around an inline chip, which the row's ellipsis cuts into rather than dropping whole as it dropped an inline-block one.

Found by the review (2026-10-19), each checked in a quiet `dev:clean` window at 100% on the `small.11` fixture before and after the fix:

- **A bar's hover card stayed open.** The arrowhead was a `span` under the same key as the bar's `button`, so when a bar became the arrowhead React replaced the element, and fired no leave for the one that had gone. Resting on a bar until its card opened and clicking it, a quick click before the card's 100 ms, or focus by the store (as Shift+J or a list row would give it) each left the card open over the next paragraphs with the pointer elsewhere, through a wheel scroll too, until another suggestion was hovered. The arrowhead is now the same button, with no pointer: after the click the card closed with the pointer still, the quick click opened none, and focus by the store closed it as the pointer left. A mark that unmounts under the pointer closes its card itself (`markHover`, whose `gone` the mark calls as it unmounts): a bar whose change was decided under the resting pointer closed its card at once, and with `gone` made to do nothing the card stayed open after the pointer left. After Save to chapter the paragraph's bar was a new element and the card closed as the pointer left. The arrowhead still measures 11 by 39.09 CSS px, its middle 0.55 px from its line.
- **A focused small change's ghost sat on `--focus-bg`.** Category text on the dark focus yellow is 4.14:1 for spelling, 4.18 homophone, 4.28 punctuation and 4.03 other, under the 4.5 a category as text needs (light 4.70 and up), and no pair checked it. Compared in both themes on a spelling and a punctuation change: the fill dulled the ghost in dark, and a ring with no fill read as a keycap round the whole ghost, which since `small.7` means named whitespace. The ghost is now unfilled, as a word-sized change's always was; the capsule's yellow, the arrowhead and the x mark the focus.

Questions for the author, with the contact sheet of `small.11`: whether case 1 bothered him because the change was hard to find again or because "WAS -" was unreadable; "period" or "full stop" (the app says "full stop"); whether a click on a bar should accept the change instead of selecting it; and whether the page stays calm with a page full of commas.

### C.69 Default is Opus 5.5 on Pro since CLI 2.1.280 (`setup.13`, 2026-10-19)

Section 1 said that what Default means depends on the account, "Opus on Max, Sonnet on Pro". That was true of the Claude Code the plan was written against, and stopped being true at 2.1.280; 11.1's Default model row had already given the newer fact, with the reason the Pro note matters.

- **What Anthropic's page says** (model-config, re-read 2026-10-19, Appendix A). With no model chosen, Claude Code's Default is Opus 5.5 on Pro, Max, Team, Enterprise and the Anthropic API. Before 2.1.280 it was Sonnet 5 on Pro and on Team Standard seats, and Opus 5 on the rest. The same version moved the `opus` alias to Opus 5.5; `sonnet` became Sonnet 5.5 at 2.1.284 and `haiku` Haiku 5.5 at 2.1.293. No plan's Default is a Fable model.
- **What it means for the app.** A new settings file says `model: 'default'`, which the app passes as no `--model` flag at all (`modelArgs`, `setup.1`). On Claude Code 2.1.280 or newer a review on a Pro plan therefore runs on Opus 5.5, which uses a Pro plan's limits fastest; before, it ran on Sonnet 5. Two things stand between a Pro user and that: the first welcome guide preselects Sonnet when its check finds a Pro plan ready and the model is still Default (`proPreselection`, C.67), and the review dialog's note beside the model list, "On a Pro plan, Opus models (including Default) use your limits fastest. Sonnet is usually enough for copyediting." (`PRO_PLAN_NOTE`), shows for Default and every Opus model. Section 1's row now says this.
- **What else decides Default, as the app runs Claude Code.** The page orders the choices: `--model` (the app passes it for every model but Default), `ANTHROPIC_MODEL` (removed from the child's environment, 11.3 c), a `model` in a settings file, which `/model` writes (not read, as the app passes `--setting-sources=`), then `ANTHROPIC_DEFAULT_MODEL` (2.1.236 and later), which passes through unchanged, so a user who set it gets that model as Default in the app too. An Enterprise organisation's default model (2.1.196 and later) and a model recorded on an Enterprise account by `/model` (2.1.280 and later) also change it. The model list labels Default with what Claude Code's `initialize` reply says it is on that machine and account (round 5), so the review dialog shows the model Default stands for.
- **Between 2.1.266 and 2.1.279.** `MIN_CLAUDE_CODE` is 2.1.266, so a Claude Code the app accepts can still make Sonnet 5 a Pro plan's Default, and there the note's "(including Default)" was wrong. Such a copy is older than `RECOMMENDED_CLAUDE_CODE` (2.1.283), so the review dialog and Setup show the update note with `claude update`, and a copy from Anthropic's installer updates itself; `setup.13` left the note as it was. `setup.17` makes it follow the model list, whose Default entry is labelled from the `initialize` reply (round 5): `defaultIsOpus` reads the family from that label ("Default: Sonnet 5"), and where it is not Opus, `proPlanNote` shows nothing while Default is chosen and, for an Opus model, "On a Pro plan, Opus models use your limits fastest. Sonnet is usually enough for copyediting." (`PRO_PLAN_NOTE_OPUS_ONLY`), without the parenthesis. Where the list has not come yet, or its Default label names no version, the note stays as it was, since Default is Opus 5.5 on every plan from 2.1.280. The same rule covers an `ANTHROPIC_DEFAULT_MODEL` that makes Default something other than Opus. Left as it is: the usage-limit card's advice for a limit every model shares (`WAIT_ADVICE`, `setup.9`) also says "Opus models (including Default)", shown on any plan after a review stopped at a limit; it is built where no model list is read (`usageLimitCard`, `setupStatus`), and on such a copy the update note already shows; a `MIN_CLAUDE_CODE` of 2.1.280 or later would retire the case for both.
- **Checked against the installed Claude Code** (2026-10-19; `claude --version` and `claude --help`, with no session started): 2.1.302, newer than 2.1.280. Its `--help` describes `--model` as an alias for the latest model, giving `fable`, `opus` and `sonnet` as examples, or a model's full name, and says nothing about the account's default, which only the `initialize` reply and the page give. This machine is signed in on a Max plan, so a Pro plan's Default was not seen; no review ran and no model list was asked for.

### C.70 No in-app sign-in launcher (`setup.13`, 2026-10-19)

11.0 cuts it in one line ("the legal page bars offering Claude login. Setup shows a command to copy."). This records what was weighed and what the app does instead.

- **What a launcher would have been.** A button on Setup or in the welcome guide that signs the author in: running `claude auth login` as a child of the app, opening a terminal with the command already typed, or opening the browser at Anthropic's sign-in page. Each makes the sign-in start from the app.
- **Why not.** The legal page (re-read 2026-10-19, Appendix A) says Anthropic does not let third-party developers offer Claude.ai login in their own applications, and that sign-in to a Claude account has to complete through Anthropic's own flow; it also says none of that stops an end user signing in to the unmodified Claude Code with their own subscription. A button in the app that starts the sign-in reads as the first; the user running Anthropic's command in their own terminal is the second. The Usage Policy that takes effect on 2026-11-12 also counts circumventing the log-in process among its bypasses (Appendix A). Nothing about the sign-in passes through the app: Claude Code keeps the login in `%USERPROFILE%\.claude\.credentials.json` (authentication page), which the app never reads (CLAUDE.md rule 2 (a); `test/shared/policy.test.ts` keeps the credential file's name, `setup-token` and `logout` out of the source).
- **What the app does instead** (5.6). Setup shows the view's command, `claude auth login` or the one line that installs Claude Code and signs in, with Copy, on the tab of the user's system, and the full-path form where a terminal may not find `claude`. The author runs it in their own terminal, where Claude Code opens the browser at Anthropic's page, or prints the link and reads a pasted code. Setup checks again as its window comes back to the front, and Test the connection shows a request going through. `runClaudeCli` refuses every command but `--version` and `auth status --json`, and the tests of Setup and the welcome guide (`setupScreen.render.test.ts`, `welcome.test.ts`) find no button labelled like a sign-in.
- **Checked against the installed Claude Code** (2.1.302, 2026-10-19; help output only, no sign-in started). `claude --help` lists `auth` and `setup-token`; `claude auth --help` lists `login`, `logout` and `status`; `claude auth login --help` gives `--claudeai` (a Claude subscription, the default), `--console` (Console billing), `--email` and `--sso`; `claude auth status --help` gives `--json` (the default) and `--text`. So the commands Setup shows exist as written, and `claude auth login` with no flag signs in with a Claude plan. The top-level help also says `--bare` takes Anthropic sign-in only from `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` or an `apiKeyHelper` and never reads OAuth, which is why the app never passes it (CLAUDE.md rule 6).
- **The cost.** A trip to a terminal on the first run, and again whenever a sign-in ends. The install line signs in as soon as it has installed, so a first run is one paste, and Setup's Troubleshooting covers a browser that does not open.

### C.71 An ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN is the token, not a Claude plan (`setup.17`, 2026-10-19)

The `setup.13` review left open how the check reads an `ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN`, the bearer token that Anthropic's authentication page ranks above an API key and the subscription sign-in, for a gateway or proxy (Appendix A, Authentication). `setup.17` added `--auth-token-dummy` to `dev:clean`, which sets it to a dummy token as `--api-key-dummy` sets a dummy key, and looked.

- **What Claude Code says** (2.1.302, 2026-10-19). Its two answers were also read outside the app, with the app's flags and no prompt, in an empty configuration folder of the scratch directory's own (`auth status --json` and the `initialize` exchange; dummy token and key; only the fields the app keeps were printed). With the token, `auth status` gives `loggedIn` true, `authMethod` `oauth_token`, `apiProvider` `firstParty` and no key; the `initialize` account gives `tokenSource` `ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN` and `apiProvider`, with no email, plan or key. Over this machine's own Max sign-in the token wins: the same answers, no email, and a line on stderr that the claude.ai connectors are off because another auth source takes precedence over the claude.ai login. Beside an `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`, both answers add `apiKeySource` `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`, and `auth status` still says `oauth_token`. For comparison: signed out, `tokenSource` `none`; the key alone, `tokenSource` `none` with the key's source; and this machine's plain sign-in, `email`, `organization`, `subscriptionType` (`Claude Max`) and `apiProvider`, with neither `tokenSource` nor `apiKeySource`. So 2.1.302 never gives the `apiKeySource` `none` that made Settings' Claude account row read "key from none" (`test/main/claudeRuntime.test.ts` keeps one in its fixture; the row now passes over it, `setup.17` (d)).
- **What the app made of it.** In a quiet `dev:clean --auth-token-dummy --claude-config <empty folder>` window, before the fix: ready, with the credential `subscription`, from `oauth_token`; no launch card; the status bar "Claude ready"; Setup "Claude is ready", "Claude Code 2.1.302 is signed in. Review with AI can use Claude.", Advanced "a Claude plan, auth method oauth_token" and Test the connection's note "counts against your plan"; Settings' row "signed in". The token is not a plan's: it displaces the sign-in, and its requests are billed to whoever issued it. So `classifyClaude` misread it, and `setup.17` fixes that.
- **The fix.** `ClaudeCredential` gains `auth-token`, which `classifyClaude` gives when the account's `tokenSource` is `ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN` and no cloud provider is named, ahead of the API key rule, in the page's order (cloud provider, token, key). The view stays `ready`, so the welcome guide and the launch card are unchanged; the card says "Claude Code 2.1.302 signs in with the token in ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN, such as a gateway or proxy hands out, so reviews are billed to the account behind that token, not through your Claude sign-in. Review with AI can use Claude." and "To use your Claude sign-in instead, remove ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN from your environment and start <APP_NAME> again."; the status bar "Claude ready (token)"; Advanced "a token from ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN, auth method oauth_token"; the test note "Sends one very small request to Claude, which is billed to the account behind your ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN like any other."; Settings' row "signed in, token from ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN". The same window after the fix showed exactly these. Without the `initialize` account, when only `auth status` answers, `oauth_token` still reads as a plan, as nothing there tells the token from a plan's own.
- **Not done.** No model request was sent: the check sends none and Test the connection was not pressed, so how a request with a token that is refused fails is not known. `buildClaudeEnv` passes `ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN` through unchanged, as it does `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` (11.3 c), so a review uses it as the check found it.

### C.72 What the syntax detector counts where 11.3 (k) left it open (`files.6`, 2026-10-19)

11.3 (k) lists the kinds of syntax a model's suggestion must leave alone; `src/shared/text/obsidian.ts` had to settle their edges. CommonMark and Obsidian's help (Tags, Internal links and Callouts, read 2026-10-19) settled most of them. These are the choices that were the plan's own, each pinned by `test/shared/obsidian.test.ts`. The `files.6` review found 19 mutations of the detector, one rule each, that passed every test; since its fix, 35 such mutations, those 19 among them, each make a test fail.

- **Unclosed openers.** (k) has an unclosed `%%`, `<!--` or `$$` protect only its opening marker. An unclosed code fence does the same, although CommonMark and Obsidian run one to the end of the note: otherwise a stray fence, or a `~~~` used once as a scene break, would make the rest of the chapter code, hidden from the reviewer (`files.8`) and closed to every suggestion. Two such lines still enclose code, as Obsidian shows them. A closed fence's span is whole lines, from the start of its opening line to the end of its closing one, so a paragraph inside it lies wholly inside the span.
- **HTML.** Attribute syntax means a `name=value` attribute. A real element counts with no attributes or only ones with values (`<br/>`, `<span class="aside">`, `</span>`, in any case: `<BR>`), and any name counts with at least one `name=value` (`<x-note data-id="1">`). A bare word after the name is not an attribute here: CommonMark would read `<I know.>` as an `<i>` tag with an attribute `know.`, and angle-bracket dialogue is prose (`files.8`). The cost is that a tag whose only attributes are bare, such as `<details open>`, goes unprotected, though a suggestion that touches its `<` or `>` is still kept out by the markup rule.
- **Frontmatter and `bodyStart`.** The frontmatter is what `frontmatterRange` finds, as for `splitParagraphs`. Its span takes the line break after the closing `---`, and `bodyStart` is just past that break, so an insertion straight after the `---`, which would break the fence, comes before the body and is kept out as frontmatter. Where the body starts on the very next line, with no blank line between, `splitParagraphs` started the first paragraph at that line break, one character before `bodyStart`, until `files.22` started it at `bodyStart` (C.76). A paragraph does not start a note, so the guard reads one alone with `{ frontmatter: false }` (`syntaxSpans` and `syntaxSignature` both take it; the default, for a whole chapter, looks for frontmatter). Read as a note, a body paragraph that starts with a `---` line and has another below it, such as `---\nThree days later.\n---` between scene breaks, would be frontmatter, prose and all, where the chapter has two horizontal rules, and every copyedit in it would be kept out as frontmatter. Read with the option, a body paragraph that no span of its chapter crosses finds just what the chapter finds in it. One that a comment, maths or code fence runs into or out of across a blank line can read differently, as a construct is found only where it opens and closes inside the text given; the overlap rule, which uses the chapter's spans, keeps out a suggestion inside such a span first.
- **Tags.** By Obsidian's help a tag's name holds letters and digits of any script, emoji, `_`, `-` and `/`, and something besides digits (`#1984` is not a tag, `#y1984` is). The name ends at whitespace, at any other ASCII punctuation, and at the general and supplemental punctuation blocks (dashes, curly quotes, the ellipsis). A `#` counts at the start of a line, after whitespace or `(`, as (k) says, and also straight after a line's quote markers (`>#todo`).
- **Line markers.** A block quote marker's span takes the one space after it, as a heading's `#`s do. After quote markers the rest of the line is read as a line of its own, so headings, horizontal rules and footnote definitions are found in quotes, and a callout's `[!type]` only there. Up to three spaces may come before a marker; a tab makes the line indented prose, so a paragraph indented with a tab has none. A `---` under a line of text, which CommonMark reads as that line's heading underline, is a horizontal rule here; it is syntax either way.
- **Links and the rest.** Link destinations follow CommonMark: in angle brackets, or without spaces and with balanced parentheses (Obsidian's help asks for `%20`), then an optional title. Inline code, link text and an inline footnote never cross a blank line; comments, maths and fences do. Block IDs are Latin letters, digits and dashes after a space or at the start of a line, with nothing after them on the line but spaces. A bare web address ends at whitespace, `<`, `>`, `"`, a backtick, `|` or a span already found, and leaves out the punctuation that ends a sentence and a `)` or `]` that closes nothing inside it, as GitHub's autolinks do.
- **Escapes.** A character after an odd number of backslashes opens nothing: `\#draft` is no tag. The backslash is not in `MARKUP_CHARS`, so a suggestion that adds or removes one is caught by the signature check instead (the last rule of (k)): `\#draft` and `#draft` have different signatures.
- **Labels.** `SYNTAX_LABELS` uses Obsidian's names where it has them, for the kept-out note: "an internal link", "an embed", "a callout", "a block ID", "a horizontal rule", with "a web address" for a URL and "maths" for `$$`.
- **Speed.** About 6 ms for a 60,000-character chapter (Chapter 01 forty times over, with links, tags, footnotes, comments and callouts added). Each unmatched `[` or backtick looks to the end of its paragraph for a close, so a made-up 95,000-character paragraph holding 5,000 of each took about 220 ms.

### C.73 What the guard settled where 11.3 (k) left it open (`files.7`, 2026-10-19)

`src/shared/diff/protect.ts` applies the guard rules of 11.3 (k) to a model's suggestions. These are the choices that were its own, each pinned by `test/shared/protect.test.ts`.

- **A paragraph count that changes gives `paragraph-break`.** (k) had a change to the signature or the paragraph count give "the kind or `markup`". A signature that changes always names a kind (next point), so `markup` would have been left for a suggestion that adds or removes a paragraph without touching syntax, such as deleting a one-line paragraph, or the only words on a line inside one, where "a markup character" would name a character the suggestion does not hold. It gives `paragraph-break`, as a suggestion that crosses a blank line does: both change where paragraphs break. The count is `countParagraphs` in `text/paragraphs.ts`, which splits as `splitParagraphs` does with no frontmatter looked for. `markup` is left for the markup characters.
- **Which kind a changed signature names.** The paragraph's spans before and after the suggestion, each as kind and text, compared from both ends: the first that differs as it was, or the first one the suggestion adds when it takes nothing away. A word run into `#draft` names a tag; `example.com` made into `https://example.com` names a web address; `example.com #draft` made into `https://example.com#draft` names the tag the address now runs through, not the address; taking the backslash from `\#draft` in front of an address names the tag, not the address that stays.
- **An insertion at the edge of a span.** "Strictly inside" leaves an insertion at either edge of a span to the signature rule, which keeps `[[Mill]]s` and `See the [[Mill]]`, where the link is as it was, and keeps out `x#draft` (no tag any more) and `#drafts` (another tag).
- **A paragraph the chapter reads in a wider context** (the `files.7` review). A paragraph read alone shows what its chapter shows there only while nothing outside it reaches in (C.72). The review found a suggestion the signature rule let through: in a chapter whose code block holds a blank line, `.` or ` x` added after the closing fence. Read alone, the paragraph's closing fence is an unclosed opener whose run stays as it was, and the suggestion holds no markup character, yet the fence would no longer close, and the code after the blank line would read as prose. So, last of the rules, a suggestion in such a paragraph must also keep the chapter's `syntaxSignature` read whole, and is kept out with the kind of what changed otherwise, named as for a paragraph but over the whole chapter (`code` here). Two things make the wider context. One is a span of the chapter crossing the paragraph's start or end, a fence, comment or maths holding a blank line; adding an indent to the opening fence of one that runs out of its paragraph changes the block's text, which only the end crossing shows. The other is an opener the chapter leaves unclosed before the paragraph, which a line of it could close: the same check found `~~~ The end` made into `~~~`, and `- >` or `->` made into `-->`, closing an earlier `~~~` or `<!--` and turning the paragraphs between into code or a comment. Only a code fence or `<!--` can be closed by a line that reads as nothing new alone, so only those count, and only when the suggestion's line, as it would read, is a fence line or holds `-->`; a new `%%` or `$$` is an opener when read alone too, so the paragraph's own signature changes. Without that last condition one stray `~~~` near the top, a scene break perhaps, made every later suggestion read the whole chapter.
- **The touching rule.** The later of the two hunks is kept out, and only when the guard screens it; the one before may be any hunk on the page, an accepted suggestion or the author's own edit included, since the page may show that hunk's replacement beside it. A hunk this rule keeps out is off the page, so of three suggestions side by side the second goes and the third stays. Hunks are taken by position, whatever their order in the review. "On the line" holds unless the hunk before ends with a line break, which only one the guard does not screen can hold. The rule has the false positives 11.5 expects: two punctuation fixes side by side, `dark,stormy` made into `dark; stormy` by two suggestions, keep the second out. It runs within the overlap pass (`touchingRule`, `AnchorOptions.touching`, the `files.7` review), so a hunk it keeps out is off the page before the hunks after it are measured, and pushes none of them off as an overlap: of `ab`, `cd` and `d e` in `abcd efgh`, each made into capitals, `cd` touches `ab` and is kept out, and `d`, which overlapped only `cd`, stays. Run after the pass, as `files.7` first had it, `d` went too, as an overlap of a hunk that was no longer on the page. A loaded review's hunks never overlap, so `guardTouching` applies the same rule to them without a pass.
- **Labels and the reason.** The three reasons that are not a kind of syntax read "a paragraph break", "a markup character" and "together with the suggestion before it" (`KEPT_OUT_LABELS`). A reason that a later version writes and this one does not know gets the note without the brackets. The note is worded from `keptOut` when the side panel draws it, unlike "Could not find this text in the chapter." and "Overlapped an earlier suggestion.", which go into `reason` in brackets, so a kept-out suggestion keeps the model's own reason.
- **Kept out through a rebase.** `files.20` lists "kept-out hunks are never re-located" among its rebase rules. Without it, the next change on disk would find a kept-out suggestion's words and put it back on the page with `keptOut` still set; the guard passes over such a hunk, so it would stay on the page, out of Unanchored and without its note. A review that comes back while the file has changed is rebased at once, too (App.tsx). So `rebaseReview` leaves a hunk with `keptOut` as it is from `files.7` on; `files.20` gave the rebase the rest of the guard's rules (C.74).
- **Where it runs.** `createAiReview` screens before `resolveOverlaps` and runs the touching rule within it, and since `files.20` so does `rebaseReview` (C.74); `upgradeLoadedReview` runs `guardLoadedReview` on every review main reads, History's summaries included, which are cached by modification time and size. A chapter's suggestions kept out by the screen come first under Unanchored in a new review, since `resolveOverlaps` sorts them by their offset 0, then those kept out by the touching rule and those overlapped, in the order of their places, then those never found.
- **Speed.** On a 60,000-character chapter (Chapter 01 with links, tags, a footnote, a comment, code and a callout, repeated) with 300 pending suggestions, `guardLoadedReview` took about 6 ms (16 ms on its first run), and `createAiReview` with 150 changes about 4 ms. After the `files.7` review the same took about 5 ms and 4.5 ms, and about 5 ms with a stray unclosed `~~~` at the top, where reading the whole chapter for every later suggestion, without asking for a fence line or `-->`, took about 360 ms. Reading the chapter whole costs about 1.3 ms a suggestion at that length, paid only by one in a paragraph a span runs into or out of: 300 of them, all beside 35 code blocks that hold blank lines, took about 390 ms, a made-up worst case.

### C.74 What a rebase may place, and what its cards count (`files.20`, 2026-10-19)

`files.20` gave `rebaseReview` the rest of the guard's rules (4.5 steps 2 and 3, 6.2). These are the choices that were its own, each pinned by `test/shared/rebase.test.ts`, `protect.test.ts`, `properties.test.ts` or `rebaseCard.test.ts`.

- **The body only, for every source.** The rule is about where a hunk may go, so it holds for the author's own edits, the hunks of a manual review and decided suggestions as well as for those the guard screens: a change on disk that left a hunk's words only in the frontmatter (an alias, a title, a summary copied from the chapter) put the hunk there, out of sight in the page's frontmatter block, and Save would have written an accepted one into the properties. So the rebase reads nothing before `bodyStart` of the new text: no occurrence of a hunk's words that starts there is a candidate, a place may be found through surroundings that start there but may not lie there, no copy of the words there is weighed against a place (`settleCopies`), occurrences there do not count against "the only such words in the file", and the fuzzy search reads the body alone. That last differs from 4.3 step 3, which refuses a fuzzy match before `bodyStart`: reading the body alone finds words changed a little in the body even where an exact copy stands in the frontmatter, which a refused match would have sent to Unanchored. `bodyStart` itself is in the body: a hunk on the first word of a body that follows the closing `---` at once, the usual layout in Obsidian, an insertion at its top and a fuzzy match from it are placed there. The `files.20` review found three mutations that refused just that offset, for places, words and the fuzzy search, passing every test; a case in `rebase.test.ts` and the property's frontmatters that end on the closing line now pin it.
- **What it gives up.** A hunk that already starts before `bodyStart` goes to Unanchored at the next change on disk. Two are made today: the deletion of the line break after the closing `---`, which the paragraph box makes when the body starts on the next line, and a paragraph a manual review adds at the top of the body, which the full-text diff places at the end of the frontmatter, where the page does not show it. Off the page, the first can no longer reach the file at a later Save. `files.22` is to stop both being made. It did, and a review saved with one now loads with it off the page as well (C.76).
- **Decided suggestions are the author's.** The screen keeps to the guard's own set (11.3 k): a suggestion accepted or dismissed before the change on disk is placed where it is found, inside syntax the author has just made or not, as when a review loads, and Save writes an accepted one there as it would have before the change. The CHANGELOG line first said that a suggestion the change put into syntax is kept out, whatever its decision; since the `files.20` review it names the undecided ones and says to look over an accepted one before saving.
- **Off the page, never taken as made** (the `files.20` review). `apply.23`'s "only such words in the file" let a hunk's other side win where it stood once, and a hunk already off the page has no place in the old text, so in practice only that rule could apply to it: a model's never-found "teh river" was taken as made once "the river" stood once in the chapter, and dismissed, Save would have written "teh river", text the chapter never held. `files.20` widened it, since a copy in the frontmatter, a summary perhaps, no longer counted against the one in the body, and its tick wrongly said it had not changed it. Nothing about a hunk off the page shows that its other side, wherever it stands, is the change made or undone there, so `plainlyOnDisk` refuses it: it comes back only on its own side's words, its decision as it was, and a saved change off the page is not turned back into a suggestion where its old words stand either.
- **What the cards count.** `newlyStale` is the hunks on the page before the rebase and off it after, not kept out: those it could not find or could not place plainly (4.5 step 3), and those pushed off as an overlap. One already under Unanchored is not news, whether it was never found, overlapped or kept out, and the cards counted them all until `files.20`, so the reload card warned at every change on disk while one was there ("3 could not be found" in the `files.7` window check, all three kept out). `keptOut` is the suggestions this rebase kept out, one that was off the page and is found again inside syntax included, but not those kept out before. Kept out, a suggestion has its own sentence on the card and no warning: it is under Unanchored with the note that says why, as the guard meant. The history card stays an information card and the saving card a warning; the opened and reloaded cards take their tone from `newlyStale` (`rebaseCardTone`).
- **A run of reloads** (the `files.20` review). "One already under Unanchored is not news" held only for a card the author saw: each reload replaces the reload card, and Obsidian saves on a debounce while the author types, so a card that warned "2 could not be found" was replaced two seconds later by "Reloaded from disk. 0 suggestions re-anchored, 0 could not be found." as an information card (seen in a quiet `dev:clean` window). Before `files.20` the count was every suggestion under Unanchored, so it never fell short. So while the card is up, the next reload's card reports the run since it went up (`mergeReloadRun`, from the ids in `RebaseResult.changes`). The review proposed adding each reload's counts; that counts a suggestion twice when one reload takes it off the page and a later one keeps it out, and counts as lost one a later reload found again, as when a paragraph is cut in Obsidian, saved, and pasted back. The run therefore keeps ids: "could not be found" is those any reload of the run took off the page and that are off it still and not kept out, the kept-out sentence those any of them kept out, and the decisions those any of them changed, each once, while "re-anchored" is the latest reload's. The tone follows, so a run warns while a suggestion it lost is still lost. App keeps the run with the card's id; a reload of another review, the card closed with its X, or a chapter or a review opened starts a new one. The opened, history and saving cards have no key and stay, so they need no run.
- **Speed.** On a 60,000-character chapter (Chapter 01 repeated, with a frontmatter and, in each copy, an internal link, a tag, a web address, a footnote, a comment, a callout and a code block) with 300 suggestions, 222 on the page, a rebase after a line typed near the top took about 17.5 ms, against 12.2 ms before `files.20`; the screen and the overlap pass took about 4.3 ms of it.

### C.75 What the prompt hides, and what its Obsidian rule says (`files.8`, 2026-10-19)

`files.8` gave the prompt the Obsidian rule (5.4) and the hidden line for a paragraph lying wholly inside a comment, code or maths (5.2). These are the choices that were its own, each pinned by `test/shared/prompt.test.ts`.

- **"Wholly inside" is every character but white space, in one span or several.** Read as "inside one span", an indented `%%` note, one with spaces after its closing `%%`, or a paragraph of two `%%` lines or of a `%%` line and an HTML comment would have been sent, though nothing in them is prose. So a paragraph is hidden when every character of it but white space lies inside a `comment`, `code` or `math` span, whichever. The spans are the chapter's, read whole (`syntaxSpans(text)`), never the paragraph's alone: a code block or a comment that holds a blank line is two paragraphs, and read alone the second would start with words and end with an opener nothing closes (C.72), so it would be sent. Read whole, each paragraph of it is hidden. A paragraph of an inline code span alone, `` `like this` ``, is hidden too: it is code.
- **What is still sent.** A note beside prose in one paragraph (`Rain %% Ellen %% fell.`) is sent as written, note and all, as is the part of a note in a paragraph that a comment runs into or out of when prose follows it: hiding it would hide the prose, and anchoring needs the paragraph as it is. The rule tells the model to leave a note alone, and the guard keeps out any suggestion inside one (11.3 k). An unclosed `%%`, `<!--`, `$$` or code fence is a span of its marker alone (C.72), so the words after a stray one are sent, and a paragraph that is nothing but a lone marker is hidden, with nothing in it to correct. Two `~~~` lines used as scene breaks enclose code, as Obsidian shows them (C.72), so the paragraphs between them are hidden from the model as well as closed to suggestions. Frontmatter is left out as before, and no other kind of syntax hides a paragraph: one that is only a link, an embed, a tag, a rule, a callout's marker, a web address or HTML is sent.
- **Numbers and count.** A hidden paragraph keeps its number and counts in `paragraphs="..."`, so a comment that cites "paragraph 12" still means the paragraph labelled 12 on the page (5.2). Leaving it out would have renumbered everything after it.
- **The rule is in the static part.** The guidelines template has had an Obsidian bullet since `setup.10`, but an author's own `GUIDELINES.md` is never changed, and the samples' copy predates it. The static part states it for every review, guidelines or none. It gives an example of each kind of syntax as it is written in a note, since the chapter shows the model the syntax, not its name.
- **One sentence beyond the task's list: the markup rule as the guard applies it.** The rule also tells the model never to add, remove or change one of `[ ] % $ ^ # < > | ~`, a backtick or a line break, nor to let one change alter words on both sides of one, as the app sets such a change aside; to change only words and ordinary punctuation and give each place its own change; and that quoting those characters unchanged around the words it changes is fine. That is the guard's markup rule (11.3 k) as the guard reads it: on a suggestion's `original` and `replacement` after `anchorChanges` has trimmed them to the part that differs, widened back only over word characters (`trimCommonAffixes`), so a markup character quoted unchanged at either edge is gone before the guard looks. `<where are you>` to `<Where are you?>` gives `where are you` to `Where are you?`, `|teh mill` to `|the mill` and `[teh old map]` to `[the old map]` give `teh` to `the`, and a fix to a footnote's or a callout's words that quotes its marker stays on the page too. What is set aside is a change whose differing part holds or spans one: `5 dollars` to `$5`, `<come here>` made into `"Come here."`, or `teh word #draft and teh` as one change (kept out as a tag), where one change for each `teh` would have stayed on the page. The sentence is there to head those off. As first written it said a change was set aside whenever its `before` or `after` held one of the characters, and told the model to quote only the words, so the reason given here was that a fix quoting angle brackets or an alias's `|` would always be kept out. Neither held, and the sentence pulled against the first rule for `changes` (copy `before` exactly, Markdown markers included, and keep it unique): a model could leave out the context that made its quote unique, for no gain. The `files.8` review found it; in a quiet `dev:clean` window against the repository's OpenAI mock, each of the fixes above that quoted brackets, a `|`, `^[`, `[^1]:` or `> [!note]` was on the page, and `$5` and the change across the tag were under Unanchored, before the fix and after it. The link bullet's "Quote only those words" became "Change only those words" for the same reason. `test/shared/protect.test.ts` pins the guard's side through `createAiReview`.
- **A footnote and a callout by their markers alone.** The guard protects a footnote reference such as `[^1]` whole, the `[^1]:` that starts a definition's line, an inline footnote's `^[` and its `]`, and a callout's `[!type]` and the `>` before each of its lines (11.3 k); the words of a footnote, an inline footnote and a callout's title and body are prose it leaves open (`files.6`). As first written the rule listed footnotes and callouts among what to leave exactly as written, with `^[...]` contents and all, so a model following it would skip a typo the app lets through. It now names their markers, and lists their words among the words a reader sees, which may be corrected (the `files.8` review). The guidelines template's Obsidian bullet (`setup.10`) still names footnotes and callouts whole. Where an author's `GUIDELINES.md` carries it, it follows the rule and takes precedence, so the model may leave those words alone, which is the safe side; the template is not changed here.
- **The hidden line is one constant.** `HIDDEN_PARAGRAPH` in `prompt/chapter.ts` is what `renderChapter` sends and what `STATIC_INSTRUCTIONS` quotes, so the two cannot drift apart.
- **Checked once, live.** One review through the author's Claude Code (Sonnet 5.5, effort low, about 3 s) of a scratch Chapter 01 with a `%%` note, holding `teh`, added as paragraph 6: the prompt held `[6] (author's note or code, hidden; skip it)` and none of the note; the reply named the six seeded errors (`had began`, `should of`, `the the`, `would loose`, `Its a sound`, `water come`) and `nodded her head`, in paragraphs 1, 2, 3, 4, 8, 10 and 7, numbered as the prompt numbered them, all on the page, and nothing for paragraph 6, with no comments at all. Sonnet 5.5 was used in place of Haiku: the verification runs allow a real review only on Haiku at effort low, as `apply.18` ran one, and no reason for the choice was recorded. The `files.8` review found it; no second live review was run. Chapter 01, rather than a three-paragraph chapter, follows `files.8`'s own text.
- **Speed.** About 2 ms to render a 61,000-character chapter (Chapter 01 repeated, with a link, a tag, a note, a code block holding a blank line, maths and an inline note in each copy; 164 paragraphs hidden).

### C.76 Where the first paragraph starts, and where the full-text diff puts a paragraph added at the top (`files.22`, 2026-10-19)

`files.22` was to stop the paragraph box and the full-text diff making hunks before `bodyStart`, either by starting the first paragraph at `bodyStart` in `splitParagraphs` or by leaving the line break alone in `planBlockEdit` and `diffToHunks`. These are the choices it made, each pinned by `test/shared/paragraphs.test.ts`, `edit.test.ts`, `wordDiff.test.ts`, `protect.test.ts`, `prompt.test.ts`, `drafts.test.ts`, `properties.test.ts` or `test/renderer/store.test.ts`.

- **`splitParagraphs`, not the box and the diff.** The line break inside the first paragraph was one cause with more effects than the two the task named. The box opened with an empty first line and Done deleted it; the page drew an empty line above the first words, as paragraphs are `pre-wrap`; the prompt sent `[1] ` and a line break; a manual review whose text had a blank line under the frontmatter compared `\nFirst` with `First` and deleted the break, and, in the same layout, one that added a paragraph at the top found no first paragraph equal to its own, so it paired the new paragraph with the first one as a rewrite and put the first one back after it; and a comment's 40-character key compared the two as well (`remapComment`). Leaving the break alone in `planBlockEdit` and `diffToHunks` would have mended the two named and left the rest, each needing the same rule again. So the first paragraph starts at `bodyStart`, and every reader of the paragraphs has it at once.
- **Both ends, and lines of spaces.** The rule is that no paragraph starts or ends with a line break: blank lines at either end of a span, which a separator of two line breaks or more does not take, belong to no paragraph. Besides the line break after the closing `---`, that takes in a text that starts with a blank line (no frontmatter) and one that ends with one, past the final newline `normalizeText` keeps apart, a file ending in two line breaks: in both Done with nothing typed deleted that line break too, at the top or at the end. A line of spaces or tabs is blank, as for the separator; spaces before the first words stay, as indentation, which `normalizeDraft` keeps as well.
- **Every caller checked.** No paragraph appears or goes, only the edges of the first and the last move, so every index is as it was: the numbers in the prompt and on the rail, `Hunk.paragraph` and each comment's paragraph (a property in `paragraphs.test.ts` counts the paragraphs against `countParagraphs` over 1,000 layouts). `buildRenderBlocks` starts the first block at `bodyStart`, and through it `blockSpanFor`, the box, `placeDrafts` and the page; `deletionSpan` keeps the break when the first paragraph is emptied, where it took it before, and `---Second` was written. `renderChapter` sends `[1] First words`. `anchorChanges` looks for a quote in the paragraph's words, and an offset at the break still gives paragraph 0 (`paragraphIndexAt`). `rebaseReview`, `remapAfterCommit` and `repairCommentAnchors` split the old and the new text alike. `stats.ts` counts the same words. `screenModelHunks` reads the first paragraph as it reads any other: the frontmatter span ends at `bodyStart`, so it no longer crosses the paragraph's start, and `readsWider` no longer reads the whole chapter for each suggestion there. The verdicts are the same, as a paragraph that no span crosses finds what the chapter finds (C.72); only the time differs, which no test sees, so `protect.test.ts`'s first-paragraph case pins the verdicts on a body that follows the closing line at once.
- **Where the full-text diff puts an added paragraph.** After the paragraph before it, behind a blank line, as before. At the top of the body, before the first body paragraph, at its start and followed by a blank line, as was done at offset 0 for a text with no frontmatter; several go in at the same place in their order, each its own suggestion (compose keeps the order of hunks at one place). In a body with no paragraph at all, at the end of the text, which is never before `bodyStart`: the first with no blank line before it when the text is empty or ends with a line break, behind one otherwise (`---` then a blank line). Such a chapter, frontmatter alone, has no block of the page to draw it in, so it is listed only in the suggestions list, a case the task did not name. Once saved, the paragraph is there to draw it in, and the save moves it to the paragraph's start ("After Save", below).
- **A deletion at the end of the text.** The `files.22` property found that an unpaired removed paragraph at the end of a text that ends in blank lines was deleted together with them, past the end of the paragraph's block, so the page did not draw it, before `files.22` as well. It took the blank line after it only where a paragraph follows, and so, at the end of the text, none at all, which the `files.22` review found left a deletion the page does not draw once saved, before `files.22` too: the blank line before it then ended the chapter, with the deletion past the last paragraph (in a quiet window, the last paragraph of a scratch chapter deleted with Submit manual review and saved, the file ended `noon.` and three line breaks, and the accepted deletion was drawn nowhere). Where no paragraph follows the block, a deletion now takes the blank line before it, as the paragraph box deletes a last paragraph (`deletionSpan`), except the first paragraph of the body, which has none before it: accepted and saved, the chapter ends at the words that stay, and the deletion is drawn at the end of the paragraph before it. That holds whatever is decided for each of several such deletions; the review's property found that the blank line after one, taken where only deleted paragraphs follow it, ended the chapter once it was kept and those after it were deleted and saved.
- **Reviews saved before.** With the first block starting at `bodyStart`, a hunk at the break is in no block: the page no longer draws it, and Save would still write it, putting the first words on the `---` line. The same holds at both ends of the rule (the `files.22` review): in a text with no frontmatter that starts with a blank line, and in one that ends with a blank line, a file that ends in two line breaks, the old box's Done deleted that line break, alone or joined to the first or last words (`First` made into `Early` as `\nFirst` to `Early`, `words.` made into `words!` as `.\n` to `!`), and the page draws neither, while Save writes them and a box opened on that paragraph again could make a hunk that overlaps one (CLAUDE.md rule 5; the review showed it in node, and in a quiet window such a review opened on a page that read `Last words.` with "1 not saved to chapter", and Save wrote `Last words!`). As first written the load step took off only a hunk that starts before `bodyStart`, which is 0 without a frontmatter and never reaches the end. So `upgradeLoadedReview` runs `unanchorOutsideBody` before the guard: a hunk still on the page that the page does not draw, one that starts before the first body paragraph or ends past the last, is taken off it as a rebase takes one, `anchor: 'stale'` at offset 0, its words and decision kept, and listed under Unanchored, where the author can make it again with the pen. A zero-width hunk at the very start of the first paragraph or the very end of the last is drawn there and stays. In a body with no paragraph, where the page has no block, only a hunk that starts before `bodyStart` is taken off. That also takes off the full-text diff's deletion of a last paragraph that took the blank lines ending the text ("A deletion at the end of the text"), which the page did not draw either. A model suggestion the guard screens is left to the screen, which keeps it out as `frontmatter`, or as `paragraph-break` when it lies in no paragraph. Nothing the app makes since `files.22` has such a hunk, before Save or after it ("After Save", below). Mending such a hunk in place, by taking the break out of its `original`, was not chosen: the decision was made on the hunk as it was, and changing what it does on load would be a guess at what the author meant.
- **After Save.** The `files.22` review found, in a window, that a chapter of frontmatter alone ended up with an Unanchored hunk the app had made and saved itself: Submit manual review added a paragraph, inserted at the end of the text `---\ntitle: Empty\n---` as `\n\nA new start.`, accepted and saved. Once written, that suggestion holds the line break that closes the frontmatter and the blank line, so it starts before `bodyStart` and before the paragraph: the page drew it nowhere, and opened again it was under Unanchored, counted there and no longer as accepted. No place at which the diff could insert it avoids that, since the paragraph needs the closing line break, so the save moves it (`intoFirstParagraph`, run by `remapAfterCommit`): a hunk the save leaves starting in the blank text before the first body paragraph starts at the paragraph instead, the blank text left out of the side the base holds (here `A new start.` from `(nothing)`, accepted, drawn at the top of paragraph 1). Taken out again, its words go and the frontmatter's closing line break and the blank line stay. A zero-width one at that place, a paragraph added there ahead of the one accepted and left undecided or dismissed, goes to the paragraph's start too, its words followed by that blank text (`\n\nA.` becomes `A.\n\n`), so paragraphs keep their order when it is accepted later; where the text ended with a line break, so that its words went in with no blank line before them, accepting it later keeps the blank line the saved paragraph brought before them, and that is all that differs. The same happens to a deletion that takes the blank line before it ("A deletion at the end of the text"), left undecided while every paragraph before it was deleted and saved. Narrowing the load step and the page to skip such a hunk was the other way the review named; it would have drawn the frontmatter's closing line break in the first paragraph's block.
- **Paragraph boxes kept from before.** A box kept on disk (`apply.16`) for the first paragraph of such a chapter opened on the line break and the words, and no longer reads as its block does, so `placeDrafts` sets it aside as a .txt when it was typed in and drops it otherwise, `apply.16`'s rule for a box whose paragraph changed, rather than a special case for the few boxes kept before `files.22`.
- **Speed.** `splitParagraphs` takes about 0.1 ms on a 55,000-character chapter of 400 paragraphs (Chapter 01 forty times over, with a frontmatter and the body on the next line).

### C.77 What a review says when the chapter or its reply does not fit (`files.10`, 2026-10-19)

`files.10` gave the two thresholds and asked for clearer output-limit errors, and left the rest open.
