- **What Claude Code sends.** Read from the bundled code of the installed Claude Code 2.1.302, since no run here could provoke it: that would take a chapter long enough to spend a large share of the author's plan. A reply that stops at `max_tokens` is held back and resumed, up to three times, by a hidden "Output token limit hit. Resume directly" message. Once those attempts are used up, Claude Code sends an assistant message with `error` and `api_error` both `max_output_tokens` and the text "API Error: Claude's response exceeded the 32000 output token maximum. To configure this behavior, set the CLAUDE_CODE_MAX_OUTPUT_TOKENS environment variable." (with the limit in force), adding " The last attempt reached the limit while still thinking. Lower the effort level to leave room for a reply." when thinking used it up; the error result repeats the text and carries the same `api_error`. A full context window comes with the same error and "API Error: The model has reached its context window limit."; a chapter too long to send is an `invalid_request` whose text starts "Prompt is too long". Running out of turns is `error_max_turns` with "Reached maximum number of turns (3)", and of schema retries `error_max_structured_output_retries` with "Failed to provide valid structured output after N attempts". `test/helpers/fakeClaude.ts` plays these shapes. `MIN_CLAUDE_CODE` stays: a Claude Code that sends only the error or only the text is read the same way, and one that sends neither gets the messages it got before.
- **Strong and weak signs.** The text, the assistant `error` and the result's `api_error` say the run ended at a limit, and are read before the assistant-error table (`claudeReplyLimit`); the text tells a full context window from the output limit, which share the error. A last reply that stopped at `max_tokens` says only that the reply was cut off, since Claude Code may resume it and go on to succeed or to fail for another reason, so it is read after the assistant errors and the text rules and before the subtype, which is how running out of turns or schema retries after a cut-off reply comes to name the limit. The last reply's reason counts, the result's `stop_reason` ahead of the last streamed `message_delta`'s. A successful result whose structured output is missing or does not parse names the limit when its reply was cut off (`cutOffReply`). A run that ended with no result at all says so, unless Claude Code's words or error name the limit. An assistant message's `api_error` is not read: where it says `max_output_tokens`, so does its `error`.
- **Codes stay.** The failures keep `claude-failed` and `openai-failed`. No card, Setup view or log line needs to tell them apart, and a new code would reach each of them; the words are the change.
- **The words.** One function for both providers, `replyLimitMessage` in `src/shared/ai/replyLimit.ts`: who ran out (Claude, or the OpenAI model that answered), the limit when the provider named it, and what helps. A lower effort, since the model's thinking counts against the same limit (Claude Code caps the thinking budget below the output limit; OpenAI counts reasoning tokens in it), unless the review already ran at low; splitting the chapter into two files from 12,000 words, the dialog's first threshold; and with neither, "Try again, or choose another model.". The providers pass the chapter's words, counted as the dialog counts them, and the effort. Claude Code's own words, which name an environment variable the app does not set (CLAUDE.md rule 6) and the author should not need to, go to `detail`, which is not shown. A chapter too long to read can only be split.
- **The thresholds.** 12,000 and 40,000 words, from the task, each inclusive, counting the body as the dialog's line does, and the same for both providers. The reply grows with the number of fixes a chapter needs, which no word count predicts, so the dialog's lines say "may" and give no token figure. By Claude Code 2.1.302's model table a model's default output limit is 32,000 to 128,000 tokens; gpt-5's is 128,000.
- **OpenAI.** A response that ends `incomplete` at `max_output_tokens` names the tokens the reply had used, the model's own limit, since the app asks for no `max_output_tokens`; `content_filter` has its own sentence, and any other reason is named. A review's 400 `context_length_exceeded`, or one whose message names the context window or length, says the chapter is too long for the model to read; from the model list or a connection test, which send no chapter, it keeps the usual words. The mock's `outputlimit` key streams half of the canned reply and ends `incomplete`.

### C.78 What sync hygiene recognises, and what it does with it (`files.11`, 2026-10-19)

`files.11` named the three tools, the two marker lines and the Excalidraw suffix, and said never to hide or delete anything; the rest was settled here.

- **The names, from each tool's own description.** Obsidian Sync, with its Conflict resolution setting on "Create conflict file" (Obsidian 1.9.7 and later; the default merges instead): `<name> (Conflicted copy <device> <YYYYMMDDHHMM>).md`, from the help page's troubleshooting section, whose example is `Meeting notes (Conflicted copy MyMacBook2 202411281430).md`. Dropbox: the editor's name, "conflicted copy" and the date added to the name, `<name> (<who>'s conflicted copy <YYYY-MM-DD>).md`, with ` (1)` after the date for a second copy that day; its help page gives the parts, not the exact pattern, so this is the shape Dropbox has long written. Syncthing: `<name>.sync-conflict-<YYYYMMDD>-<HHMMSS>-<device>.md`, from its documentation and its `conflictName`, where the device is a short ID of seven capitals and digits (`0` for none), and copies from before 0.14 have no device. The words are matched in any case, Dropbox's apostrophe straight or curly; the date and time must have their digits, and the name must end in an extension, as every chapter's does. Nothing else is recognised (the task said "patterns only"): not OneDrive's or iCloud's renamed copies, not Proton Drive's "Edit conflict" or "Name clash", not a copy made by hand, not git's `.orig` files.
- **Which chapter it copies.** The chapter's name takes as much of the copy's name as it can, so brackets and dots in the chapter's own name stay in it (`Chapter 1 (draft) (Jane Doe's conflicted copy 2026-10-19).md` copies `Chapter 1 (draft).md`), and a copy of a copy, by the same tool or another, is named as a copy of the first copy, whose words come before the last tool's. The three patterns cannot match the same name, since each ends at the extension in its own way, so their order does not matter.
- **The badge.** "conflict copy" on a line of its own under the name, with the pending count, which a copy has when it has a review of its own, beside both as on any row; a rose pill (11.3 e) on one line, which ends in an ellipsis only in a list narrower than itself. Its tooltip is "Obsidian Sync made this copy of Chapter 12.md when the file was changed in two places at once. Compare the two and keep the words you want. Lapidary does not hide or delete either." The row still shows the copy's own name, and a copy opens, is reviewed and is saved as any chapter is (it is one, for Save's rule in 6.1). The badge first sat after the name and kept its width, so the name gave way to it, and the `files.11` review found the name too short to tell which chapter a copy belonged to: in the drawer at 200% (section 7, Narrow windows) every copy read "Chapt..." and the subfolder's copy "Part T...", and at 100% a copy with the unsaved dot and a tick kept 73 px of its name. Under the name, the name has the width any chapter's has, for a row about twice as tall (44 px against 25 at 100%): at 100% the three copies of `Chapter 02 - After.md` read "Chapter 02 - After (Conflicted co...", "Chapter 02 - After (Jane ..." and "Chapter 02 - After.sync-conflict-...", so they no longer read alike, and in the drawer at 200% each names its chapter, "Chapter 02 - After (Co...", "Chapter 03 - Obs..." beside a tick, "Part Two/Chapter 05 -...". A shorter badge, or one that shrank, would still have taken from the name the width it needs at 200%; a badge that moved under the name only in a narrow list would have given copies one line or two by the width and the marks beside them. The row's tooltip still has the whole name.
- **Merge markers.** A line that starts with exactly seven `<` or `>` and a space, as git writes `<<<<<<< HEAD` and `>>>>>>> origin/main`; either alone counts. `=======` does not, since under a line of prose it is a Markdown heading, nor git's `|||||||` base line, nor a marker indented, followed by nothing or by a tab, or inside a line. Markers inside a code block count too: a novel rarely quotes git, and a card too many costs less than a clash missed. The review is sent the marker lines with the rest; the syntax detector (11.3 k) reads the `>>>>>>> ` of a closing line as block quote markers, so the guard keeps out a suggestion that would change them, and the other marker lines as prose. Save writes them back as they are, since the app never removes text the author has not decided on.
- **When the card shows.** The task said on open. It also follows the text whenever the page takes the chapter's text from disk again, so markers that arrive while the chapter is open are not missed: a reload from disk (6.2), a review opened from History, which reads the chapter again, and Save to chapter finding the file changed (6.3 step 2), whose rebase makes the watcher's reload of the same bytes do nothing. Each compares the text with the text on screen before it (`mergeMarkersCard`): markers that were not there show the card, no markers close it, and markers still there leave it as the author left it, so a card closed with its X does not come back at each save in Obsidian; opening a chapter always shows it for a chapter with markers, and a chapter without them closes a card left from another. One key, `merge-markers`, so there is never more than one. Save goes ahead with markers the page already shows: the card asks the author to resolve them, and refusing would only hold back decisions that do not touch them. A Save that finds the file changed, the change bringing markers, stops before writing (the `files.11` review): it went straight on to its second try and wrote the chapter, so the card it had just put up, saying "Lapidary has not changed the file" and to remove the markers "before you review or save", stood beside "Saved to the chapter file." about markers the author had not yet seen. Now the rebase card leaves out "Retrying.", "Nothing was saved: the change on disk brought merge markers. They are on the page now." goes up under `SAVE_CARD`, the save ends `failed`, and the next Save goes ahead, the author having seen them. Giving the save its own wording, that the decisions were saved around the markers, was the other way; stopping was taken because the card's words and advice then hold and nothing is written over a clash the author has not looked at. A card the author leaves up and then saves past, after this stop or after opening the chapter, keeps its words, true when it went up; the Saved card beside it says what that save did.
- **Excalidraw.** A drawing of the Excalidraw plugin is a Markdown file whose frontmatter says `excalidraw-plugin` and whose body holds the drawing's text elements and its compressed data, not prose. `listChapters` leaves out any file whose name ends `.excalidraw.md`, in any case, and nothing else (`Notes on excalidraw.md` and `Sketch.excalidraw.txt` stay). The file is never read or touched. The watcher still refreshes the list when one appears or goes, which lists nothing new, and Save's rule (6.1) does not name drawings, since none can be opened from the list.

### C.79 When the watcher has not started, and how the page learns it (`files.21`, 2026-10-19)

`files.21` said to start the watcher whenever a list read succeeds and none is running, and to say so in the list's notice while it is not; what "not running" is, who starts it, and how the page knows were settled here.

- **What chokidar does with a held folder.** Measured with chokidar 5.0.0 and Node 24.21 on Windows 11, against a folder opened with no sharing: one `error`, `EBUSY` on `scandir` with the folder as its `path`, no `ready`, and nothing at all for a change made after the folder was released; a new watcher started then saw a change within a second. A folder that is not there is no error: chokidar watches the folder above and takes the folder up when it appears, which was checked the same way, so that is a start that worked and the list's own words cover it (6.1).
- **What fails a start.** An error whose `path` is the manuscript folder itself, compared as `pathKey` compares, before chokidar is ready. Not an error for a subfolder, which the list skips too (6.1), since failing on it would make every Try again fail again; not one that names no path; and not the folder's own once ready, since chokidar's watch on the folder is already open and keeps working, and closing it would stop a watcher that still works.
- **Who starts it again.** Only a list read that works (`listAndWatch`, then `ensure`), as the task said, and only of the folder `start` was last given, after that start failed. `settings:get` and `settings:set` keep `start`, which leaves the folder in hand alone even after a failed start: Settings does not know the folder can be read, and it saves the theme, the model and every other setting through `settings:set`, so it would try again, and log another error, at each change while the folder is held. The folder chosen again still starts it, through the list read that follows. `reviews:index` reads the list too, so it may start it as well; the two reads of one refresh make one start, since the second finds it starting. `ensure` first started whatever folder the read was of, and the `files.21` review found that a read begun before Settings changed folder, and ended after the new folder's own read, moved the watcher back to the old folder, where `watching()` was true, so no line showed while changes in the new folder went unseen until some later read of it; a read that ended after Settings chose no folder started one too. In a `dev:clean` window, a list read of a scratch folder of 4,500 chapters, Settings choosing a copy of `samples/manuscript` 190 ms later and that folder's own read, the old read ended about 400 ms after Settings and the log read `watcher.start` for the new folder and then the old one again, and a chapter written in the new folder refreshed nothing. Now a read of any folder but the one `start` was last given changes nothing; the page reads Settings, which calls `start`, before its first list read, so the folder a read is of has always been given to `start` first. The same steps left the watcher on the new folder, whose new chapter refreshed the list.
- **The hashes.** `ensure` keeps the hashes of what the app loaded and saved while nothing watched, each with the path it was given, so a chapter opened meanwhile whose file is touched without a change does not reload; Settings choosing another folder (`start`) starts with none, as before.
- **Catching up once ready (the `files.21` review).** chokidar starts with `ignoreInitial` and reports nothing that happened before it was ready, so an edit made outside to a chapter open while nothing watched was never reported once Try again had worked: the line went and the page kept the old text. A chapter can be open then because a file in a held folder can still be created, read and written, only the folder itself refusing to be listed: New chapter makes and opens one, and a chapter opened after a list read that worked stays open when the start then fails. In a `dev:clean` window with the folder held at start-up, New chapter made and opened `Chapter 04 - Held.md`, a paragraph was appended to its file from outside, the folder was released and Try again pressed: the log had `watcher.start` and `watcher.ready`, and the page still one paragraph and no card. Now, at each `ready`, every file whose hash is kept is read again (`catchUp`): bytes other than those kept go to the page as `file:changed` (`change`), whose reload is the one of 6.2, rebase, card and merge-marker check; a file that is not there (`ENOENT`, `ENOTDIR`) as `unlink`, with the list read again; any other refusal is logged as `watcher.read-failed` (debug), as for an event; and nothing is reported once that watcher has been closed or replaced. The same steps then brought "Reloaded from disk. 0 suggestions re-anchored, 0 could not be found." and the second paragraph, and the new chapter deleted from outside instead brought "The chapter was deleted, renamed or moved on disk. ...". The check runs at a first start's `ready` too, where it finds only what was loaded while chokidar was starting. The page reading the open chapter again when told it is watched was the other way; it was not taken because the page is told when the start begins, before chokidar is ready, so an edit made in between would still be missed. A chapter still open from a folder Settings has left is not caught up when Settings comes back to that folder, since `start` forgets the hashes, as it did before `files.21`.
- **Dropped events.** Every event of a chokidar watcher that has been closed or replaced is dropped, its errors among them, so the log has one `watcher.error` per failed start, and a late change from a folder no longer watched is not reported.
- **How the page learns it.** `files:watching-changed` at each change, and `files:watching`, which the page asks once each list answer is in, whether the read worked or not: the event alone would be missed by a page that loads again while main's watcher has failed (a reload, or a page that crashed), and the list would then say nothing. The page takes the folder as watched until told otherwise, so nothing flashes at start-up.
- **Where the line goes.** Under main's words when the folder could not be read, under the empty-folder line, or above the rows: a list read can work while the start fails, when another program takes the folder again between the two reads, so the line must stand with rows as well. There is one Try again under the lines, 8 px above the rows when they show. With no folder chosen the list asks for one and says nothing of watching.
- **The log.** `watcher.start` (info, the folder) at each start, `watcher.ready` (debug) when chokidar is ready, and `stopped=true` on the `watcher.error` that failed a start. A held start then reads `watcher.start`, `watcher.error ... code=EBUSY ... stopped=true`, and after Try again `watcher.start` and `watcher.ready`.

### C.80 What Copy diagnostics holds, and how it is opened (`hardening.5`, 2026-10-20)

`hardening.5` listed the fields and said never the email, the key's last four characters, drafts or backups; the rest was settled here.

- **Made in main, scrubbed there.** `collectDiagnostics` (`src/main/diagnostics.ts`, Electron-free) gathers the facts and `diagnosticsReport` (`src/shared/diagnostics/report.ts`, pure) writes them as plain text: a title, the line saying what is left out, the time it was made, then a section per subject (App, Display, Reviews, Claude, OpenAI, Manuscript folder, Recent warnings), a `Label: value` line per fact. Only main knows the home folder, so the text is scrubbed there, every line as the log's values are (`scrub`: key shapes, Bearer tokens, email addresses, the home folder as `~`) and cut at 500 characters, and only the finished text crosses to the page (`app:diagnostics` answers `{text}`). The scrub is a second guard: no fact the report reads carries an email or a key. Of a `RuntimeStatus` it takes the state, the credential, the Claude Code path and version, the auth method, the plan, the free-plan warning, the time of the check and, for OpenAI, where the key comes from; never `email`, `keyLast4` or `message`, which can carry what a probe said. Chapter names are left out though Appendix D question 17 allows them: the count says whether chapters are missing, and a list of titles is the author's work. Nothing of drafts or backups, not even a count. Of each warning from the log the report keeps its time, level and event and only the fields in `REPORT_WARNING_FIELDS` (`warningLine`): channel, code, name, errno, syscall, provider, stage, quitting, stopped, kept, names and durationMs, and since `hardening.4` reason, exitCode, outcome and components, as the log wrote them. The message, the frames and a thrown value stay in the log file, because an app error's message is the sentence the page shows, and those name the chapter ("Chapter 07.md is saved as UTF-16"), its review file or its backup folder, so a chapter that will not open, the very case Copy diagnostics is for, would otherwise put its name under the line saying no chapter names are included (`hardening.5` review). A field a later event adds stays out until it is listed.
- **No check.** It reads `lastRuntime` and `lastFailure` (`providers/index.ts`, `hardening.3b`) and the last lookup (`installedCli`), so it costs nothing, starts no `claude` and logs no `ai.runtime`; before the first check of the run it says "not checked yet". `claudeDiagnostics` (`setup.4`) writes the Claude section, and now says "Claude Code: not found" for a missing Claude Code, where it said "unknown version".
- **The versions** (`app:info`, `src/main/appInfo.ts`). The app's from its package.json (`app.getVersion()`), Electron's, Chromium's and Node's from `process.versions`, the system's from `os.release()` (Windows 11 still calls itself 10.0, so a build of 22000 or later is named Windows 11), the `openai` package's read once from its own package.json (the package's `exports` do not list that file, so `readPackageVersion` walks up from the entry point Node resolves and takes the first package.json of that name), and the user's Claude Code from `installedCli`. `setup.3` kept no such record: one is now kept of what the last lookup found, whether a terminal finds `claude` by name, and what `--version` said for that path (`createInstalledRecord`, through `afterLookup` and `afterVersion`, in `claudeBinary.ts`). The runtime check writes to it itself (`createClaudeRuntimeCheck`'s `installed`, which claude.ts must pass), so a test of the check covers what `app:info` and the report read; claude.ts writes only a lookup made before the first check, for a model list, a review or a test (`hardening.5` review: the first version kept it in two lines of claude.ts that no test reached). Nothing is written in at build time.
- **The folder.** Markers are looked for in the manuscript folder and every folder above it, since a manuscript folder is often a folder inside the vault: `.obsidian` (a folder only), `.git` (a folder, or the file a worktree has) and Syncthing's `.stfolder`; the report says where ("yes, in the folder above it"). Obsidian Sync is the `sync` core plugin in that vault's `.obsidian/core-plugins.json`, an object of every core plugin with `true` or `false` (Obsidian 1.4 and later) or a list of those turned on (earlier); no file, no key or a file that is not JSON is `unknown`, and no vault "no vault". On means the plugin is enabled, not that a remote vault is connected. Cloud hints are folder names in the path, whole names in any case: OneDrive (and `OneDrive - <organisation>`), Dropbox (and `Dropbox (Personal)`), iCloud Drive (`iCloudDrive`, `Mobile Documents`, `iCloud~md~obsidian`), Google Drive (`My Drive`, `Shared drives`, `Google Drive`), Box, pCloud, MEGA, Proton Drive, Nextcloud and ownCloud, and Syncthing by its marker; a hint, not a finding, since a folder of that name made by hand reads the same. The chapter count is `listChapters`' own, without the watcher start that a list read makes (C.79); a folder that cannot be listed gives its own error code, such as `ENOENT` or `EPERM`. The guidelines file is "changed from the template" when its text, read as the app reads it and with blank lines at either end aside, differs from `GUIDELINES.default.md`, with its length in characters and the style sheet's state (section 10), never its words.
- **The window.** The Appearance setting, whether the dark colours are in use (`shouldUseDarkColors`), Windows' contrast themes (`inForcedColorsMode`, "Contrast theme" in the report, as Windows names them), the window's zoom, the scale of the display it is on, its inside size in device-independent pixels (and in CSS pixels at a zoom other than 100%), and Chromium's GPU compositing status (`app.getGPUFeatureStatus().gpu_compositing`).
- **Copy and Show.** Setup's link is named Copy diagnostics, so it copies: it opens the dialog with `copyOnOpen`, which copies once, when the report first arrives, and the line beside Copy says so. A card's Show diagnostics opens the same dialog and copies nothing until Copy is pressed. Copying straight from the link, with no dialog, was the other way; the dialog was kept so the author sees what they paste. The copy is `navigator.clipboard.writeText`, which needs the window to have the focus, as it has after a click. In the first window check the text on the clipboard and the text in the dialog differed in their time: a development run's StrictMode asks for the report twice, the copy took the first answer and the dialog showed the second. Only the latest request's answer is now kept, so what is shown is what was copied.

### C.81 What crash handling settled where the plan left it open (`hardening.4`, 2026-10-20)

`hardening.4` named the parts: `crash.ts`, `log:renderer` and its cap, `createErrorFilter`, the window listeners and `onUncaughtError`, an `ErrorBoundary` whose fallback writes and offers Reload window and Copy diagnostics, and Reload or Quit after `render-process-gone`. The rest was settled here; 7.7 "When the page fails" has what the author sees.

- **Which errors leave a card.** An error nothing caught leaves one, in the page as in main: in the page it is most often a button's handler that failed, so what the author did last may not have finished, and a card says so. A rejection nothing handled is only logged, in both processes, as the text gave main's: a cancelled request is one, and a card for it would cry wolf. Checked in a window: a review cancelled from the lock card, a close answered Close, keep for later with a review running, and a close with nothing at risk left no rejection in the log of either process.
- **Repeats and the caps.** The same error is one with the same kind, name, code, message and first frame; it is let through once a minute, counted from the last time it was. Chromium's "ResizeObserver loop" notice, which comes as a window error with no error object, is never reported. Each process writes at most 30 unexpected-error lines in any minute and says once when it stops (`main.errors-capped`, `renderer.log-capped`); each process's card comes at most once a minute, whatever the errors (`NOTICE_INTERVAL_MS` in main, `PAGE_CARD_INTERVAL_MS` in `createErrorReporter`). The page's card first came for every error the filter let through, so a card closed came straight back with the next different error; 7.7 and section 5 said once a minute, and the review fix made the page's card keep to it.
- **What crosses from the page.** The page sends the error's loggable fields (`pageErrorFields`, by the one policy) and main keeps only `RENDERER_LOG_FIELDS` that hold a scalar, then scrubs them as it writes, so a page that sent more could still not put chapter text in the log. The page's `ApiError` carries main's code and message, so the policy now treats it as `AppFailure`: an error whose message quotes the model's reply logs its code only. A render error adds the app's own component names, innermost first (`StatusBar < App < ErrorBoundary`), never an element or a file's address.
- **The crash page holds the close guard.** When the boundary takes App down, App's guard goes with it, and main would have asked a page that no longer answers, then shown "not responding". The crash page installs the guard again with `crashedPageState`: once its writes are made, decisions are in their review and boxes in their drafts, which is what Close, keep for later would keep, and nothing can be saved to the chapter from a page in that state, so the close goes at once; a write still waiting or failed, or a review still running, is asked about in the questions it draws itself, with no Save. A question the failed page had open is answered Cancel, so a close it held is kept and the next one is the crash page's. Answering Cancel did not end that close at first: the failed page's run of `prepareToLeaveApp` went on with App's deps, and since Cancel in "Still writing your decisions" is Wait, it wrote again and then asked App's close question, "Save 1 change and close" among its buttons, in the crash page's dialog, and Save would have run the failed page's `saveChapter`; a run in its write race when the page failed went on the same way. Seen in a `dev:clean` window (a review file made read-only, WM_CLOSE, the file put back, then the page made to fail). Now `installCrashedPageGuard` ends the run under way first (`leavingRun`): every step after an await goes on only while the run has not been ended (`goOn`), a write race or a save it waits on stops at once (`run.stopped`), and an ended run answers false with no card (`RunEnded`). The bare page, for an error in the crash page itself, has nothing to ask with, so its guard takes every question as Close anyway (`questions: false`): a close still gives the writes their 5 s.
- **The boundary catches once.** React hands a boundary that has `getDerivedStateFromError` any error under it in a render where it has not already caught one, and then draws its fallback afresh, with new state. So an error in the crash page on a later render (as its writes end, its report arrives or its question opens) was caught by the same boundary, and each fresh crash page wrote again, took the close guard again and asked main for the report again; an error that came back on that render went round for good, never reaching the bare page, and the repeat filter kept the log to one line. A temporary throw in the crash page once its writes had ended mounted it about 5,000 times in 4.5 s in a window. Now `componentDidCatch` keeps an error after the first and the boundary's own render throws it, and React never hands a boundary its own render's error: it goes to the root's `onUncaughtError`, logged as `renderer.render-uncaught` with the crash page's frames, and the bare page shows. The crash page drawn afresh for that error runs its effects once more first. In the same window the throw now gave one more mount, then the bare page with Reload window focused.
- **What the crash page does is tested in node.** Its effects never run in a test, since the renderer has no DOM there, so three mutations of the first version (the guard never taken over, the writes never made, `CRASH_WRITES` without `flushDraftWrites`) passed every test. What it does as it opens, when no question is open and on Try again is now `createCrashPage` (`src/renderer/state/crashPage.ts`), which `CrashFallback` calls from its effects with `CRASH_PAGE` (`pageIo.ts`); a source check pins that wiring. Reload window takes the focus whenever no question is open and the focus is on nothing, and Try again gives it the focus before it writes again. The first version focused it on the first render, when a question the failed page had open was still in the store and the page under it inert, so the focus was lost, and Try again's link took the focus with it when it went. The focus shows its ring however it came (`focusVisible`, as the confirm dialog's default button), since after a click on Try again Chromium would leave it off.
- **Errors React does not report.** When the crash page fails on its first render, nothing is committed, so the boundary's `componentDidCatch` never runs for the first error, and React hands `onUncaughtError` only the second: the log then has `renderer.render-uncaught` for the crash page's error and nothing for the one that started it. Logging from `getDerivedStateFromError`, which runs during render, was the other way, and was not taken for a page whose first fallback has already failed.
- **Reload or Quit.** Reload window is the default and what Escape and the box's own close button give, since a window whose page has gone shows nothing; a box that fails to open reloads. Besides the text's three conditions (quitting, a clean exit, a close under way going ahead), the box is not shown at the end of a Windows session (`isSessionEnding`, added to the close guard for it) or for a window that has gone; it is taken away with its window through its signal, and an answer that comes after the window closed or the app began quitting does nothing. A review that was running keeps running in main; Reload drops its answer with the old page, and quitting stops it (`abortAll`).
- **Verification notes.** Main's inspector is opened by starting `dev:clean` with `V8_INSPECTOR_PORT=9229` in the environment, which electron-vite passes to Electron as `--inspect`; a throw evaluated there reaches `uncaughtException`. A file a page throw is put in for a check must be a component: an edit to a module `main.tsx` imports (`src/shared/ui/crash.ts`) reloads the whole page instead of updating it. The box after `render-process-gone` takes the foreground (C.61), so it was checked by unit tests, not raised in a window. In a development window the page's own modules can be imported over CDP (`await import('/state/store.ts')` gives the page's store), and a card whose text is an object (`upsertNotification(key, 'info', { not: 'a string' })`) makes App fail to draw without a file being edited, which the review and its fix used.

### C.82 What the OpenAI default and the verification message settled where the plan left it open (`hardening.10`, 2026-10-20)

`hardening.10` named the pattern the default skips, the order full gpt-5 then mini or nano, `isStreamingVerificationError` and the mock scenario `unverified`. The rest was settled here; 5.0 has the rules.

- **Mini before nano, and what comes after gpt-5.** "Mini or nano" is read as a mini, then a nano: a copyedit wants the larger model. Each tier is newest first by `created`. After the gpt-5 tiers comes any other gpt-5 the pattern does not name (a preview, say), and with no gpt-5 at all, as for a project limited to older models, another family's newest model that is neither a mini nor a nano, then a mini, then a nano: newest first alone would have taken gpt-4.1-nano, which OpenAI listed a little after gpt-4.1. Tiers match the id without its snapshot date, and a dated snapshot gives way to its undated alias when both are listed, so the default reads `gpt-5.5` whichever of the two OpenAI created last.
- **Skipped is still listed.** The pattern only keeps a model from being chosen for the author; the list and the select still offer it. `isTextModel` already left the deep research models out of the list, as search models, and `gpt-5.1-codex-mini` with `codex-mini-latest` (its `codex-mini`); the pattern names them too. `chatgpt-4o-latest` is not named (its `chat` follows no dash, and `chat-latest` does not occur in it), so a key with no gpt-5 could still default to it if nothing newer qualifies; the pattern is the task's, left as written. The `chat-latest` half of it adds nothing for OpenAI's own ids: each that holds `chat-latest` is a `-chat-latest`, which `-chat-` names already, so only a made-up id whose `chat` follows no dash, as `gpt-5-groupchat-latest`, tells the two halves apart. The tests use one, and made-up -chat ids that are no -chat-latest alias (`gpt-5-chat`, `gpt-5.1-chat-2025-11-13`) for the word `chat`, since every -chat id OpenAI lists ends in -chat-latest (the review). README and CHANGELOG say "chat model" for the ones the pattern names.
- **When nothing else qualifies.** The task's "`defaultOpenAiModel` skips" the pattern is read as: while the list holds any other text model. The first version had no default for a list of skipped models only, so the review dialog's select showed the list's first row (`selectedModel`) and main sent that row (`openAiModelToSend`). Newest first, that row is most likely a `-pro` model, the dearest, which the task meant to keep from being chosen, and README and CHANGELOG said a pro, codex or chat model was never chosen. The review fix: the same tiers then pick among the skipped models, a codex or chat model before any `-pro` one, so a pro model is the default only for a key that can use nothing else. The list marks that row "(default)", the dialog selects it and main sends it, keeping what the dialog shows what is sent (C.28); README and CHANGELOG say when such a model is used. `defaultOpenAiModel` is null only when no text model is listed, when the dialog has no row and cannot start, and `gpt-5` stays the guess for a list that cannot be read or holds no text model.
- **The refusal.** OpenAI answers a streamed request from an organisation that has not verified its identity with status 400, `invalid_request_error`, `param` `stream`, code `unsupported_value` and "Your organization must be verified to stream this model. Please go to: https://platform.openai.com/settings/organization/general and click on Verify Organization. If you just verified, it can take up to 15 minutes for access to propagate." Developers reported it for o3, gpt-5 and gpt-5-mini in 2025, with the same model answering when not streamed (https://community.openai.com/t/need-verification-for-o3-streaming-despite-being-tier-5/1230334 , https://community.openai.com/t/why-can-non-verified-organisations-use-gpt-5-and-gpt-5-mini-but-not-stream-them/1338294 , https://community.openai.com/t/need-help-with-verification-to-access-gpt-5-via-an-api/1362059 ; community posts, read 2026-10-20, not OpenAI's documentation). So the gpt-5 mini the default falls back to does not avoid it, and the message says another model may not need it rather than naming one. `isStreamingVerificationError` takes a 400 with those words ("organization must be verified to stream", in either spelling) or a refusal of `param` `stream` that mentions verifying; no run may use a real key, so it was checked only against the mock and OpenAI's words as reported. One post says a key made before the organisation was verified kept failing until a new key was made; the message does not say so. The app's words use its own spelling, "organisation", and name OpenAI's button as OpenAI spells it; the card shows the address as text, not as a link.
- **The refusal to use a model** (the review). OpenAI has a related refusal with the same cause and the same fix, "Your organization must be verified to use the model `o3`", followed by the same address and advice, which developers report for o3 and gpt-image-1 among others, mostly as a 403, streamed or not (https://community.openai.com/t/we-are-verified-and-yet-error-403-your-organization-must-be-verified-to-use-the-model-help/1366731 , https://community.openai.com/t/gpt-images-1-403-what-are-the-conditions-for-requesting-this-model-gpt-image-1/1245846 ; community posts, read 2026-10-20, not OpenAI's documentation). As a 403 it fell to "OpenAI rejected the API key" and its Open Settings button, which sends the author to replace a key that works. `isStreamingVerificationError` now takes "must be verified to stream" or "to use" on a 400 or a 403, and a refusal of `param` `stream` that mentions verifying on a 400 only; any other 403 is still a refused key. Its name stays the task's though it now also takes a refusal that is not about streaming; the message never mentioned streaming, so it fits both. Checked against OpenAI's words as reported and, in a window, a scratch server that answers with them.
- **Only a review meets it.** The refusal is mapped for every request, but only a streamed one is refused. Test the connection sends one unstreamed request (5.0), so on an unverified organisation it would pass while a review is refused; OpenAI's test is offered by no button yet, and a button that offers it should first stream, as a review does. Falling back to an unstreamed request on this refusal would also let an unverified organisation review, without the progress count; the task asked for the message, so that is left as a choice for later. The provider tests pin the gap, so whoever adds OpenAI's test button meets it: the `unverified` key's connection test answers while its review is refused. A model refused outright ("to use") fails the connection test too, with the same message.
- **The mock.** `unverified` refuses a streamed `POST /v1/responses` with OpenAI's words and answers the model list and an unstreamed request, as the API does. The mock's model list gained `gpt-5.5-pro`, `gpt-5-codex`, `gpt-5-chat-latest` and `o3-deep-research`, each newer than a model the default could take, so a development window shows the default passing over them. The review added `skippedonly`, whose list holds only `gpt-5.5-pro`, `gpt-5-codex`, `gpt-5-chat-latest` and `whisper-1` (`SKIPPED_ONLY_MODELS`) and which otherwise answers as the default scenario does, so a window and the provider tests show the codex marked "(default)" under the newer pro.

### C.83 What the experimental label settled where the plan left it open (`hardening.11`, 2026-10-20)

`hardening.11` named the constant, the provider option "OpenAI (API key, experimental)", a note under the select and the Settings row label. Appendix D 16 cut the real-key check, so 1.0 ships with `OPENAI_MATURITY = 'experimental'`. The rest was settled here.

- **Every label reads it, the welcome guide's too.** The welcome guide already said so in two literals, its button "Use OpenAI instead (experimental, pay per use)" and the OpenAI step's "OpenAI in Lapidary is experimental."; both now come from the constant (`openAiChoiceLabel` and `openAiStepText` in `src/shared/ui/welcome.ts`) with their words unchanged, so a flip leaves no label behind. The status bar, History and Copy diagnostics name the provider by its short name, "OpenAI" (`PROVIDER_NAMES`), and say nothing about it. README and CHANGELOG are prose and are edited by hand when it flips.
- **What `tested` reads.** `OPENAI_MATURITIES` is `experimental` then `tested`, and `tested` drops the word: "OpenAI (API key)", "OpenAI API key", "Use OpenAI instead (pay per use)", the step without its sentence, and no note. Each label function takes the maturity, defaulting to the constant, so the tests read both.
- **The note.** A grey note (`modal__note`) right under the provider row and before the API key row, only while OpenAI is chosen: "OpenAI in Lapidary is experimental. It has been tested only with a stand-in for OpenAI's service, not with a real key, so a review may fail in ways not yet seen." With Claude chosen the option list still says experimental and there is no note.
- **Settings' row.** "OpenAI API key (experimental)" is wider than the 150 px name column, so it wraps after "key" onto two lines; the row stays centred on them. The password field keeps its accessible name, "OpenAI API key".
- **The guard.** `test/openaiMaturity.test.ts` parses every `.ts` and `.tsx` file under `src` with the TypeScript compiler and fails on a string, template or regular-expression literal, or JSX text, that spells "experimental" anywhere but the declarations of `OPENAI_MATURITY` and `OPENAI_MATURITIES`, and on the word outside a comment in a `.html` or `.css` file. Comments may name it, as the stylesheet's note on the welcome button's width does, and tests are not scanned, since they pin the labels.

### C.84 The log file: what a line may hold, and how it is written (`hardening.2` and `hardening.3b`, recorded by `hardening.12`, 2026-10-20)

`hardening.2` built the log, and `hardening.3b` and `hardening.4` gave it the events 11.3 (m) lists, with no entry here. This records what the code settled, checked against `src/main/log.ts`, `src/shared/diagnostics/redact.ts`, `test/main/log.test.ts` and `test/shared/redact.test.ts`, and, where those have no test, a scratch test run on 2026-10-20 and removed. CLAUDE.md rule 9 is the rule for new code.

- **One file, rotated once.** `createLogger` (no electron import) appends to `<userData>/logs/main.log`. When a write would take a file that is not empty past 1 MiB (`DEFAULT_MAX_BYTES`), it first renames the file to `main.1.log`, over any earlier one, so there are never more than the two (the scratch test put an old `main.1.log` in the folder and found it replaced). Every level, debug to error, goes to the file; nothing filters by level. There is no logging package (11.1): a logger of the app's own has no transport, format or option that could write something `log` did not format.
- **Buffered, and never throws.** `log` adds the line to a buffer and to an in-memory tail of the last 500 lines, and the buffer is written by one `appendFileSync` on a later turn of the event loop (`setTimeout(..., 0)`). `flushLog` writes it at once; `will-quit` calls it after logging `app.quit`. A write that fails (the folder is a file, the disk is full, access is refused) turns writing off for the rest of the run, and lines then go only to the tail, from which Copy diagnostics still takes its warnings, saying "Log file: stopped after a write failed" (`logWriting`). Nothing in the logger throws, so a log that cannot be written cannot take the app down. Lines logged before `initLog` are held, at most 200, and written once it runs; it runs in `start()`, after the single-instance lock, so a copy that loses the lock writes nothing (11.3 a).
- **A line.** `<ISO time, UTC> <LEVEL> <event> k=v ...`. An event name has to match `^[A-Za-z][\w.-]*$`, else it is written `invalid.event`; the app's are `area.what`, as `file.save` or `watcher.close-failed`. `formatFields` keeps a field only when its key matches `^[A-Za-z][\w.]*$` and its value is a string, a number, a boolean or null: an object or a list is dropped whole, never looked into, since it could hold anything. A string is scrubbed, cut to 300 characters (`MAX_FIELD_CHARS`, the last of them an ellipsis) and written in JSON's quotes and escapes when it is empty or holds white space, `=`, a quote or a backslash, so a line always splits back into its fields, which `warningLine` in Copy diagnostics relies on.
- **The scrub** (`scrub`). `sk-` followed by 16 or more letters, digits, `_` or `-`, the shape of OpenAI's and Anthropic's keys, becomes `[key]`; `Bearer` and a token of 8 or more characters, `Bearer [token]`; an email address, `[email]`; and the home folder `~`, found with back or forward slashes, doubled backslashes, percent-encoded separators and colon, and in `file:///` addresses, in any case, but not where it is only the start of a longer folder name. The home folder is `os.homedir()`, handed to `createLogger` by `initLog`. The scrub is the second guard: what a caller passes is counts, codes and names it chose.
- **Errors.** An error reaches a line only through `loggableErrorFields`, the one policy, whose four kinds 11.3 (m) gives. Besides: frames are the stack's `at` lines after the message, at most eight (`MAX_FRAMES`), each scrubbed and cut to 200 characters; an errno error, as Node's file system errors are, keeps its name, code, errno and syscall and never its message, which names the path; and a thrown value that is not an object is logged as `error`, its string form scrubbed and cut. A failed request is logged by `runHandler` as `ipc.failed` and a review's failure by `withLogging` as `ai.review.failed`, so a handler need not log its own (a few still log a step of their own first, as `backups.failed` before a save gives up), and the page's unexpected errors come by `log:renderer` already reduced by `pageErrorFields`, of which main keeps only `RENDERER_LOG_FIELDS` (C.81).
- **What the log may name.** It never holds chapter text, prompts, guidelines, replies, `detail`, drafts, backups, the account email or the key (11.3 m), but it is not free of names. The policy keeps an app error's message, the sentence the page shows, which often names the chapter, its review file or its backup folder (C.80); `watcher.start`, `watcher.ready` and `watcher.error` carry the manuscript folder, `watcher.read-failed`, at debug, a chapter's path, and `ai.runtime`, after each check of Claude, Claude Code's full path as `executable` (`runtimeFields`, `src/main/providers/logged.ts`), each with the home folder as `~`. That is the file in the author's own data folder. Copy diagnostics, the text an author is asked to paste, takes none of this from the log: of each warning it keeps only the time, level, event and the fields `REPORT_WARNING_FIELDS` lists (C.80). Its own sections do name the manuscript folder, the reviews folder and the guidelines file (its Manuscript folder section, `src/shared/diagnostics/report.ts`) and Claude Code's path (`Claude Code: <version> at <path>`, `claudeDiagnostics`), with the home folder as `~`, as Appendix D 17 allows.

### C.85 What main does with a path the page sends (`files.2`, `apply.11`, `apply.16` and `hardening.8`, recorded by `hardening.12`, 2026-10-20)

11.1 counts "IPC path guards" among the security choices. They came with several tasks and had no entry here; this gathers, channel by channel, what main does with a path or a file name the page sends, checked against `src/main/ipc.ts` and the functions named. The page is the app's own and loads nothing else (C.41), so these guards hold the hard rules against a fault in it rather than against a page someone else wrote.

- **Before any handler.** `runHandler` first runs `checkPayload` (`src/main/ipcGuard.ts`, `hardening.8`, 11.3 m): a channel that takes nothing must be sent nothing and any other a plain object, and no field `PATH_FIELDS` lists may hold a NUL, which no file system takes and a native call could read as the end of the path. The refusal is `invalid-input` and names the channel and the field, never the value. `files:check-name` is not in the table, since it answers any name typed in New chapter in words of its own.
- **Writes.** `files:save` writes only a `.md` or `.txt` file that is not the guidelines file and lies in the manuscript folder or was read or created from it in this run (`assertSavableChapter`, `OpenedChapters`, `files.2`, 6.1); paths are compared after `path.resolve` by `isInsidePath` and `samePath` (`src/shared/paths.ts`), without case on Windows and macOS (`caseInsensitiveFs`), and the backups root must lie outside the manuscript folder and the chapter's folder (`assertOutside`, 6.5). `files:create` takes a name, never a path: `checkChapterName` refuses `\` and `/`, the characters Windows forbids, control characters, a name of dots only, one ending in a dot or a space and Windows' reserved names, and the file is created in the manuscript folder with `wx`. `reviews:save` writes over the path it is sent only when that is a `.review.json` directly in the chapter's folder in the reviews folder (`folderFor`, named by the slug of the chapter's file name) and holds that chapter's review or nothing yet (`mayOverwrite`; a file there that cannot be read stops the save, `apply.25`); anything else goes to a new entry in that folder named by the review's `createdAt` (`newEntryPath`, and the last item below). `reviews:shown` records only a `.review.json` directly in that folder that belongs to the chapter (`recordShown`). The drafts channels never name a file: a chapter's boxes are kept in `drafts/<the first 16 hex digits of the SHA-256 of its path key>.json`, and a set-aside text is created with `wx` in `drafts/set-aside`, named after the chapter with every character a file name cannot hold made `_` (`setAsideFileName`).
- **A chapter's reviews, found by its path.** `reviews:list` and `reviews:load-latest` read only the folder named by the slug of the `sourcePath` they are sent (`folderFor`, `chapterSlug`, whose `slugify` leaves no separator and never `.` or `..`), so they stay in the reviews folder, and of the reviews there they take only those whose own `sourcePath` is the one sent (`belongs`). `reviews:load-latest` also writes: when no review there belongs to the chapter, it may create that folder and move into it the reviews of another path whose file is gone, chosen by `findAdoptable` with the `hash` the page sent, through the adoption journal (`adopt`, `.adoption.json` in the reviews folder, C.45), each rewritten with the path sent and its old file removed once the copy is on disk. Like the other review-store writes, these stay inside the reviews folder. Both channels first finish an adoption a crash interrupted (`finishAdoption`).
- **What is opened outside the app.** `shell:reveal` shows fixed places (the data, logs, backups and drafts folders, settings.json, or the data folder once it is gone, for the card of section 7 (`hardening.15` review), and the reviews folder, the manuscript folder and the guidelines file the settings name), a chapter's own backup folder, worked out from its full path and checked to lie directly under the backups root (`chapterBackups`, `assertChapterBackupFolder`, `apply.11`), or a set-aside text named by a bare `.txt` file name, with no folder in it and not `.` or `..`, that is a file in `drafts/set-aside` (`setAsideFile`, `apply.16`). `guidelines:open` is sent nothing (`polish.3`; until then which way to open the file, with `.md` needed for Obsidian): the file is the one the settings name, and `ensureGuidelinesFile` refuses one that is not `.md` or `.txt` before anything is made from the template.
- **Settings.** `settings:set` refuses a folder that is not a full path or holds a NUL, and a guidelines file that is not a full path, with no NUL, to a `.md` or `.txt` file (`refuseDroppedPath`); a settings.json edited by hand to hold one reads as null (11.3 d, `hardening.8`).
- **Read with no folder check.** `files:read` reads any file it is sent, up to 4 MiB and only as UTF-8 text (`readChapter`, 11.3 l), and `reviews:load` reads any file as a review (`loadReviewFile`); neither writes. `files:read` records a path inside the manuscript folder as opened, which is what lets Save write that chapter after Settings has moved to another folder. The dialogs hand `defaultPath` to the system's picker as where it opens, `ai:review` uses `sourcePath` only for the chapter's name in the prompt, and `app:guard-state`'s `chapter` is kept by the close guard. No folder check was added to the reads: what they read goes only to the app's own page, and 11.0 cut the IPC sender check because the window has no remote content.
- **A review's time as a file name.** `newEntryPath` makes `createdAt` into the file name with its colons and dots made dashes, which is why `createdAt` joined `PATH_FIELDS` (`hardening.8` review). No `..` survives that, so a new entry never leaves the chapter's folder, but a `/` or `\` in `createdAt` names a subfolder of it: the save fails when that subfolder is not there, as it never is unless made by hand, and lands in it when it is. The scratch test of C.84 saw a review whose `createdAt` was `a/b` refused, then written to `a/b.review.json` in the chapter's folder once `a` had been made, and one whose `createdAt` was `../c` written to `--/c.review.json`. A review the app makes has `toISOString()`'s time, so only a review file edited by hand could carry such a time. Found here; `hardening.15` refuses such a time: `stampFor` throws `invalid-input` for a `createdAt` holding `/` or `\`, in words that name the field and never the value, and `saveReview` asks for the stamp only when the review needs a new entry, before the chapter's folder is made or anything is written, so a review saved over its own entry, which its time does not name, is still saved. Only the separators are refused: no other character can lead out of the folder, a NUL is refused by `checkPayload` before the handler runs, and any other character Windows refuses in a name fails the write itself. `test/main/reviews.test.ts` saves `a/b`, `a\b` and `../c` with nothing made under the reviews folder, nothing written into subfolders `a` and `--` made by hand, a refusal too when the path sent cannot be written over, and the same review saved over its own entry.

### C.86 What a settings.json that cannot be read does (`hardening.3a`, recorded by `hardening.12`, 2026-10-20)

11.3 (d) gives three rules for reading settings.json, missing, not JSON and refused, which `createSettingsStore` (`src/main/settingsStore.ts`, no electron import) keeps; `hardening.3a` left no entry here. This records the cases the rules leave open, checked against `test/main/settingsStore.test.ts` and, where that has no test, the scratch test of C.84.

- **Missing** (ENOENT). The defaults, cached; nothing is logged, and nothing is written until the first save writes the file through `atomicWriteFile`.
- **Not JSON.** A file `JSON.parse` refuses once a leading byte order mark is dropped, an empty file or one holding only the mark among them, is copied beside itself as `settings.json.corrupt-<yyyymmddhhmmss>`, in local time, with `COPYFILE_EXCL`, so no earlier copy is ever replaced: a name already taken gets `-2`, and so on up to `-20`. The copy is logged as `settings.unreadable kept=<the copy's name>`, the defaults are cached, and the next save writes a new file over the old one while the copy stays. Two ways round the copy were found here and closed by `hardening.15`: when the copy itself failed, `settings.unreadable kept=none code=<code>` was logged and the defaults were still cached, so the next save wrote over the file with no copy kept (the scratch test, with a copy that failed with EACCES); and when all twenty names were taken, nothing was logged and the same followed. Each is now a read that failed, as Save to chapter treats a backup it cannot make (6.5): nothing is cached, `loadChecked` says `readFailed` with the reason `no-copy`, so the page is told as below and its card says the file is damaged rather than held (the `hardening.15` review), and the next load reads the file and tries the copy again. A save first does the same, and with still no copy logs `settings.save-refused kept=none` and fails with "Settings could not be saved, because settings.json could not be read and no copy of it could be made, so saving would lose what it holds. Lapidary's log says why the copy failed.", the file keeping its bytes. Twenty names taken are logged as `settings.unreadable kept=none code=EEXIST names=20` (`kept`, `code` and `names` are all fields Copy diagnostics shows). Once a copy can be made, the rule above holds again (`test/main/settingsStore.test.ts`, `a settings.json that could not be read`).
- **JSON that is not an object.** `null`, a list, a number or a string parses, so it is not set aside: `normalizeSettings` reads it as no settings, the defaults are cached, nothing is logged, and the next save writes over it (the scratch test, for each of the four). Such a file holds no setting the app could have read.
- **Read refused** (any other error, such as EBUSY, EPERM, EACCES or EISDIR). The read is tried again once after 200 ms; if that fails too, `settings.read-failed code=<code>` is logged and the defaults are returned but not cached (and `loadChecked` says `readFailed` with the reason `refused`, `hardening.15`), so every later read of the settings tries the file again, twice, and logs again until it can be read (the scratch test: two loads, four reads, two lines). A save first reads in the same way; while the file still cannot be read it logs `settings.save-refused code=<code>`, the request fails with "Settings could not be saved, because settings.json could not be read and might be overwritten. Close any program that has it open and try again.", and the file keeps its bytes. Once a read works, the save puts its patch over what the file says, not over the defaults (`recovers once the lock goes away, keeping what the file said`). A zoom step whose save fails still applies to the window and logs `zoom.save-failed`.
- **The page is told** (`hardening.15`). Until then it was not; this item first recorded what that did. It was handed the defaults like any other answer: no manuscript folder, so the welcome guide shows (`onboardingDone` defaults to false without a folder, 11.3 d), and the system's theme. A save the page makes then goes over what the file says once the file can be read, so a key the page set from the defaults wins over the file's. The Pro preselection (C.67) sends `model` and `dismissedHints` without a click when Claude is ready on a Pro plan while the welcome guide is open, so after a first read that failed twice and a later one that worked it would replace the author's model and the hints they had dismissed; dismissing a hint would also replace the list. Found here from the code: it needs settings.json, in the app's own data folder, to be unreadable for more than 200 ms as the app starts and readable again later in the run. The `hardening.12` review fix then saw it in a quiet `dev:clean --no-claude-code` window, with settings.json held open from PowerShell with no sharing as the app started: main logged `settings.read-failed code=EBUSY`, sixteen times in its first two seconds, the page showed the welcome guide with no folder chosen, and once the file was let go, the patch the preselection makes from the defaults, sent through the page's bridge, replaced the file's model and its dismissed hint and kept its folder and effort. Now `settings:get` answers `settingsAnswer(await loadSettingsChecked())`: the settings, or, while the read fails, `{ readFailed: true, reason, settings: null }`, a flag and a fixed word, `refused` for a read refused and `no-copy` for a file that is not JSON with no copy made, never the error, and the watcher, the theme and the zoom are left as they are. The `hardening.15` review saw a damaged file whose twenty copy names were taken open on the card with the held file's advice, which no closing of programs ends, and nothing saying where the file is or why the copy failed; the reason gives each case its own words, and the card has Show in folder and Show diagnostics (section 7). The page's store then keeps no settings, so the welcome guide does not show, the Pro preselection is not made, and a hint put away, the split and Show the welcome guide again write nothing; the card of section 7 (Settings that could not be read) stands in place of everything else, with Try again, until a read works, when main puts back the author's theme and zoom (`applyTheme`, `applyZoom`), which the window had taken from the defaults. A save the author makes after that puts only its own keys over the file. Main's own reads of the settings still have the defaults while the file cannot be read, as before; its one write of its own, a zoom step's, is refused as above, and the step still applies to the window until a read works.
- **Paths in it.** A folder or guidelines file the normaliser cannot use is dropped on read and refused on save (11.3 d, `hardening.8`, C.85).

### C.87 The package ships no Claude Code binary (`release.4`, 2026-10-20)

Phase 5 unpacked `@anthropic-ai/claude-agent-sdk-win32-x64/**` and `@anthropic-ai/claude-agent-sdk/**` from the asar so that the SDK could start the `claude.exe` it brought with it (C.20). Under Appendix D 8 and 21 the app ships nothing of Anthropic's, and `cli.1` removed the SDK (C.42).

- **The two entries.** `cli.1` took them out with the SDK, before the repository's first public commit, so `release.4` found no `asarUnpack` to drop. The config's header now says why there is none, and `test/scripts/builderConfig.test.ts` fails if the key comes back.
- **What the build holds** (`npm run package`, electron-builder 26.17.0, 2026-10-20, checked with a one-off script over `@electron/asar`'s listing and the files of `dist/win-unpacked`). The asar has 4,138 entries, among them `/out/main/index.js` and `/package.json`, and nothing under `/samples`, `/test`, `/src`, `/dist` or `/.dev-userdata`. Its `node_modules` holds six packages, chokidar, diff, diff-match-patch, openai, readdirp and zod, the six `release.12` found. No path in the asar or on disk has `anthropic` in it, and no file is named `claude` or `claude.exe`. Beside the asar, `resources` holds `GUIDELINES.default.md`, `icon.png` (`icon.ico` since `brand.5`, C.92), `app-update.yml` and electron-builder's `elevate.exe`; the rest of the folder is Electron's own, with its `LICENSE.electron.txt` and `LICENSES.chromium.html`. `opensource.5`'s verifier makes the same checks on every build.
- **Why it matters.** `DISCLAIMER` says the app "includes no Anthropic software", and the author accepts no Anthropic terms (Appendix D 8). Each user installs Claude Code with Anthropic's installer, and the app runs that copy (11.3 q).

### C.88 One-click per-user installer (`release.4`, 2026-10-20)

11.1's Installer row and 11.3 (n) give the settings; this records what electron-builder 26.17.0 makes of them, read from its NSIS templates and seen in the build. The installer itself was not run, and `apply.14` did not run it either: it installs into the Windows account it runs in and then starts the app on that account's own data folder (`runAfterFinish`), which on the author's machine is his real settings and reviews. `apply.14` checked the packaged app as `dist/win-unpacked/Lapidary.exe --isolated-user-data=<scratch>`, and the installer's first run is `release.13`'s, on a clean account (11.4 steps 8 to 14).

- **The settings.** `win.target` is the NSIS target for x64 alone. `nsis` is `oneClick: true`, `perMachine: false`, `runAfterFinish: true`, `createDesktopShortcut: true`, `shortcutName` from `APP_NAME`, `artifactName: '${productName}-Setup-${version}.${ext}'`, `differentialPackage: true` and `deleteAppDataOnUninstall: false`. `allowToChangeInstallationDirectory` went, since it applies only to the assisted installer, and so did `win.artifactName`, which named the old installer `Lapidary-<version>-x64.exe`.
- **What it does.** It shows no pages and asks for no administrator rights: it installs for the current Windows account, adds a Start menu entry and a desktop shortcut named `APP_NAME`, and starts the app when it is done. The updater (`release.8b`) is to re-run the same installer (`quitAndInstall(false, true)`, 11.3 n), which then shows only its progress window. A new install goes to `%LOCALAPPDATA%\Programs\manuscript-review`, named from package.json's `name`, since a one-click per-user installer does not try the product name (`getWindowsInstallationDirName` in `targetUtil.js`). When the registry key named from `APP_ID` already holds an install folder, as after the 0.1.0 assisted installer, which used the product name (`%LOCALAPPDATA%\Programs\Lapidary`, or `Stet`, unless the author chose another), the new installer uses that folder (`setInstallModePerUser` in `multiUser.nsh`). As it installs, it copies itself to `%LOCALAPPDATA%\manuscript-review-updater\installer.exe` (`installer.nsh`), the old copy an update's differential download compares against.
- **Where updates come from.** The publish block, `{provider: 'github', owner, repo, releaseType: 'draft'}` from `appRepository()`, becomes `resources/app-update.yml`: `owner: MichaelBradetLegris`, `repo: lapidary`, `provider: github`, `releaseType: draft`, `updaterCacheDirName: manuscript-review-updater`, with no `publisherName`, as the build is unsigned. `dist/latest.yml` names `Lapidary-Setup-0.1.0.exe` with its sha512 and size, which match the file. Every script passes `--publish never`, so the build uploads nothing; with no token variable set, its log said nothing about publishing.
- **`package:dir` has no `app-update.yml`.** electron-builder writes it after packing only when one of the targets is NSIS (`isSuitableWindowsTarget` in `PublishManager.js`), and `--dir` builds only the folder; a scratch `--dir` build had `GUIDELINES.default.md`, `app.asar` and `icon.png` (`icon.ico` since `brand.5`, C.92) in `resources` and nothing else. So the updater (`release.8b`) finds no feed in a `package:dir` build, and a packaged test of updates needs the `dist/win-unpacked` that `npm run package` leaves.
- **Uninstall.** It removes the app folder, the shortcuts and the registry entries, and leaves `%APPDATA%\ai-grammar-checker` (`deleteAppDataOnUninstall: false`) and the updater cache (11.0 cut a custom macro for it; the README is to say how to delete both, 11.3 p). The uninstaller's `--delete-app-data` switch removes `%APPDATA%\manuscript-review` and `%APPDATA%\Lapidary`, from the package and product names (`uninstaller.nsh`), never `ai-grammar-checker`, which is why 11.1 keeps the package name unlike `APP_DATA_DIR`.
- **Sizes** (for 11.5). With `en-US.pak` alone the installer was 113,858,921 bytes (108.6 MiB), against 122,743,575 bytes (117.1 MiB) for the assisted installer with every Electron locale that `release.2` built from nearly the same code earlier the same day; its `.blockmap` was about 118 KiB (120,590 and 120,610 bytes in two builds of the same code, whose installers were the same size), and `dist/win-unpacked` was 358,152,543 bytes (341.6 MiB) in 22 files. The review fix put `en-GB.pak` back (C.90): the installer is now 114,001,506 bytes (108.7 MiB), 142,585 bytes more, its `.blockmap` 120,699 bytes, and the app it installs, `dist/win-unpacked`, 358,732,573 bytes (342.1 MiB) in 23 files, of which `Lapidary.exe` is 234.7 MiB and the asar 21.9 MiB. After an install the disk holds about 450 MiB: the app, plus the installer's copy of itself in the updater cache.

### C.89 No portable build (`release.4`, 2026-10-20)

11.0 cut the portable exe: it re-extracted the whole app into `%TEMP%` at every start and could not update. `release.4` removed its target, its `portable` block and its file name.

- **The numbers now.** The 600 MB of 11.0 was the Stet build with Claude Code inside it. Without Claude Code, the portable exe `release.2` built was 122,514,239 bytes and unpacked the app with every locale, about 389 MiB, at each start. It still could not update: electron-builder writes `app-update.yml` only for an NSIS target, and electron-updater's Windows updater installs only through the NSIS installer.
- **What takes its place.** For a user, the one-click installer, which needs no administrator rights either (C.88). For trying a build without installing, `npm run package:dir` and `dist/win-unpacked/Lapidary.exe --isolated-user-data=<folder>`, the one switch a packaged build accepts (CLAUDE.md, reference docs). A portable exe kept its settings in the same `%APPDATA%\ai-grammar-checker` as the installed app, so nothing moves for anyone who used one.
- **Docs.** README step 5, CONTRIBUTING's `package` and `package:dir` lines and the bug report form, whose "How you run it" list loses "Portable exe", no longer offer it. CLAUDE.md's command list still says `package:dir` makes "no installer, no portable exe", which stays true; `release.10` edits that list.

### C.90 Two locale files, en-US and en-GB (`release.4`, 2026-10-20)

`electronLanguages: ['en-US', 'en-GB']` keeps two of Electron's 55 locale files: `en-US.pak` (586,582 bytes), the locale Chromium falls back on, and `en-GB.pak` (580,030 bytes); the other 53 are 49,476,997 bytes (47.2 MiB). Chromium takes the page's locale from the locale files it has, and the spelling check's language from that locale, so the choice changes more than its own messages. The task text, and `release.4` as first committed, kept `en-US.pak` alone (the other 54 being 50,057,027 bytes, 47.7 MiB). Its review found that this also gave writers on a British English Windows a US spelling check on a new install, which nothing here had said, and the fix put `en-GB.pak` back, for 142,585 bytes more in the installer (C.88).

- **How Chromium chooses.** It follows Windows's display language, here en-US (`Get-UICulture`), not the en-CA format (`Get-Culture`) or the first preferred language (the list is en-CA, en-US, fr-CA). Of the files it has, it takes the one for that language or the one Chromium maps it to: `en-GB.pak` serves en-AU, en-CA, en-IE, en-IN, en-NZ and en-ZA as well as en-GB, and with no match it falls back on en-US. `release.4` first wrote that this machine's language was en-CA and that Chromium chose en-US for want of an en-CA file; it chose en-US because the display language is en-US, and with every file `--lang=en-CA` gives en-GB.
- **Measured** with a probe of a few lines that opens an offscreen window that never shows, types "colour realise color realize" into a box with the spelling check on, right-clicks each word with `sendInputEvent` to read the misspelled word Chromium reports, writes what it finds to a file and quits. It ran in scratch copies of the development Electron 44.3.0 holding every file, `en-US.pak` alone, and `en-US.pak` and `en-GB.pak`, each run on a new userData folder, with `--lang` standing in for another display language. After the fix it also ran in a scratch copy of the new `dist/win-unpacked` with the asar replaced by the probe, and gave the last column's answers for no `--lang`, en-GB, en-AU, en-CA and fr-CA. `app.getLocale()`, `navigator.language`, `Intl`'s default and `session.getSpellCheckerLanguages()` agreed in every run:

  | Display language (`--lang`) | Every file (0.1.0) | `en-US.pak` alone | `en-US.pak` and `en-GB.pak` |
  | --- | --- | --- | --- |
  | none given (en-US here), en-US | en-US | en-US | en-US |
  | en-GB, en-AU, en-CA, en-IE, en-IN, en-NZ, en-ZA | en-GB | en-US | en-GB |
  | fr-CA | fr | en-US | en-US |
  | de-DE | de | en-US | en-US |

  en-US wrote 20 October 2026 at 15:30 as "10/20/2026, 3:30:00 PM" and 12345.5 as "12,345.5", and its spelling check flagged colour and realise; en-GB wrote "20/10/2026, 15:30:00" and "12,345.5" and flagged color alone (it takes realize); fr wrote "20/10/2026 15:30:00" and "12 345,5", de "20.10.2026, 15:30:00" and "12.345,5", and both flagged all four words. The first measurement, in `release.4`, also found an empty required field's message to be "Please fill out this field." in en-US, "Please fill in this field." in en-GB and "Veuillez renseigner ce champ." in fr, and `app.getSystemLocale()`, `app.getPreferredSystemLanguages()` and main's own `Intl` and `Intl.Collator` to give the system's en-CA in every run, even under `--lang=fr-CA`, so main's sorting, such as the chapter list's `localeCompare`, does not depend on the locale files.
- **The first run's spelling language is kept.** Chromium stores it in the userData folder's `Preferences` (`spellcheck.dictionaries`) on the first run, and later runs keep it whatever files they have: a folder first used with every file under en-GB kept `["en-GB"]` with `en-US.pak` alone, with or without `--lang`, and one first used with `en-US.pak` alone under en-GB kept `["en-US"]` with both files. Dates and the word count follow the files at every start. So an install of 0.1.0, which had every file, keeps the spelling language its first run chose, and only a new install takes the table's.
- **In the app's window.** A quiet `dev:clean` window run on the scratch Electron through `ELECTRON_EXEC_PATH` (electron-vite overwrites `ELECTRON_CLI_ARGS`, so it could not be given `--lang`), with "colour realise color realize" typed into the paragraph box: with both files, the box underlined colour and realise, this machine's display language being en-US; with `en-US.pak` alone and a userData folder whose `Preferences` came from the probe's en-GB first run with every file, it underlined color alone. The paragraph box (`ParagraphEditor`) and the suggestion editor (`EditPopover`) turn `spellCheck` on, and main never calls `setSpellCheckerLanguages`, so both check the language above.
- **What it changes in the app.** Three things in the page follow the locale: `historyWhen`, the date History, the side panel's list of reviews and the questions that name a review all show; the review dialog's word count; and the spelling check in those two boxes. Against 0.1.0, a Windows in US English, in British English or in an English mapped to it sees no change. A Windows in any other language gets US dates and word counts where it had its own, and on a new install a US English spelling check where it had its language's. With `en-US.pak` alone, as first committed, the British-mapped Englishes would also have had US dates and, on a new install, a spelling check that underlines "colour" and "realise", though the app's style sheet note asks the author for their spelling variant (`setup.10b`). A development run keeps every file and follows the system as 0.1.0 did. Chromium's own messages are in English, as the app's are. CHANGELOG has a Changed line, which names the spelling check.
- **Left as it is.** A date whose day is 12 or less reads two ways to someone used to the other order, and a writer on a Windows in another language, such as French, gets a US English spelling check on a new install, which suits a book in English and not one in that language. The ways out, none part of `release.4`: a date format that does not depend on the locale, or one built from `app.getSystemLocale()` handed to the page; `session.setSpellCheckerLanguages` in main, from `app.getPreferredSystemLanguages()` filtered by `session.availableSpellCheckerLanguages`, or a spelling language in Settings; or more locale files, 0.9 MB each on average, each of which also brings that language's dates and Chromium's messages in it. The author can choose before 1.0.

### C.91 What the notices and the package verifier settled where the plan left it open (`opensource.5`, 2026-10-20)

`opensource.5` gives the notices file its contents and the licence gate its list, and 11.3 (n) the verifier's checks. This records the rest.

- **What counts as shipped.** Three kinds, each named in the file's list: Electron, which every copy runs on, with the `LICENSE` of the `electron` package (Chromium's notices are in `LICENSES.chromium.html`, which comes with Electron's own files beside the exe, as does `LICENSE.electron.txt`, and the file says where to find it); the production tree electron-builder packs, that is package.json's `dependencies` and `optionalDependencies`, theirs in turn, and peer dependencies not marked optional, each found as Node finds it, an optional one that is not installed passed over and a required one that is not installed stopping the script; and what each build's `bundled-packages.json` lists. Electron's own dependencies only download it and are not followed. openai's peers are all optional, so `undici`, which a development tool installs, is not listed, and electron-builder does not pack it either. In this build that is 11 packages: electron 44.3.0; chokidar 5.0.0, diff 9.0.0, diff-match-patch 1.0.5, openai 7.15.0, readdirp 5.1.1 and zod 4.5.4 in the asar; react 19.2.8, react-dom 19.2.8, scheduler 0.27.0 and zustand 5.0.15 in the window's bundle, which also holds diff and diff-match-patch. The main and preload bundles hold no package, since `externalizeDepsPlugin` leaves every dependency to node_modules.
- **The bundle records.** The plugin names the package folder of every module in a build's chunks, the innermost `node_modules/<name>` or `node_modules/@scope/<name>` of the id with any query dropped, relative to the project. It counts a module whatever its rendered length, so a package whose code was all shaken out would still be listed, which errs on the side of listing. Each record is an asset of its build, written into the folder Vite empties before it builds, so a record never outlives its bundle; the script stops when any of the three is missing.
